zabid: Zabid was originally a village called al-Husayb, inhabited by the Asha'ir tribe, and it later took the name of the Wadi Zabid, the valley to its south. According to tradition, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, a companion of Muhammad, built the al-Asha'ir Mosque there as the fifth mosque in the history of Islam. The present town was created around 820 by Muhammad ibn Abdallah ibn Ziyad, whom the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun had sent to suppress a rebellion of the Asha'ir and Akk tribes. It was the capital of the Ziyadids until 1016, then of the Najahid dynasty and of the Mahdids until 1174.

Its mosques, among them the al-Asha'ir Mosque and the Great Mosque, became centres of Islamic learning, and its place on the road between Mecca and Aden brought prosperity. After the Ayyubids took Yemen in 1174, Zabid remained its economic and political centre. Under the Rasulids (1229–1454) the official capital moved to Taiz, but the rulers kept Zabid as a winter residence. The city then reached its height, with more palaces, gardens and religious institutions than any other in Yemen, and the 14th-century writer al-Khazraji claimed between 230 and 240 mosques. Ottoman authority arrived in 1539.

Zabid lies on Yemen's western coastal plain, in the Tihama region, with an urban population of around 52,590. Its historic quarter was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993, and the vestiges of its university can still be visited. In 2000 the site was placed on the List of World Heritage in Danger at the request of the Yemeni government because of poor upkeep: UNESCO reported that about 40% of the houses had been replaced by concrete buildings. The town grows indigo and cotton, and by the mid-20th century, in the account given in Muhammad Abdul-Wali's novel Sana'a: An Open City, it had become a backwater.
zabulistan: Zabulistan means the land of Zābol, a name of uncertain origin that the Afghan province of Zabul and the Iranian city of Zabol still carry; in Ferdowsi's Shahnameh it is the birthplace of Rostam. Its Sanskrit name was Jāguḍa, meaning saffron, and the Chinese monk Xuanzang, who described it in 644, wrote it as Tsau-kü-ta. He placed it between the Hindu Kush and the Black Range, probably the Sulaiman mountains, with its capital at Ghazni and sometimes at Guzar, both strongly fortified. He recorded a cold climate with much frost and snow, abundant winter wheat, fruit and flowers, turmeric and asafoetida, and springs at Guzar used for irrigation.

The first mentions of the region come with its conquest by the Iranian Huns in the 4th century. Coins of the Alkhan rulers, among them Khingila I, bear the legend King of Zabol Alkhan, and after the Sasanian defeat by the Hephthalites in 484 the Nezak Shahs opened a mint at Ghazni. The Turk Shahis took the region in the 7th century. Xuanzang found Mahayana Buddhism favoured by the king, with several hundred monasteries and more than ten thousand monks, while most people worshipped the god Śuna, whose shrine on a mountain drew pilgrims and rich offerings.

Arab armies from Zaranj reached the region, but the historian André Wink describes the Zunbils and their kinsmen the Kabul-Shahs as rulers of a predominantly Indian rather than Persianate realm who effectively opposed the Arabs. C. E. Bosworth calls the Zunbils probably heirs of a southern Hephthalite or Chionite kingdom of Zabul. Under Saffarid rule, Amr ibn Layth's governor Fardaghan sacked the shrine of the god Zhun at Sakawand, and in 896 idols sent from there caused a sensation in Baghdad. The Hindu Shahi king Jayapala later fought the Ghaznavids for the region and lost, and their victories brought the Islamization of Zabulistan and the surrounding regions.
zacharias-ursinus: Zacharias Ursinus was born Zacharias Baer on 18 July 1534 in Breslau, then in Silesia under the Habsburg monarchy and now Wrocław in Poland. His Latin name came from ursus, bear, after his German surname. At fifteen he entered the University of Wittenberg and boarded for seven years with Philipp Melanchthon, who admired his gifts and commended him to scholars across Europe. He was also a lifelong protégé of the imperial physician Johannes Crato von Krafftheim, another native of Wrocław.

He went on to study at Strasbourg, Basel, Lausanne and Geneva, learned Hebrew in Lyon and Orléans and studied under Jean Mercier in Paris. Back in Wrocław, a pamphlet he published on the sacraments led Lutherans to charge him with being more Reformed than Lutheran, and their opposition drove him to Zurich, where he became a friend of Heinrich Bullinger and Pietro Martire Vermigli.

On Vermigli's recommendation, Frederick III, Elector Palatine, made him a professor in the Collegium Sapientiae at Heidelberg in 1561. Commissioned by the elector, he supplied the preliminary drafts of the Heidelberg Catechism and took part in its final revision with other theologians and church leaders. Caspar Olevianus was once held to be a co-author, a view modern scholarship has largely discarded. After Frederick's death and the accession of a Lutheran elector in 1576 Ursinus was removed, and from 1578 he held a chair at a Reformed academy at Neustadt. He died there on 6 May 1583, aged 48.

His works were published in 1587 to 1589, and a fuller edition by his son and two pupils, David Pareus and Quirinius Reuter, appeared in 1612. His collected lectures on the catechism, known in Dutch as Het Schatboeck, became one of the most prominent theological handbooks among Reformed Christians of the seventeenth century, above all in the Netherlands. Reformed German and Dutch immigrants to North America honoured his memory, and Ursinus College in Collegeville, Pennsylvania, founded in 1869, bears his name.
zadar: Zadar is the oldest continuously inhabited city in Croatia. It lies in northern Dalmatia on the Adriatic Sea, facing the islands of Ugljan and Pašman across the narrow Zadar Strait. The old city stands on a promontory that was once separated from the mainland by a deep moat, since filled in, and the harbour to the north-east is safe and spacious. Zadar was a Liburnian settlement laid out in the 9th century BCE and called Iader. By the 7th century BCE it was an important centre of trade with the Phoenicians, Etruscans and Greeks, and it became the main seat of the Liburnian sea power.

It became a Roman municipium in 59 BCE and a colony in 48 BCE, with a regular street grid, a forum and a capitolium. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476 CE it became the capital of the Byzantine Theme of Dalmatia. It was briefly under Frankish rule at the start of the 9th century, and in 998 it sought the protection of Venice against Neretvian pirates and swore allegiance to Doge Pietro II Orseolo. Control passed repeatedly between Venice and the Kingdom of Hungary. In 1202 the Venetians, with the Crusaders, reconquered and plundered the city, and in 1358 the Treaty of Zadar gave it to Hungary.

On 31 July 1409 Ladislaus of Naples sold Zadar and his dynasty's rights to Dalmatia to Venice for 100,000 ducats. It became the de facto capital of Venetian Dalmatia and, once the Ottoman Empire had conquered the hinterland, a stronghold protecting Venetian trade. Between the 15th and 17th centuries it was an important Renaissance centre, producing the sculptor Giorgio da Sebenico and Giovanni Francesco Fortunio, who wrote the first Italian grammar, and Croatian writers such as Petar Zoranić and Šime Budinić.

After the Treaty of Campo Formio in 1797 it passed to Austria, and from 1815 to 1918 it was capital of the Kingdom of Dalmatia. In the 19th century it was a centre of the Illyrian movement, amid growing polarisation between Croats and Dalmatian Italians, who then formed a majority of its citizens. Italy took it after the First World War, and the Partisans captured it on 1 November 1944. In 1947 it became part of the Socialist Republic of Croatia. About 10,000 Italians left, and the last Italian schools closed in 1953.

Zadar is the seat of Zadar County and the northern Dalmatian region, and the fifth-largest city in Croatia. The University of Zadar traces its origin to a Dominican institution of 1396, which closed in 1807 and was re-established in 1956. The Roman forum, parts of the aqueduct and the medieval churches survive, and UNESCO included its fortifications in the Venetian Works of Defence in 2017.
zadok: The Hebrew Bible makes Zadok a patrilineal descendant of Eleazar, son of Aaron, and the genealogy of his descendant Ezra places him in the ninth generation of descent from Phinehas, son of Eleazar. A Zadok who joined David at Hebron, his house then including twenty-two captains, is identified by Josephus with the priest. Noting that he does not appear in Samuel before the conquest of Jerusalem, some have proposed that he was a Jebusite priest; Frank Moore Cross criticised this Jebusite Hypothesis while calling it the dominant view among contemporary scholars.

Zadok and Abiathar, son of Ahimelech, were named priests when David first set up his cabinet. During Absalom's revolt Zadok and the Levites wished to follow the fleeing king with the Ark of the Covenant, but David sent him back to Jerusalem, and his son Ahimaaz, with Jonathan son of Abiathar, carried the king a message that saved his life. After the rebellion David sent the two priests to urge the elders of Judah to bring him back. In 1 Chronicles 16:39 Zadok leads the priests before the tabernacle at the high place at Gibeon.

His sons were Ahimaaz and Azariah, the latter one of Solomon's princes. In rabbinic literature his appointment fulfils a prophecy against the house of Eli. The Zadokites held the high priesthood until the rise of the Hasmoneans in about 167 BCE, through much of the Second Temple period from Jehoshua ben Jehozadak to Simon II, Onias III and Jason. Ezekiel praises the sons of Zadok as opponents of paganism. Abraham Geiger thought the Sadducee sect of Judaism took its name from him, though rabbinic sources trace them to a later Zadok, a student of Antigonus of Sokho.
zagan: Żagań lies on the Bóbr river in western Poland, in the historic region of Lower Silesia, roughly halfway between Cottbus and Wrocław. The Bóbr and the Kwisa meet just outside the town. The name probably means place of the burnt forest, from the burning of primeval forest by early settlers, which fits the names of nearby places such as Żary, Zgorzelec and Pożarów. It is known in German and French as Sagan.

The area belonged to Poland after the creation of the state in the 10th century. Żagań was founded in the 12th century by Bolesław IV the Curly and first mentioned in a deed of 1202, when it belonged to the Duchy of Silesia. It received town rights between 1248 and 1260. After the death of Duke Konrad I of Głogów in 1274, his youngest son Przemko became Duke of Żagań in 1278 and founded a monastery of Augustinian Canons. The duchy was divided and reunited several times among Piast heirs, and from 1329 its dukes were vassals of John of Luxembourg, King of Bohemia.

Piast rule ended when Jan II the Mad sold the duchy to Duke Albert III of Saxony of the House of Wettin. In 1549 Elector Maurice of Saxony ceded it to Ferdinand I of Habsburg, and in 1627 Emperor Ferdinand II gave the fief to Albrecht von Wallenstein. It then passed to the Bohemian Lobkowicz family. After the First Silesian War of 1742 Żagań became part of Prussia. In 1786 Peter von Biron, Duke of Courland, bought the fief, and in 1845 his daughter Dorothea was invested as Duchess of Sagan.

Żagań has 23,136 inhabitants and is the capital of Żagań County in the Lubusz Voivodeship. Its main sights are the former Augustinian monastery, a burial site of the Piast dynasty, the Ducal Palace and Park ensemble, and the POW Camps Museum. The museum stands on the site of German prisoner-of-war camps that held over 60,000 Allied soldiers, among them Stalag Luft III, the scene of the Great Escape, an episode filmed in 1963.
zagreb: Zagreb lies in the north of Croatia, along the Sava River, on the southern slopes of the Medvednica mountain and near the border with Slovenia, at an elevation of about 158 metres. Most of its districts lie low in the Sava valley, while the northern and northeastern ones spread across the foothills of Medvednica. Its position, where Central Europe, the Mediterranean and Southeast Europe meet, has made it the centre of Croatia's road, rail and air networks.

The oldest known settlement near present-day Zagreb was the Roman town of Andautonia, now Šćitarjevo, which existed between the first and fifth centuries CE. The city's own history begins in 1094, when the Hungarian King Ladislaus, returning from a campaign against the Kingdom of Croatia, founded a diocese. Beside the bishop's see grew the canonical settlement of Kaptol, north of Zagreb Cathedral, and on the neighbouring hill the fortified settlement of Gradec. The name Zagreb is first recorded in a charter by Felician, Archbishop of Esztergom.

Both settlements were attacked by the Mongols in 1242. Béla IV, king of Croatia and Hungary, had been given a safe haven in Gradec, and in gratitude granted it the Golden Bull of 1242, which exempted its citizens from county rule and gave them autonomy and their own judicial system. The name is probably from a Proto-Slavic word meaning a hill or an embankment, perhaps the remains of first-millennium fortifications on Grič.

In the mid-19th century the Ban of Croatia, Josip Jelačić, united Gradec and Kaptol, and the main city square bears his name. The University of Zagreb was founded in 1669. While Croatia was part of Yugoslavia, from 1918 to 1991, Zagreb was an important economic centre and the second largest city. After Croatia declared independence in 1991 its Parliament proclaimed Zagreb the capital.

Zagreb is the capital and largest city of Croatia and the seat of its government, parliament and Constitutional Court, which stand on St. Mark's Square. It has the special status of a city and a county, separate from Zagreb County. The University of Zagreb is the oldest continuously operating university in Croatia.
zagros-mountains: The Zagros range is 1,600 km long and spans Iran, northern Iraq and south-eastern Turkey. It begins in north-western Iran, follows Iran's western border, and runs south-east to end at the Strait of Hormuz. Its highest point is Mount Dena, at 4,409 metres. The mountains were formed mainly by the collision of the Eurasian and Arabian plates, chiefly during the Miocene, and the collision continues. They are entirely of sedimentary origin, made mainly of limestone, and are divided into many parallel sub-ranges. Salt domes are common, and Iran's main oilfields lie in the western central foothills.

Humans have lived in the Zagros since the Lower Paleolithic. The earliest human fossils found there are Neanderthal, from Shanidar Cave, Bisitun Cave and Wezmeh Cave, with the remains of ten Neanderthals at Shanidar dating from about 65,000 to 35,000 years ago. Signs of early agriculture in the foothills go back as far as 9000 BCE, and some settlements later grew into cities such as Anshan and Susa. Wine storage from between 3500 and 5400 BCE has been found at Hajji Firuz Tepe and Godin Tepe, among the earliest evidence of wine production.

In ancient times the Zagros was the home of peoples such as the Hurrians, Guti, Kassites, Elamites, Turukku and Lullubi, who periodically invaded the Sumerian, Akkadian and Assyrian cities of Mesopotamia. The mountains form a geographic barrier between the Mesopotamian plain and the Iranian plateau. A small archive of clay tablets from Tell Shemshara on the Little Zab records the interactions of these groups in the early second millennium BCE. Ancient Mesopotamians placed the entrance to the underworld in the Zagros, with a staircase leading down to its gates.

The Zagros has long been home to pastoralists and farmers, among them Lurs, Bakhtiari, Kurds and Qashqai, who move their herds from the eastern slopes in summer to the western slopes in winter. Cities at the foothills include Sulaymaniyah, Kermanshah, Khorramabad and Shiraz. Oak woodland and pistachio and almond steppe remain, though overgrazing and deforestation have degraded them, and the ancestors of wheat, barley, lentil, almond, pistachio, pomegranate and grape grow wild there.
zagwe-dynasty: The Zagwe were an Agaw monarchy that ruled the northern parts of Ethiopia and Eritrea. The name is thought to derive from the Ge'ez phrase Ze-Agaw, meaning of the Agaw, in reference to Mara Takla Haymanot, the founder of the dynasty; it does not appear in contemporary sources. Accounts of the founding differ. According to one tradition Queen Gudit destroyed the remnants of the Kingdom of Aksum and ruled for 40 years. According to another, Mara, born in the province of Lasta, was a general of the last Aksum king, Dil Na'od, married his daughter Masoba Warq and overthrew him. James Bruce records a tradition that Mara was a cousin of Gudit who succeeded her.

The Zagwe period is still shrouded in mystery, and even the number of kings is disputed. The regnal lists give eleven names in some manuscripts, five in the list that Pedro Páez and Manuel de Almeida saw at Axum, and sixteen in at least one other. Carlo Conti Rossini thought the shorter reckoning more likely, arguing that a letter to the Patriarch of Alexandria John V shortly before 1150 came from Mara Takla Haymanot, who wanted an abuna who would endorse the new dynasty.

The dynasty is best known for King Gebre Meskel Lalibela, credited with ordering the rock-hewn monolithic churches of Lalibela. In land grants of 1204 and 1225 he called himself negus and also hasani, a title meaning tutor, nurse or counsellor. His knowledge of Jerusalem inspired him, in the late twelfth century, to give his capital that city's form, attributions and toponyms. The last Zagwe king was killed at the Battle of Ansata by Yekuno Amlak in 1270. The name preserved for him, Za-Ilmaknun, is a pseudonym that Taddesse Tamrat translates as the unknown, the hidden one, and Taddesse believes the last ruler was actually Yetbarak.

The areas under direct Zagwe rule apart from Lasta probably embraced the highlands of modern Eritrea, Tigray, Wag and Bete Amhara and westwards towards Lake Tana, according to David Buxton. Taddesse Tamrat argues that succession passed from brother to brother, following Agaw inheritance law. The kings bore three names: a baptismal name, a regnal name and a surname. Unlike Aksum, the Zagwe were virtually unknown to the Mediterranean powers; regular relations seem to have been kept only with Egypt and Jerusalem. A Muslim community lived in eastern Tigray, and cemeteries at Bilet and Arra attest it.
zahir-al-umar: Daher al-Umar was born in 1689 or 1690. His father, Umar, was sheikh of the Zayadina, a family of Bedouin origin that had settled around Tiberias in the late 17th century under Daher's grandfather, Salih; his mother came from the Sardiyya, a Bedouin tribe of the Hauran. The Galilee belonged to Sidon Eyalet, whose governors farmed out tax collection to local potentates. Around 1698 Umar became a multazim, or tax farmer, and by 1703 the French vice-consul of Sidon called him the paramount sheikh of the Galilee.

Around 1730, with the support of the Saqr Bedouins, Daher took over Tiberias and ousted its subgovernor. By about 1740 he held Safed and Nazareth, and his fortified towns withstood sieges by Sulayman Pasha al-Azm, governor of Damascus, in 1742–1743. He took Acre by force in 1744, was formally made its multazim in July 1746 and moved his headquarters there around 1750. Under an agreement with the French vice-consul Joseph Blanc, the French covered his taxes and supplied firearms in return for exclusive rights to his cotton and wheat.

In 1768 the imperial government recognised him as Sheikh of Acre and of all of Galilee. When Uthman Pasha al-Kurji of Damascus moved against him in 1770, Daher turned to Ali Bey al-Kabir of Egypt and the Shia clans of Jabal Amil. In 1771 their campaigns drove Uthman Pasha and his son from Damascus and Sidon, and Daher won at Lake Hula and occupied Jaffa and Sidon. On 6 July 1772, at his request, Russian ships under Count Orlov bombarded Beirut.

His last years were troubled by his sons, who fought one another for the succession. In March 1775 Abu al-Dhahab, who had toppled Ali Bey, invaded Palestine, executed the men of Jaffa and drove Daher from Acre, but he died soon after and Daher returned. In August an Ottoman flotilla under Hasan Pasha al-Jaza'iri came before Acre to collect his tax arrears, and Daher was killed. Ahmad Pasha al-Jazzar became governor of Sidon and suppressed the last of the Zayadina in 1776.

Daher's security, flexible taxation and invitation to Christian and Jewish immigrants brought growth to Acre, Haifa, Tiberias and Nazareth. Jazzar kept his cotton monopoly, but when the southern United States became Europe's supplier in the 19th century, the region suffered a sharp downturn. Daher is regarded as a national hero among Palestinians.
zaire: Zaire was the Congolese state in Central Africa that Mobutu Sese Seko headed from 1965 to 1997. In 1965 the division of power between president and parliament in Congo-Léopoldville, a former Belgian colony, led to a stalemate, as it had in 1960. Joseph-Désiré Mobutu again seized power, but this time he took the presidency himself, following five years of upheaval after independence known as the Congo Crisis. The country was officially the Democratic Republic of the Congo until 1971. On 27 October 1971 he announced its renaming as the Republic of Zaire.

The name derives from the Congo River, sometimes called Zaire in Portuguese, which in turn comes from the Kikongo nzere o zadi, the river that swallows rivers. Under the policy of authenticité Zairians were required to adopt African names, and Mobutu himself became Mobutu Sese Seko. Cities were renamed too, so that Léopoldville became Kinshasa and Stanleyville became Kisangani.

By 1967 Mobutu had given the country a new constitution, approved by 98 per cent of those voting in a referendum in June, which centralised executive power in the president. On 17 April 1967 he created the Popular Movement of the Revolution, the MPR, as the only party. In the presidential election of 1 November 1970 only the MPR could nominate a candidate, and Mobutu was confirmed with 10,131,000 votes against 157.

They were driven out with Western military help. By 1979 purchasing power was only 4 per cent of its level in 1960, and IMF loans from 1976 were largely embezzled. After the end of the Cold War Mobutu had to declare a new republic in 1990 and allow a multi-party system. In 1996 Hutu militias that had fled Rwanda, allied with the Zairian army, attacked Congolese Tutsis in the east, and the Tutsi militias rose in the First Congo War. Laurent-Désiré Kabila led the rebellion, Mobutu fled, and the name Democratic Republic of the Congo was restored in 1997. Mobutu died less than four months later in Morocco.

Zaire was a unitary presidential state in which the president appointed and dismissed ministers, provincial governors and judges. Its doctrine, Mobutism, was set out in the Manifesto of N'sele of May 1967, which named nationalism, revolution and authenticity as its themes and declared the regime neither right nor left. Authenticity also led Zairians to abandon Western dress for the abacost. The currency was the zaïre, divided into 100 makuta.
zakarids: The family's origins have been debated. Its inscriptions in Armenian, its claims to Armenian titles and the Armenian Christian faith of most of its early members point to an Armenian origin, and the family considered itself Armenian; Cyril Toumanoff held it to be an offshoot of the Pahlavuni family. A family legend linked the Georgian name Mkhargrdzeli, meaning long-armed, to the Achaemenid king Artaxerxes II, called the Longarmed. The dynastic name honoured Zakare. The first Zakarid who can be traced is Khosrov Zakarian, in the early 11th century.

The Zakarids rose as vassals of the Bagrationi kings of Georgia. They backed George III of Georgia against the rebellion of Prince Demna and the Orbeli family in 1177 and were raised up after it, and in 1186 Sargis Zakarian was granted Lori. His sons Zakare and Ivane took Dvin in 1193, won victories at Shamkor in 1195 and Basen in 1203, and raided northern Iran in 1210. In 1201 Tamar of Georgia gave them Ani as a principality. Zakare and his heirs ruled north-western Armenia from Ani, Ivane and his heirs eastern Armenia with Dvin. Ivane converted to Georgian Orthodox Christianity while Zakare remained in the Armenian Apostolic Church.

Ivane became the first Atabeg of Georgia in 1207 and Amirspasalar, commander-in-chief, in 1217, joining the two offices; his son Avag Zakarian inherited them in 1227. The family resisted the Khwarizmians of Jalal al-Din and the Mongols, but after the Mongols took Ani in 1236 they confirmed the Zakarids in their fiefs, and in 1243 gave Akhlat to Tamta, Ivane's daughter. The Mongols later gave the atabegate to others, and from 1306 it passed for good to Sargis II Jaqeli.

Zakare and Ivane left bilingual inscriptions across the Armenian and Georgian borderlands and built churches and forts, among them the Harichavank and Akhtala monasteries in northern Armenia. Their conquests also opened the way to the first large-scale migration of Kurdish tribes into the Caucasus. The later Zakarids held Ani until they lost it to the Kara Koyunlu Turkoman tribes, who made it their capital. In the 18th century a branch of the family entered the nobility of the Russian Empire as the Argutinsky-Dolgorukov.
zakat: The word zakat comes from the Arabic root z-k-w, meaning to purify. Muslims hold that it purifies income and wealth, as ablutions purify the body and prayer the soul. The Quran discusses charity in many verses, and zakat is found in the early Medinan suras and described as obligatory. Muslims believe that those who give it can expect reward from God in the afterlife. The practice is traditionally traced to Muhammad, and Schact suggested that the idea may have entered Islam from Judaism, from the Hebrew and Aramaic word zakut, though some Islamic scholars disagree.

The caliph Abu Bakr was the first to institute a statutory zakat system, on the principle that it must be paid to the legitimate representative of Muhammad's authority. Tribes that refused to pay while remaining nominally Muslim were considered apostates, which led to the Ridda wars. Uthman ibn Affan decreed that only apparent wealth was taxable, which limited zakat mostly to agricultural land and produce. After Ali ibn Abu Talib his supporters refused to pay it to Muawiyah I.

State administration in Medina was short-lived. During the reign of Umar bin Abdul Aziz (717–720 CE) it is reported that no one in Medina needed zakat, and after him it came to be seen more as an individual responsibility. Zakat was not collected from non-Muslims, who paid the jizya, and Muslims were also encouraged to give voluntary sadaqat.

Zakat on wealth is customarily 2.5 per cent, or one fortieth, of disposable income after essential needs. It is payable on assets held for a lunar year above the nisab, a minimum value, and on agricultural goods, precious metals, minerals and livestock the rate varies between 2.5 and 20 per cent. Scholars differ on the nisab and on which kinds of wealth are zakatable.

Verse 9:60 of the Quran is read as naming eight categories of recipient: the poor, the needy, the collectors, those whose hearts are to be won, those to be freed from slavery, debtors, those in the cause of God, and stranded travellers. The Shafi'i school requires equal division among the categories, while the Hanafi school permits giving to any or only one. Shia Muslims have traditionally given zakat to deputies of the imams rather than to the state.
zakopane: Zakopane lies in a valley between the Tatra Mountains and Gubałówka Hill, 800 to 1,100 metres above sea level, near Poland's border with Slovakia. It centres on the crossing of Krupówki and Kościuszko Streets and is connected by rail and road to Kraków. Its altitude makes it almost 3 °C colder than Kraków, and its position on the northern slope of the Tatras brings far more precipitation than the lowlands to the north. A warm foehn wind, known locally as halny, can sharply raise winter temperatures. The town is a centre of Goral culture and is often called the winter capital of Poland.

The earliest documents mentioning Zakopane date from the 17th century and describe a glade called Zakopisko. In 1676 it was a village of 43 inhabitants, and in 1818 it had 1,805 inhabitants. The first church was built in 1847. In the 19th century it became a centre of mining and metallurgy, the largest in Galicia, and by 1889 it had grown into a climatic health resort. Rail services began on 1 October 1899, and by the end of the 1800s the population was about 3,000.

The ski jump on Wielka Krokiew opened in 1925, the cable car to Kasprowy Wierch was finished in 1936 and the funicular to Gubałówka in 1938. By 1930 there were about 60,000 tourists a year. Germany invaded in September 1939, and the Germans set up a prison camp for Poles in the town. The Polish resistance attacked a German prison on 29 November 1939 and used Zakopane as an underground staging point between Poland and Hungary. In 1944 the Germans deported thousands of people from Warsaw to the town after the Warsaw Uprising, and the occupation ended in January 1945.

The Zakopane Style of architecture, inspired by the regional art of Podhale, was pioneered by Stanisław Witkiewicz, and its main examples include Villa Koliba of 1892–93, Villa Oksza of 1894–95 and the Chapel in Jaszczurówka of 1904–07. Many artists lived or worked in the town during the Young Poland period, among them the composer Karol Szymanowski, whose Villa Atma is now a museum. The Old Cemetery in Pęksowy Brzyzek holds the graves of many artists and mountaineers. Zakopane hosted the Nordic World Ski Championships in 1929, 1939 and 1962. It is part of Lesser Poland Voivodeship.
zakynthos: Zakynthos lies in the eastern Ionian Sea about 20 kilometres west of the Peloponnese, with Kefalonia 15 kilometres to the north. It is about 40 kilometres long and 20 wide, covers 405.55 square kilometres and has an arrowhead shape, with Cape Skinari at its north-western tip. The west is a mountainous plateau with steep cliffs, while the east is a fertile plain with long sandy beaches, overlooked by the hill of Bochali. Its highest point is Vrachionas, at 758 metres. The town of Zakynthos, also called Chora, is the capital.

Homer mentions the island in the Iliad and the Odyssey, and tradition names its first settler as Zakynthos, son of the Arcadian king Dardanos. During the First Peloponnesian War the Athenian commander Tolmides made an alliance with the island. It gave Athens a source of tar, dredged from a lake now called Lake Keri, which protected the planking of the Athenian triremes. In 430 BCE a Spartan force under the admiral Cnemus burned much of the countryside but failed to take the city. Rome finally conquered the island in 191 BCE under Marcus Fulvius Nobilior.

In 459 the Vandals under Geiseric plundered the island and carried off 500 aristocrats. After Margaritus of Brindisi captured it in 1185 it formed part of the County Palatine of Cephalonia and Zakynthos, and a Latin bishopric stood beside the Orthodox one. Venetian rule lasted until the fall of the Republic of Venice in 1797. The island then passed through French rule, the Septinsular Republic from 1800, French rule again in 1807 and British control from 1809, until the Union of the Ionian Islands with Greece in 1864.

Under Venice, Zakynthos had closer contact with western literary trends than other areas inhabited by Greek people, and in the late 18th century it produced the Heptanese School of poetry. Its best-known poet is Dionysios Solomos, whose statue stands in the main town square. During the Axis occupation in the Second World War, the mayor Loukas Karrer and Bishop Chrysostomos Dimitriou refused to hand over a list of the town's Jewish community and hid its members in rural villages. According to some sources all 275 Jews of the island survived, and both men were recognised as Righteous among the Nations.
zalavar: Zalavár is a village in Zala County in south-western Hungary, about 9 kilometres south-west of Lake Balaton. In the 9th century written sources call the settlement Mosapurc, in the phrase Mosapurc regia civitate. Later records and modern sources also give Moosburg, Urbs Paludarum, Braslavespurch and Blatengrad, and Slovak, Serbo-Croatian and Bulgarian writers use Blatnohrad or Blatnograd.

In the 9th century Mosapurc was a fortified settlement on the Zala river, the capital of the Lower Pannonian Principality, a Frankish vassal ruled by the Slavic prince Pribina. A Salzburg chronicle describes it as the stronghold of Pribina, a fortress in the woods and marsh of the Zala. His son Kocel ruled from 861 to 876. In the summer of 867 the town briefly hosted the brothers Cyril and Methodius on their way from Great Moravia to the pope in Rome, where they went to defend the use of Slavonic as a liturgical language.

The brothers and their disciples made Blatnograd one of the centres that spread the new Slavonic script, the Glagolitic alphabet, and its literature, and educated many future missionaries in their own language. Some writers claim that Mosapurc, called Brazlavo's burg in the sources, was the site of the Battle of Pressburg rather than Bratislava. The only contemporary source that places the battle is the Annales iuvavenses maximi, the Annals of Salzburg, which locate it near the castle of Duke Brazlavo (Braslav), west of Lake Balaton; but the annals survive only in fragments copied in the 12th century, so their reliability is questioned.
zalesye: Zalesye, also called Opolye, the area in the fields, covers the north and west of present-day Vladimir Oblast, the north-east of Moscow Oblast and the south of Yaroslavl Oblast. Its deep woods once separated the medieval Principality of Rostov from the Republic of Novgorod and from the principalities on the Dnieper. Merians, Muroma and other Volga Finnic tribes also lived in the area, and Slavs and Finnic peoples interacted closely there.

In the twelfth century this fertile land, protected by its forests from Turkic raids, drew Slavs migrating from the southern borders of Kievan Rus. Its population grew so fast that by 1124 Yuri Dolgoruki found it worthwhile to move his princely seat from Rostov to Suzdal, the oldest and most senior town of Zalesye. Yuri founded further towns, among them Pereslavl-Zalessky, Yuriev-Polsky and Starodub-on-the-Klyazma in 1152 and Dmitrov in 1154. The descriptors Zalessky and Polsky set these new towns apart from their namesakes in the south, in what is now Ukraine.

Yuri was constantly at odds with the boyars of Suzdal and thought of moving his capital to Pereslavl-Zalessky, but his unexpected death in 1157 prevented it. His son Andrew the Pious moved the princely seat to the young town of Vladimir that year. The old nobility of Rostov and Suzdal arranged Andrew's assassination in 1174, and a brief civil war for supremacy in Zalesye followed. As the kernel of Vladimir-Suzdal, the region played a vital part in the growth of Russian statehood.

From the time of the Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus', between 1223 and 1240, the woods were gradually cleared and new centres grew up in Moscow, Tver and elsewhere, so the strategic importance of Zalesye declined. Later towns developed around monasteries, such as Sergiev Posad and Kirzhach, or near royal residences, such as Alexandrov and Radonezh.
zaleucus: Almost nothing about the life of Zaleucus is certain. According to the Suda, he worked as a shepherd and was kept as a slave before he received an education and turned to making laws. Some ancient writers made him a Pythagorean philosopher, while older ones placed him before Pythagoras, and some denied that he had existed at all. The ancient sources also gave his laws a divine origin.

The Locrian code itself is lost and is known only from later mentions and imitations, which seem plainly anachronistic. These describe sumptuary rules: a free-born woman could not be accompanied by more than one female slave unless she was drunk, nor leave the city at night unless she was an adulteress, nor wear gold jewellery or a garment with a purple border unless she was a courtesan. Drinking undiluted wine was forbidden except as medicine.

Although the code favoured the aristocracy, Zaleucus was remembered for reconciling the factions of his city. One rule guarded the laws themselves: anyone proposing a new law or a change to an old one had to appear before the Citizen's Council with a rope round his neck, and was strangled at once if the council voted against him. Demosthenes, in his speech Against Timocrates, cited this Locrian custom to warn the Athenians against changing laws on small pretexts, claiming that only one new law had been made at Locri in more than two hundred years. Hierocles and Polybius attributed the rule to Zaleucus.

Legends told of Zaleucus keeping his own laws at great cost. He forbade anyone to enter the Senate House armed; when an emergency drove him to do so and he was reminded of the law, he fell on his own sword as a sacrifice to the claims of social order. A similar story was told of the lawgiver Charondas. Another legend held that he punished adultery with the loss of sight, and the tale of his own son's condemnation belongs to the same body of stories, whose value is uncertain.
zalmoxis: The earliest account is Book IV of the Histories of Herodotus, written before 425 BCE. In the story he heard from the Greeks of the Hellespont and the Black Sea, Zalmoxis, once freed, grew rich and returned home, built a banquet hall and told the chiefs that neither they nor their descendants would die but would live forever in happiness. He then hid for three years in an underground dwelling and reappeared in the fourth, so that the Thracians believed him. Herodotus himself thought Zalmoxis had lived long before Pythagoras and left open whether he was a man or a native god.

Some Getae, Herodotus adds, called the same being Gebeleizis, and in thunder they shot arrows at the sky and threatened the god, as they knew no other. The historian Dan Dana calls Herodotus the only pertinent ancient source, and it is certain only that the cult predates him.

Since the beginning of the 20th century scholars have debated a Zalmoxian religion. Vasile Pârvan and others held the Getae to be monotheistic; others point to Diodorus Siculus, who says they also worshipped Hestia. The arrows and the messenger have suggested a sky god, the underground chamber a chthonic one. Mircea Eliade, who wrote the first coherent reading of the myth, saw in the disappearance and return a rite of passage, and some read a mystery cult founded on the model of Pythagoras.

The name's spelling is uncertain. Most manuscripts of Herodotus give Salmoxis and later writers prefer Zamolxis, though most Thracologists take the -l-m- form to be the older. Porphyrius linked the name to zalmon, the Thracian word for hide, from the bearskin in which he was wrapped at birth.

Plato made Zalmoxis a physician who healed body and soul together, and Iamblichus said the Getae ranked him first among the gods for giving them laws. Mnaseas of Patrae and Hesychius identified him with Cronos, and Celsus counted his followers among deceivers of simple people. Strabo tells of Deceneus, a magician hired by King Burebista, at whose order the people destroyed all their wine, and many modern Romanian writers regard him as a priest who reformed the worship of Zalmoxis.
zaman-shah-durrani: Zaman Shah was an ethnic Pashtun of the Sadozai clan, the fifth son of Timur Shah Durrani and a grandson of Ahmad Shah Durrani. As a child he dreamed of conquering Hindustan like his grandfather, but his father did not allow him to join his campaigns in the Punjab. When Timur Shah died, many of Zaman's brothers opposed him, among them Mahmud Shah Durrani and Humayun, who had their own regional zones of influence. An election was held in Kabul, and by then the influence of the Barakzai tribal leaders and of Zaman had grown, so that he won the vote with the support of Chief Payandah Khan.

Zaman Shah took the throne in 1793 and imprisoned his opposing brothers at Kabul, starving them on two to three ounces of bread a day until they recognised him on the sixth day. He replaced his ministers with loyal Pashtuns and put to death chiefs who still opposed him. He then marched on Kandahar, where his brother Humayun came out to meet him and was defeated at Qalati Ghilji. Revolts followed in Kashmir and the Punjab, Sindh severed its ties with the empire, and the Uzbeks crossed the Oxus. Humayun seized Kandahar again with Talpur help; Zaman retook it and had him put to death. He spared the Talpur on condition that they paid tribute, and defeated Mahmud Shah at Gurak Village, later pardoning him.

Zaman Shah advanced to Lahore on campaigns into the Punjab and planned to invade India, but he was recalled each time, once by a Persian threat to Khorasan under Fath-Ali Shah Qajar. The historian Hari Gupta writes that his costly failed campaigns against the Sikhs led him to lose his crown as well as his eyes. In his later years Barakzai chiefs plotted to depose him and make the crown elective. His prime minister Wafadar Khan executed them, among them Payandah Khan. Payandah's son Fathi Khan joined Mahmud Shah, who took Kandahar after a siege of 43 days.

Zaman Shah raised about 30,000 men, but one of his commanders, Ahmad Khan, deserted to Mahmud Shah near Zabul. Mahmud Shah captured Kabul and Zaman Shah was taken prisoner and blinded on his orders. Zaman Shah escaped and took refuge at Rawalpindi, where Ranjit Singh gave him a house and later a monthly allowance of 1,500 rupees at Lahore. He then moved to Ludhiana, where he lived for the rest of his life and died on 13 September 1845. He is buried at the Ahmad al-Fārūqī al-Sirhindī Mazar in Sirhind, Punjab.
zambezi: The river is 2,574 km long and drains a basin of 1,390,000 km2, slightly less than half the size of the Nile's. It rises in a marshy dambo in miombo woodland in North-Western Province, Zambia, and flows south-west into Angola for about 240 km before turning south. It then runs along the north-eastern border of Namibia and the northern border of Botswana, follows the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe, and crosses Mozambique to the Indian Ocean.

The upper river falls about 400 m between its source and the Chavuma Falls, then only another 180 m across some 800 km to Victoria Falls, which mark the boundary with the middle river. Below the falls the river runs for about 200 km through the Batoka Gorge, between basalt walls 20 to 60 m apart. The lower river, 650 km from Cahora Bassa to the sea, is navigable but shallow in the dry season.

Vasco da Gama anchored in January 1498 at what he called the Rio dos Bons Sinais, now the Quelimane, which was then linked to the Zambezi by navigable channels. By the 16th century the river was called the Cuama, after a Swahili coast outpost in its delta. Medieval geographers knew the region as the Empire of Monomotapa, and early maps probably drew on Arab information. The Portuguese degredado António Fernandes visited the inland river in 1511 and 1513 to report on trade; his findings showed the importance of the upper Zambezi ports to the East African gold trade.

The rapids prevented the river from becoming a long-distance route. David Livingstone's Zambezi expedition tried to open it to paddle steamers but was defeated by the Cahora Bassa rapids. A paddle-barge service later ran between the Katombora Rapids and the rapids above Katima Mulilo, with Lozi paddlers and teams of oxen hauling barges round the Ngonye Falls.

Lake Kariba, created in 1959 behind the Kariba Dam, is one of the largest man-made lakes in the world, and the Cahora Bassa Dam in Mozambique was completed in 1973. Together the dams control the seasonal floods, and the delta is now about half as broad as before. Filling Cahora Bassa in a single flood season cut mangrove cover by 40 per cent and the prawn catch by 60 per cent.
zambia: Zambia covers 752,614 square kilometres and consists mostly of high plateaus with some hills and mountains, dissected by river valleys. About three-quarters of the country drains to the Zambezi and Kafue basin and about a quarter to the Congo basin. The Zambezi flows through the west and forms the southern border with Namibia, Botswana and Zimbabwe, and two of its largest tributaries, the Kafue and the Luangwa, flow mainly in Zambia. In the east the plateau rises from about 900 metres in the south to 1,800 metres in the north near Mbala. The highest point is Mafinga Central, at 2,339 metres, in the Mafinga Hills.

The fossil skull of Broken Hill Man, also called Kabwe Man, dated between 300,000 and 125,000 years ago, shows that early humans lived in the area. Zambia was inhabited by the Khoisan and Batwa peoples until around 300 CE, when migrating Bantu began to settle. Rock art such as the Mwela Rock Paintings, the Mumbwa Caves and Nachikufu Cave is attributed to these early hunter-gatherers.

The Bantu originally lived around present-day Cameroon and Nigeria and about 5,000 years ago began a millennia-long expansion across much of the continent, one of the largest human migrations in history, and are believed to have been the first to bring iron working into large parts of Africa. The first Bantu communities in Zambia lived in villages without an organised unit under a chief, moved as slash-and-burn farming exhausted the soil, kept cattle, and were highly self-sufficient.

After European expeditions in the eighteenth century, the British Empire began to consolidate control following the 1890 British Ultimatum against the Portuguese. Britain formed the protectorates of Barotziland–North-Western Rhodesia and North-Eastern Rhodesia, merged in 1911 as Northern Rhodesia. For most of the colonial period an administration appointed from London governed the territory with the advice of the British South Africa Company. Industrial copper mining began on the Copperbelt in the late 1920s and triggered rapid urbanisation. Zambia became independent on 24 October 1964 with Kenneth Kaunda as the first president, and from 1972 to 1991 it was a one-party state.

Lusaka is the capital, in the south-central part of the country, and the population is concentrated around it and in the Copperbelt Province. The name Zambia derives from the Zambezi river, and the territory was called Northern Rhodesia from 1911 to 1964. The country nominally includes about 73 ethnic groups, most of them Bantu-speaking, of which the Bemba, Nyanja and Tonga are the largest. The Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa has its headquarters in Lusaka.
zamboanga-city: The southwest and eastern sides of the city are bounded by irregular, generally rocky coastlines with occasional sandy or gravelly beaches, and the coast usually descends abruptly towards the sea. The terrain ranges from rolling to very steep, with a highest elevation of 1,200 metres. The city has mangrove areas at Tagasilay and eastern Vitali Island, and the Pasonanca Watershed Forest Reserve. The name is the Hispanicized spelling of the Sinama samboangan, meaning mooring place, from samboang, a mooring pole.

The Zamboanga Peninsula was settled in the late 12th or early 13th century by the Subanen people, and it was also the homeland of the ancestors of the Yakan, the Balanguingui and other closely related Sama-Bajau peoples. Spanish explorers led by Ferdinand Magellan reached the Philippine archipelago in 1521, and in 1569 Zamboanga was chosen as the site of a Spanish settlement and garrison at La Caldera, now part of Barangay Recodo. Spain gave the former local polity protectorate status against the Sulu Sultanate, its former overlord. The city became one of the main Spanish strongholds in Mindanao, supporting colonial efforts in the south, paving the way for Christian settlements and serving as an outpost against foreign invaders and Moro pirates.

The Republic of Zamboanga was proclaimed on 28 May 1899, after Zamboangueño revolutionary forces defeated the last Spanish government there. Fort Pilar was turned over to General Vicente Álvarez, who was its first president until November 1899. The republic lasted until 1903, with Isidoro Midel as second president under a puppet government of the United States, followed by Mariano Arquiza. After its dissolution Zamboanga became the capital of the Moro Province, a semi-military government of five districts, and General John J. Pershing was its military governor from 1909 to 1914.

Zamboanga became a chartered city on 12 October 1936 under Commonwealth Act No. 39, with a territory that included the whole island of Basilan. Japanese forces landed there on 2 March 1942, and the city became a branch hub of Unit 731, where Japanese doctors carried out human experimentation on Filipinos. Basilan was made a separate city on 16 July 1948.

The 2024 census counted 1,018,894 people. Roman Catholicism is the predominant religion, with 56.93% of the population, followed by Islam and Evangelical Protestantism. The lingua franca is Chavacano, whose lexifier is Spanish and whose grammar is influenced by Subanon and other Austronesian languages of the Philippines; Tausug is the second most spoken language. Sardine canning is concentrated on the west coast, and the traditional sailboat, the vinta, is known around Zamboanga for its colourful sails.
zamboanga-del-norte: Zamboanga del Norte lies in the Zamboanga Peninsula region of Mindanao and covers 7,301 square kilometres in the northern part of the peninsula. It borders Zamboanga del Sur and Zamboanga Sibugay to the south, Misamis Occidental to the northeast and the Sulu Sea to the north and west. Its irregular coastline runs some 400 kilometres from north to south. The average elevation is 243.8 metres, the highest peak being Mount Dabiak in Katipunan at 2,600 metres, and the land near the coast is plain. Rainfall is evenly distributed through the year, giving a mild climate.

The name Zamboanga is the Hispanicized form of the Sinama term samboangan, "mooring place", from samboang, "mooring pole"; it is attested in historical records from the 17th century. Islam was the predominant religion until the Spanish spread Christianity through the Jesuits, Augustinians and Dominicans. The Jesuit missionary Francesco Palliola of Nola was active in Dapitan and died at Ponot, now the town of Jose Dalman.

Before its creation as a province, the area formed the northern portion of the historical province of Zamboanga. Republic Act No. 711, issued on 6 June 1952, divided Zamboanga into two provinces, one of them Zamboanga del Sur. During the martial law that began in September 1972, the human rights lawyers Jacobo Amatong and Zorro Aguilar were shot dead by two soldiers who were never caught, and the acupuncturist Leo Alto, who helped Subanon communities defend their ancestral lands, was killed by the Philippine Constabulary at Polanco on 1 August 1975.

The capital and largest city is Dipolog. The province has 25 municipalities and 2 cities, and the 2020 census counted 1,047,455 people. Cebuano is the main language, with Chavacano, Subanon, Tausug, Samal, Filipino and English also spoken, and about half the people are Roman Catholic. Dapitan is the town where the national hero José Rizal was exiled by the Spanish colonial authorities. About half the land is farmed, mainly for corn, coconut and rice, and yellow fin tuna is the main catch of the commercial fishery.
zamfara-state: Zamfara State lies in the North-West geopolitical zone of Nigeria. It is bordered by Sokoto to the north-west and west, Kebbi to the south-west, Niger and Kaduna to the south and Katsina to the east, and a short stretch of its northern border forms part of the international border with the Niger. It takes its name from the Zamfara River, which flows through it, and from the historic Kingdom of Zamfara. The state lies almost entirely within the West Sudanian savanna and contains the Ka, Rima, Sokoto and Zamfara rivers. Its population is mainly Hausa and Fulani, and the great majority are Muslim.

The Kingdom of Zamfara was one of the old Hausa kingdoms, like Kano, Katsina, Gobir, Kebbi and Zazzau. It was established in the 11th century and flourished as a city-state until the 16th century, and its capital moved between places such as Dutsi and Birnin Zamfara. In the 16th century it became a tributary of the Kebbi Kingdom under Kanta Kotal, and it regained its independence by a revolt around 1715. Gobir destroyed Birnin Zamfara in the first half of the 18th century, and the court eventually moved to Anka. Zamfara was incorporated into the Sokoto Caliphate in the Fulani jihad of 1804 led by Usman dan Fodio.

After the British conquered the Caliphate in 1903 the area became part of the Northern Nigeria Protectorate, and Nigeria became independent in 1960. It formed part of the Northern Region until 1967, then of the North-Western State, and from 1976 of Sokoto State. On 1 October 1996 the military government of Sani Abacha separated the eastern local government areas as Zamfara State, with an area of 38,418 square kilometres. Its first governor was Jibril Yakubu.

Gusau is the state capital and largest city. It grew under British rule into a commercial and administrative centre on the road and rail network. The state has fourteen local government areas, and more than 80 per cent of its people are engaged in agriculture, growing millet, guinea corn, maize, rice, groundnuts and cotton and herding livestock. Its slogan is Farming is Our Pride. Zamfara was the first Nigerian state to adopt Sharia criminal law.
zamindar: The word zamindar is Persian for landowner, and it came into use under the Mughal Empire, when Persian was the official language. When Babur conquered North India there were many autonomous and semi-autonomous rulers known locally as Rai, Raja, Rana, Rao or Rawat, whom the Persian chronicles called zamindars. They were mostly hereditary vassals. Babur recorded that of the 52 crores of revenue from his lands in 1528, eight or nine crores came from the parganas of the rais and rajas who had submitted to the Sultans of Delhi.

The word covered very different people. According to Arif Qandhari, a historian of Akbar's reign, two to three hundred rajas, rais and zamindars ruled from strong forts under the emperor's suzerainty, each with an army of clansmen, and Abul Fazl puts their combined troops at forty-four lakhs, including 384,558 cavalry and 1,863 elephants. The historian Irfan Habib divided zamindars into autonomous chiefs with sovereign power in their territories and ordinary zamindars, mostly appointed by the Mughals, who held superior rights in land and collected revenue from the peasants.

S. Nurul Hasan distinguished three groups: autonomous chiefs, intermediary zamindars and primary zamindars. Under the Mughals the emperor was regarded as the supreme owner of the land, and zamindars had only the right to collect revenue. The system was more common in the north, where Mughal influence was stronger.

The East India Company began as a zamindar of three villages, Calcutta, Sultani and Govindpur, and obtained control of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa in 1765. Under Lord Cornwallis the Permanent Settlement of 1793 made zamindars proprietors in return for a fixed annual rent, creating the zamindari system as it later became known. An estate whose rent was not paid by sunset could be partly auctioned, which produced a new class of zamindars. After 1857 most zamindars lost their armies. The British gave loyal zamindars titles such as Raja, Maharaja and Nawab, and in the south mostly used the ryotwari method, taxing cultivators directly.

The system was ended by land reforms in East Pakistan, India and West Pakistan during the 1950s. In India this followed the First Amendment of the Constitution, and in East Pakistan the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act of 1950. Zamindars were patrons of the arts, and the Tagore family, whose estate Rabindranath Tagore often used as a base, produced India's first Nobel laureate in literature, in 1913.
zamorin: The title first appears in the writings of Ibn Battuta in 1342. It was once thought to come from the Sanskrit samudra, sea, but the historian K. V. Krishna Iyer derived it from svami and sri and gave the full title as Svami Tiri Tirumulapad, august emperor. The Zamorins belonged to the Eradi subcaste of the Samantan section of the Nair aristocracy and were at first the hereditary chiefs of Eranad within the Kodungallur Chera kingdom; the Cochin Jewish copper plate of about 1000 is the earliest reference to that chiefdom. Succession passed to the king's sister's son, and every ruler took the name Manavikrama.

According to the Keralolpathi, the Eradi besieged the Polarthiri of Polanadu for 48 years, then won over his followers and even his consort, and moved his seat from Nediyiruppu to Kozhikode, where he built the fort of Koyil Kotta.

Deva Raya II of Vijayanagara defeated the rulers of Venadu and Calicut in 1443, but as Vijayanagara weakened the Zamorins rose again and built a fort at Ponnani in 1498. Zheng He brought an imperial mandate to the king of Calicut from the Yongle Emperor in 1407. In 1602 a Zamorin offered the Dutch a fort at Calicut, but the two factors sent were captured by the chief of Tanur, handed to the Portuguese and hanged at Goa. Mysore forces first entered Kerala in 1732, and in 1756 the Zamorin promised Hyder Ali 12 lakh rupees, which he could not pay. The original ruling family ended with the 114th Zamorin; the 115th was the eldest of the princes adopted from Nileshwaram in 1706.

At their height, according to M. G. Raghava Varier, the Zamorins ruled from Kollam to Panthalayini Kollam, with local chiefs acknowledging their overlordship and supplying warriors in war. Most revenue came from taxing the spice trade through Calicut and smaller ports such as Ponnani and Tanur, while trade itself was left to Middle Eastern and Kerala Muslims. The Shahbandar Koya, a Muslim merchant and port commissioner, supervised customs and fixed prices. The army was mainly feudal levies of Nair foot soldiers, and in the 16th century the Kunjali Marakkars led the fleet of light Mappila vessels that harried Portuguese shipping.
zanabazar: Zanabazar was born Eshidorji in 1635 in present-day Yesönzüil, Övörkhangai, the second son of Gombodorj and his wife Khandojamtso. His father traced his line to Genghis Khan and was a grandson of Abtai Sain Khan, who had opened Khalkha lands to Gelugpa Buddhism. In 1639 an assembly of Khalkha nobles at Shireet Tsagaan nuur recognised the four-year-old as Öndör Gegeen, high saint and supreme religious leader of the Khalkha, a choice that gave the nobility added religious legitimacy.

In 1649 he went to Tibet to study under the 5th Dalai Lama and the 4th Panchen Lama at Drepung Monastery. The Dalai Lama identified him as the reincarnation of the scholar Taranatha and gave him the Sanskrit name Jñānavajra, from which Zanabazar comes.

After journeys to Tibet in 1651 and 1656 he founded Gelug-influenced monasteries, temples and shrines across Mongol territory, among them the Saridgiin Monastery in the Khentii mountains, completed in 1680. His travelling residence, the Örgöö, later known as Urga, eventually became the capital Ulaanbaatar. He revived metal image making in Mongolia, and his workshop at Tövkhön Monastery produced works such as the White Tara of 1685 and the Five Dhyani Buddhas.

When the Dzungar leader Galdan Boshugtu Khan invaded Khalkha in 1688, Zanabazar fled south with nearly 20,000 refugees to seek the protection of the Kangxi Emperor, and Dzungar forces pillaged Erdene Zuu. After the submission at Dolon Nor he stayed in China until 1701, wintering in Beijing and spending summers with the emperor at Jehol as his spiritual mentor.

He returned to Khalkha in 1701 to restore Erdene Zuu, then journeyed to Beijing after the Kangxi Emperor's death and died there on 18 February 1723; some believe he was poisoned. The Yongzheng Emperor ordered Amarbayasgalant Monastery built in his honour, where his body was laid to rest in 1779. Communists ransacked it in 1937, and his remains were allegedly burned. Socialist authorities portrayed him as a traitor for the submission to the Qing, a view since revised, and the Fine Arts Zanabazar Museum in Ulaanbaatar holds the largest collection of his works.
zande-people: The Azande, also called Zande, speak the Zande languages, whose classification is uncertain. They live in south-eastern Central African Republic, north-eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and south-central and south-western South Sudan. The name Azande means the people who possess much land and refers to their history as conquering warriors.

The Azande were formed by military conquest during the first half of the 18th century, under two dynasties of different origin and political strategy. The Vungara clan created most of the political, linguistic and cultural parts, while a non-Zande dynasty, the Bandia, expanded into the north and adopted some Zande customs. In the early 19th century the Bandia ruled over the Vungara, and the two groups became the Azande.

When a king died, his sons fought for the succession, and the losing son often founded a kingdom in a neighbouring region, which carried the Azande kingdoms eastward and northward. Sudanese raids halted part of the northward expansion later in the 19th century, and European colonialism divided Zande territory among Belgium, France and Anglo-Egyptian Sudan.

In 1938 the Governor of Sudan ordered a survey of the region, and the British chose the Azande area for the Zande Scheme, an agricultural programme built around cotton, palm oil and cattle. They resettled 60,000 Azande into new villages of 50 families called gbarias. The scheme largely failed, partly because of poor roads and distance from ports, and the British abandoned it. In 2015 conflict between Azande and Dinka in Yambio, in Western Equatoria, led to orders to open fire on insubordinate soldiers, and Amnesty International documented war crimes against the Azande in 2021.

Azande society was organised in chiefdoms, also called kingdoms, in which the Avongara formed the hereditary nobility and chiefs were military, economic and political leaders. Most Azande are small-scale farmers who grow maize, rice, groundnuts, sesame, cassava and sweet potatoes. Zande metalworkers are known for the throwing knife called the shongo, and the Azande also make sculpture in wood and clay and thumb pianos called sansa.

Traditional belief includes Mbori, an omnipotent god, together with magic, oracles and witchcraft. Mangu, or bad magic, is believed to be an inherited substance in the belly. The poison oracle, benge, consulted only by men, is the most powerful of three oracles, and its decisions were always accepted. The anthropologist E. E. Evans-Pritchard studied these beliefs. About 85 percent of Azande consider themselves Christian, and more than half are Catholic.
zanj: Zanj was a term used by medieval Muslim geographers for part of south-eastern Africa, chiefly the Swahili coast, and for its Bantu-speaking inhabitants. Arab sources also used it more widely for sub-Saharan peoples. The word comes from Middle Persian zang, meaning black one, though Anthony Christie argued that it may be of South-East Asian origin, noting a Chinese form recorded as early as 607 CE. Arab and Chinese sources placed Zanj south of Misr (Egypt), Al-Habasha (Abyssinia) and Barbara (Somalia). Its core ran from south of present-day Ras Kamboni to Pemba Island in Tanzania. The 10th-century geographer al-Mas'ūdī described Sofala as the limit of Zanj settlement.

The Zanj traded with Persians, Arabs and Indians, and by the late medieval period their coast held at least 37 substantial Swahili trading towns, among them Kilwa, Malindi, Gedi and Mombasa. The coast sent ivory, gold and slaves to the Indian Ocean world. Zanj were shipped as slaves around the Indian Ocean, and the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphs recruited many as soldiers. Slave revolts of the Zanj in Iraq are recorded as early as 696. The Zanj Rebellion near Basra ran from 869 to 883. Many Zanj in Iraq had earned their freedom and stayed, and the term there is thought to mean Africans in general, because the Swahili coast then had no large slave trade.

Ibn Battuta visited Kilwa around 1331 and praised the generosity, humility and religion of its ruler, Sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman. He also reported that the sultan raided the mainland, taking slaves and booty, and that he described the enslaved Zanj as jet-black with scarification on their faces. Kilwa traded in gold and ivory, and in this period the Palace of Husuni Kubwa was built and the Great Mosque of Kilwa extended.

The name survives in Zanzibar, meaning coast of the Zanji, and the sea off south-eastern Africa was called the Sea of Zanj. During the anti-apartheid struggle it was proposed that South Africa take the name Azania, to recall ancient Zanj. The Lemba people still use Zenj for neighbouring peoples. A 2023 study of ancient DNA from 80 people in six coastal towns from 1250 to 1800 found that peoples of African and Asian, mostly Persian, origin had begun to mix by about 1000. More than half the DNA of many individuals came from African women, and 80 to 90 per cent of the Asian DNA came from Persian men.
zanj-rebellion: Africans were brought to the Abbasid Caliphate through the Indian Ocean slave trade, mainly to work the plantations of the Sawad, southern Iraq. Wealthy residents of Basra had acquired abandoned marshlands that could be made arable by intensive labour. Their enslaved workers were put in camps to clear away the nitrous topsoil, and others worked the salt flats near Basra. Conditions of work and life were considered extremely miserable, and two earlier revolts, in 689-90 and 694, failed quickly. From 861 the caliphate was weakened by the Anarchy at Samarra, in which six caliphs followed one another, troops mutinied and the government became virtually bankrupt, so that it could not commit enough troops to subdue the rebels.

The leader was Ali ibn Muhammad, whose ancestry accounts report differently. After a failed rising in Bahrayn in 863 and a flight from Basra in 868, he returned in 869 and began to seek out black slaves in the Basra marshes and ask about their working conditions. He promised them wealth and was called Sahib al-Zanj, Chief of the Zanj. His movement also drew freed slaves, craftsmen, some peasants and Bedouin. He used Kharijite slogans on his banner and coins while still claiming to be a Zaydi. The revolt began in September 869.

The Zanj fought by guerrilla warfare, raiding towns and camps, often at night. They built fortresses and a navy, collected taxes and minted coins. They sacked al-Ubulla in 870 and Suq al-Ahwaz in 871, and Basra fell in September 871 after a long blockade, when the city was burned and its inhabitants massacred. A campaign by the regent al-Muwaffaq in 872 failed. By 879 the rebels had sacked Wasit and Ramhurmuz and come within fifty miles of Baghdad. In late 879 al-Muwaffaq sent his son Abu al-'Abbas against them, and the rebels were driven back to their capital, al-Mukhtarah, which was besieged from February 881. Al-Muwaffaq offered generous terms to those who submitted, and many abandoned the struggle. Al-Mukhtarah fell in August 883.

Ali ibn Muhammad's head was impaled on a lance and carried by boat along the canals, and on 30 November 883 it was displayed again in a victory parade at Baghdad. The number of dead is hard to estimate. Al-Masudi gave a moderate estimate of 500,000, adding that exact counting was impossible, and al-Suli gave 1,500,000; modern historians consider such figures gross exaggerations. The revolt disrupted economic activity and caused extensive damage. Medieval historians such as al-Tabari and al-Masudi counted it among the most vicious uprisings the Abbasid government faced, and modern scholars have called it one of the bloodiest and most destructive rebellions in the history of Western Asia.
zanu-pf: The movement began with the City Youth League formed in Salisbury in August 1955, which merged in 1957 with the Southern Rhodesia chapter of the African National Congress, with Joshua Nkomo as president. The government banned it in February 1959, the National Democratic Party in December 1961 and the Zimbabwe African People's Union in September 1962. In April 1963 critics of Nkomo, who disliked his foreign travel and his handling of a government in exile in Tanganyika, met at Dar es Salaam, and a majority of the executive voted to remove him.

On 8 August 1963 Ndabaningi Sithole, Herbert Chitepo, Leopold Takawira, Edgar Tekere, Henry Hamadziripi and Mukudzei Midzi met at the Highfield home of Enos Nkala to form the Zimbabwe African National Union. Violent clashes followed between its supporters and Nkomo's in the towns. ZAPU found disproportionate support among the Ndebele and ZANU among the Shona. At its first congress in May 1964 ZANU elected Sithole president and Robert Mugabe secretary-general.

The Patriotic Front was an alliance of ZAPU, backed by the Soviet Union, and ZANU, backed by China, against the white minority government of Prime Minister Ian Smith. After the Lancaster House Agreement of December 1979 the two parties competed separately in the 1980 election, which Mugabe and ZANU–PF won. ZAPU was absorbed in December 1987 by the Unity Accord, after the conflict known as Gukurahundi.

In the 2008 parliamentary election the party lost its majority for the first time. Morgan Tsvangirai of the Movement for Democratic Change led the first round of the presidential vote but withdrew from the run-off, citing violence and intimidation, and Mugabe was re-elected unopposed. A government of national unity followed. A struggle over the succession between Emmerson Mnangagwa's faction and Grace Mugabe's faction ended in the military coup of 15 November 2017. Mugabe resigned on 21 November and Mnangagwa was sworn in as president on 24 November. Mugabe died on 6 September 2019.

The party constitution sets out a hierarchy running from the National People's Congress, the National People's Conference and the Central Committee down to provincial, district, branch and village committees. The party also has a Women's League and a Youth League, and a War Veterans' League was added in 2022. It belongs to the Former Liberation Movements of Southern Africa, an association of parties involved in the region's anti-colonial movements.
zanzibar-revolution: Zanzibar became a British protectorate in 1890 and was fully independent in 1963. Arab rule there dated from 1698. By 1964 it was a constitutional monarchy under Sultan Jamshid bin Abdullah, with about 230,000 Africans, some of whom claimed Persian ancestry and were called Shirazis, and minorities of 50,000 Arabs and 20,000 South Asians. The Arabs were the major landowners, generally wealthier and with better health and education than Africans. As the British withdrew, the parties formed along ethnic lines, the Zanzibar Nationalist Party being mainly Arab and the Afro-Shirazi Party (ASP) African. In the July 1963 election the Arab minority kept power despite its share of the vote.

Around 3:00 am on 12 January 1964, 600 to 800 poorly armed, mainly African insurgents, helped by recently dismissed policemen, attacked police stations on Unguja to seize weapons, and then the radio station. They carried spears, knives, machetes and tire irons but had numbers and surprise. John Okello led the attack on the Ziwani police headquarters, the largest armoury on the island, and at about 7:00 am made his first radio broadcast, calling himself only the field marshal. The insurgents took the main buildings of Zanzibar Town and overthrew the Sultan and his government.

A Revolutionary Council with Abeid Karume as president renamed the country the People's Republic of Zanzibar and Pemba, banished the Sultan and banned the Zanzibar Nationalist Party. Okello's followers carried out beatings, rapes, murders and looting against Arabs and South Asians on Unguja. Estimates of the dead range from several hundred to 20,000, and some Western newspapers gave 2,000 to 4,000. About 10,000 people fled.

Britain drew up intervention plans but did not act, as British and American citizens were evacuated and the feared communist government never appeared. East Germany, the Soviet Union and China recognised the new government and sent advisers. Karume later negotiated a merger with Tanganyika that formed Tanzania. The revolution broke the power of the Arab and South Asian ruling class. The civil service became almost entirely African, land was redistributed, and the government offered free healthcare and wider school places for Africans. One-party rule lasted until 1992. Historians have analysed the revolution as social, the African proletariat rising against the ruling and trading classes, or as racial and worsened by economic inequality. An annual public holiday commemorates it.
zapatista-army-of-national-liberation: Chiapas had seen earlier uprisings, among them the Caste War or Chamula Rebellion of 1867–1870 and the Pajarito War of 1911. The EZLN emerged under the Institutional Revolutionary Party, which had ruled Mexico for more than sixty years, and many young people considered legal channels of political participation closed. The National Liberation Forces, founded in Monterrey on 6 August 1969, were one of the clandestine groups that sought to overthrow the regime. The EZLN was founded on 17 November 1983 by non-indigenous members of those forces from the urban north and by indigenous inhabitants of the Las Cañadas and Lacandon Jungle regions of eastern Chiapas.

The group grew slowly, building on peasant organisations and the Catholic Church. Through the efforts of the Diocese of San Cristóbal de Las Casas, most indigenous communities in the Lacandon forest were already politically active in the 1970s. In 1992 an amendment of Article 27 of the Constitution ended land reform, which increased unrest among indigenous peasants.

The EZLN went public on 1 January 1994, issuing its First Declaration and Revolutionary Laws from the Lacandon Jungle, which amounted to a declaration of war on a government it considered illegitimate. About 3,000 armed insurgents seized six towns and cities in the Chiapas highlands and soon retreated to the forest to avoid a federal offensive. Its demands included work, land, housing, food, healthcare, education, independence, liberty, democracy, justice and peace. After a ceasefire on 12 January, peace talks began with the Catholic bishop Samuel Ruiz acting for the Zapatistas and Manuel Camacho Solis for the state.

In 1995 the army besieged the group in the Lacandon Jungle, but President Zedillo abandoned the offensive for a diplomatic approach. After the election of Vicente Fox in 2001 the army withdrew from some positions, but the EZLN rejected the resulting agreement and created 32 autonomous municipalities. In 2005 it issued the Sixth Declaration of the Lacandon Jungle, extending its cause to all the exploited and dispossessed of Mexico.

The Zapatistas describe themselves as a decentralised organisation. Political decisions are deliberated in community assemblies, while military and organisational matters are decided by the General Command, a committee of area elders. Its ideology, called Neozapatismo, combines Maya tradition with elements of Catholic liberation theology and indigenous autonomism, and it has avoided adherence to a specific political ideology beyond the left. One Zapatista slogan is Para todos todo, para nosotros nada, meaning everything for everyone, nothing for us.
zaporozhian-cossacks: The name comes from Zaporizhzhia, "the land beyond the rapids", where the fortress of the Zaporozhians, the Sich, stood. Cossack is traced to a Turkic word meaning a free man, and the Cossacks were predominantly Ruthenians who included other groups. It is not clear when the first Cossack communities formed on the Lower Dnieper; similar people lived on the steppe from the 12th century, and the part played by nomads such as the Cumans, Pechenegs and Khazars in their origins is disputed. Many were escaped serfs who preferred the dangerous freedom of the steppe to life under Polish or Polonised aristocrats, and newcomers had to accept Eastern Orthodoxy. In the 16th century Dmytro Vyshnevetsky, a Ruthenian noble, united these groups into a strong military organization.

In the 16th century the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth regarded the Zaporozhians as its subjects, though tentatively, and registered Cossacks were part of its army until 1699. From the later 16th century their raids on Ottoman territory, which Tatar raids answered, strained relations between the Commonwealth and the Ottoman Empire and helped lead to wars such as the Battle of Cecora in 1620. After the Treaty of Pereyaslav in 1654 the Host became a suzerainty under the protection of the tsar of Russia, though it long kept near-complete autonomy.

By the late 18th century much of the Cossack officer class in Ukraine had been absorbed into the Russian nobility, and many rank-and-file Cossacks had been reduced to peasant status. The Sich sheltered runaway serfs, which angered Catherine II. Her council decided on 7 May 1775 to disband it. General Peter Tekeli surrounded the Sich with artillery and infantry on 5 June, and the Cossacks were overwhelmed. In 1784 Grigory Potemkin formed the Host of the Loyal Zaporozhians between the Southern Bug and the Dniester.

The Host was governed by the unwritten Cossack Code. It had 38 kurins and five to eight palankas, and all officers were elected by the General Military Council for a year on 1 January. Its leader never officially held the title of hetman, though Cossack leaders were unofficially called so. The highest body was the Sich Rada, the council that decided matters of foreign and internal policy, elections, the division of land and the punishment of grave crimes, which is why some sources call the Sich a Cossack republic. Hetmans and kish otamans carried the bulawa, or mace; the one carried by Bohdan Khmelnytsky from 1648 was silver, covered in gold and set with pearls and gems.
zapotec-civilization: The Zapotec civilization arose in the Central Valleys of Oaxaca, three broad valleys, Etla in the west, Ocotlán in the south and Mitla in the east, that meet about 200 km south of Mexico City. The land suited agriculture and is considered one of the cradles of maize. The three valleys held three societies separated by a no-man's-land, and burned temples and sacrificed war captives suggest that they competed. At the end of the Rosario phase, 700 to 500 BCE, the largest settlement, San José Mogote, lost most of its population.

At the same time a new settlement grew on a mountain in the no-man's-land: Monte Albán. Its early pottery resembles that of San José Mogote, which suggests settlers came from there. Walls and fortifications of the Monte Albán 2 phase, about 100 BCE to 200 CE, suggest that the city was built in response to a military threat.

The state formed at Monte Albán began to expand in the late Monte Albán 1 phase, 400 to 100 BCE, and grew through Monte Albán 2.
