The historian Chen Shou wrote that Zhang Fei was brutal and heartless towards his men, a flaw that led to his downfall, and Liu Bei had warned him against excessive punishments. Rafe de Crespigny calls him arrogant, impetuous and brutal, though courteous to the virtuous.
zhang-jinghui: Zhang Jinghui was born on 21 June 1871 in Tai'an, south-west of Mukden in Liaoning Province, an area that became a battlefield in the First Sino-Japanese War. At an early age he joined the Honghuzi irregular cavalry of the Manchurian warlord Zhang Zuolin, forces that the Japanese recruited as mercenaries during the Russo-Japanese War of 1904 to 1905. When Yuan Shikai died in 1916 the Beiyang Army split into mutually hostile factions.

Zhang Jinghui deserted Zhang Zuolin for the Zhili clique of Wu Peifu, but later rejoined him. He served as minister of war in the Beiyang Government from May 1926 to June 1927 and as minister of industry in the National Pacification Army Government from June 1927 to June 1928, and was then appointed governor of the Harbin and China Eastern Railway Special District in northern Manchuria. After Zhang Zuolin was killed in the Huanggutun Incident on 4 June 1928, his relations with the son and successor, Zhang Xueliang, deteriorated.

Following the Mukden Incident and the invasion of Manchuria by the Japanese Kwantung Army in 1931, Zhang called a conference on 27 September to form an emergency committee aiming at the secession of Manchuria from China. He proclaimed his territory self-governing and was inaugurated as governor on 7 January 1932. He then came to terms with Japan and accepted the governorship of Heilongjiang Province in Manchukuo. His refusal to leave Harbin for Qiqihar caused friction with the Kwantung Army, and he was set aside when General Ma Zhanshan accepted the post on 14 February 1932. Ma revolted in April, and Zhang replaced him as minister of defence.

His appointment as prime minister on 21 May 1935 was made at the instigation of the Kwantung Army and over the objections of Emperor Puyi. He is said to have spent his days copying Buddhist sutras and was nicknamed the Tofu Prime Minister in his own lifetime. He is recorded as speaking out against the Japanese administration only once, to criticise the forced sale of land to Japanese colonists. In 1943 he represented Manchukuo at the Greater East Asia Conference in Tokyo; in the same year Time magazine published a false report that he had killed his family and his Japanese adviser and then himself.

After the war the Soviet Union held him in Siberia until 1950, when he was extradited to the People's Republic of China and imprisoned at the Fushun War Criminals Management Centre. He died there of heart failure on 11 January 1959.
zhang-juzheng: Zhang Juzheng studied Confucianism, passed the provincial examination in 1540 and failed the metropolitan examination in 1544 before succeeding at an unusually young age three years later. He served at the Hanlin Academy, resigned through illness in 1554 and returned six years later to the Guozijian, the Imperial University; he never held office outside Beijing. Senior Grand Secretary Xu Jie, his patron since the late 1540s, had him draft the final edict of the Jiajing Emperor, which proclaimed the Longqing Emperor's accession. In 1572 Zhang and Feng Bao, head of the Directorate of Ceremonial, removed Gao Gong as senior grand secretary.

Zhang could give orders only in the emperor's name or informally, but he chose his colleagues in the Grand Secretariat and placed his followers in the Ministry of Rites, the Censorate and the provinces. Monthly and half-yearly reports measured each county and prefecture on tax collection and the suppression of bandits. Against the followers of Wang Yangming, who stressed inner self-improvement, he set the pragmatic service of the state, citing the laws of the Hongwu Emperor as his model. When his father died in 1577 the fourteen-year-old emperor cancelled his mourning; critics attacked him for disrespect to his parent and were beaten, and a review of high officials let Zhang remove about fifty opponents.

The reserves he built up included nine years of grain around the capital and 6 million liang of silver in the Ministry of Revenue. His attempt to expand the copper coinage through new mints from 1576 failed: copper ran short, provincial coins were poor, and in 1579 he acknowledged the failure. On the frontier he promoted commanders such as Qi Jiguang and Li Chengliang, opened border markets and kept an armed peace with the Mongols.

Zhang died on 9 July 1582 and was soon accused of bribery, luxury, favouritism and suppressing dissent; his supporters lost their posts and Feng Bao was sent to Nanjing in early 1583. In April 1584 the concubine of Zhu Xianjie, prince of Liao, accused him of embezzling the prince's property. Zhang was stripped of his titles, his eldest son Zhang Jingxiu took his own life, and ten descendants starved to death in confinement. Historians judge the reforms only partly successful, resting on his personal authority rather than on institutions, though the Wanli Emperor kept many of his views.
zhang-qian: Zhang Qian was born in Chenggu district, just east of Hanzhong in what is now Shaanxi. He entered the capital, Chang'an, between 140 and 134 BCE as a Gentleman serving Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty. At that time the nomadic Xiongnu controlled what is now Inner Mongolia and dominated the Western Regions, the lands neighbouring Han territory, and their hostility blocked outside contact. The emperor wished to establish commercial ties with distant lands and to find allies against the Xiongnu.

In 138 BCE the Han court sent Zhang Qian, a military officer familiar with the Xiongnu, with a party of ninety-nine to seek an alliance with the Yuezhi. His guide was a captured Xiongnu named Ganfu. The Xiongnu seized them on the way and held Zhang for thirteen years, during which he married a Xiongnu wife and had a son. When he escaped he went by Dayuan to the Yuezhi, who were too settled to wish to fight the Xiongnu. He spent a year among them and in neighbouring Bactria, recording their customs and economy. On the return he was captured again, and escaped in the disorder after the Xiongnu leader died. Of just over a hundred men, only he and Ganfu returned.

He brought the emperor detailed news of sophisticated states to the west, which according to the Shiji were rich in unusual products and militarily weak. He was made a palace counsellor. A later mission sought a route to India through Sichuan and failed, and another, between 119 and 115 BCE, went to the Wusun. In 121 BCE he took part in a campaign against the Xiongnu, but he lost his way and failed to meet the general Li Guang, whose force was surrounded and defeated. Zhang was sentenced to death and escaped by paying a ransom, which cost him his titles.

Zhang Qian's reports are quoted extensively by Sima Qian in the Shiji. He visited Dayuan in Fergana, the Yuezhi north of the Oxus, Bactria and Kangju, and reported on lands he had not seen, including Parthia, Mesopotamia and India. He described the horses of Dayuan, which led Emperor Wu to launch two campaigns to obtain them, and brought back alfalfa seeds for fodder. The Shiji says he was honoured with the post of grand messenger after his final expedition and died a year or so later.

After his embassy, Chinese missions went west in numbers, and the largest numbered several hundred people. Because silk became the main product traded from China, the route later became known as the Silk Road, although exchanges along parts of it had occurred before Zhang Qian.
zhang-xianzhong: Zhang Xianzhong was born in 1606 into a poor family at Liushujian, in modern Dingbian, Shaanxi. Tall, with a yellow complexion and an impressive beard, he was nicknamed the Yellow Tiger. He enlisted in the Ming army in the mid-1620s and was sentenced to death for breaching military law, but a senior officer had him reprieved. Drought, famine and epidemics in the late Ming drove peasants in Shaanxi to revolt against grain and tax collections, and around 1630 Zhang deserted to the rebels, styling himself the Eighth Great King.

For more than a decade Zhang led one of the mobile rebel armies the Ming called roving bandits, raiding towns across Shaanxi, Henan, Anhui and Huguang. In 1635 he joined a confederation with Li Zicheng that burned the Ming ancestral temple at Fengyang. He surrendered when it suited him, as in 1631 and 1638, then rebelled again. In 1641 he took Xiangyang and executed the imperial Prince of Xiang there, and in 1643 he captured Wuchang, killed its prince and proclaimed himself King of the West.

In 1644 he led about 100,000 troops into Sichuan, took Chongqing on 25 July and Chengdu on 9 September, renamed Chengdu the Western Capital and later declared himself emperor with the reign title Dashun. The Portuguese Jesuit Gabriel de Magalhães, pressed into his service, wrote that he began his rule with liberality and won many officials to his side. After Ming loyalists retook Chongqing in 1645 he turned to a campaign of terror against suspected resistance, which grew worse in 1646 as his government fell apart.

Zhang abandoned Sichuan in October 1646 before an advancing Qing army under Haoge, and in January 1647 he was killed in a clash with Qing forces at Xichong. Later accounts of his massacres were lurid, and the Ming history's figure of 600 million dead is an obvious exaggeration; one modern estimate puts the toll at possibly one million of a provincial population of three million. Many historians hold that more people died after his death from war, famine and disease. Sichuan was resettled by millions of migrants under the Qing, beginning around 1670.
zhang-zhidong: Zhang Zhidong was born on 2 September 1837 in Xingyi Prefecture, Guizhou, though his family's roots lay in Nanpi in Zhili. He came first in the provincial examination of 1852 and in 1863 placed third in the palace examination, entering the Hanlin Academy as an editor. In 1882 he became governor of Shanxi. During the Ili Crisis he demanded the execution of the envoy Chonghou, who had signed a treaty granting Russia extraterritorial rights and an indemnity, and urged the government to declare it invalid.

After China's defeat in the Sino-French War of 1885 Zhang called for a modern army. He founded the Guangdong Military Academy and the Guangdong Victorious Army with German officers as instructors, and in 1896 the Hubei Military Academy. At Wuchang he trained modern units of engineers, cavalry, artillery and infantry armed with Mauser rifles; of his 60,000 men, 20,000 were trained directly by foreign officers. He was put in charge of a railway from Hankou towards Beijing, finished in 1906.
In the First Sino-Japanese War he urged foreign loans, arms purchases and alliances, and in 1895 he proposed borrowing from the British in return for their navy's defence of Taiwan.

During the Boxer Rebellion in 1900 he joined Li Hongzhang and other governors in the Mutual Protection of Southeast China, refusing to take part in the court's war against the Eight-Nation Alliance. His informant Yang Rui, one of the Six Martyrs, carried out his instructions during the Hundred Days' Reform of 1898. Exhortation to Study proposed new schools funded from Buddhist and Taoist monasteries, of which 30 percent would be kept. In 1901 he succeeded Liu Kunyi as viceroy of Liangjiang at Nanjing, where he helped found Sanjiang Normal College, and in 1906 he became Minister of Military Affairs in Beijing.

Zhang died of illness in Beijing on 4 October 1909, aged 72, and received the posthumous name Wenxiang. Historians commonly see his reforms as an attempt to reconcile modernity with China's existing social fabric. In 1911 the Wuchang garrison he had built led the Wuchang Uprising, which set off the Xinhai Revolution. Red Guards destroyed his tomb in 1966; his remains were found again in 2007 and reburied.
zhang-zuolin: Zhang Zuolin was born in 1875 in Haicheng, in southern Fengtian province, to poor parents. He received little formal education and learned only a small amount of veterinary science. At twenty he enlisted as a cavalry soldier in the First Sino-Japanese War, and afterwards he returned home and became a mounted bandit. By his late twenties he had formed a small personal army. In 1900 his gang joined the imperial army during the Boxer Rebellion, and in the Russo-Japanese War of 1904-05 the Japanese Army employed him and his men as mercenaries. At the end of the Qing dynasty his men were recognised as a regiment of the regular army.

During the 1911 Revolution Zhang's regiment was used to intimidate would-be rebels in Manchuria, and he was named Vice Minister of Military Affairs. He backed Yuan Shikai, who made him military governor of Fengtian, and after Yuan's death in June 1916 the new government named him military and civil governor of Liaoning. By 1918 his control of Manchuria was complete except for the areas held by Japan, and in 1920 he was appointed Governor-General of the Three Eastern Provinces. His Fengtian Army numbered about 100,000 men in 1922.

Zhang defeated Duan Qirui in 1920 with Cao Kun, but the Zhili Army defeated the Fengtian Army in the First Zhili-Fengtian War in May 1922, and he declared Manchuria independent from Beijing. His financial adviser Wang Yongjiang reformed the province's currency and taxes, and tillage rose from 20 million to 35 million acres between 1924 and 1929. After the Second Zhili-Fengtian War of 1924, the cost of war broke the economy, and Wang resigned in 1926. In 1927 Zhang proclaimed himself Generalissimo and led the Beiyang government.

Nationalist forces under Chiang Kai-shek attacked in 1928, and the Fengtian Army retreated towards Beijing. Under Japanese pressure, Zhang left Beijing on 3 June 1928. On the morning of 4 June, a bomb planted by Colonel Kōmoto Daisaku of the Japanese Kwantung Army exploded as his train passed a railroad bridge near Shenyang, and he died a few hours later. Okada Keisuke testified at the Tokyo War Crimes Tribunal in 1946 that the Kwantung Army had been angered by his failure to stop Chiang's army. His death was kept secret for two weeks.

His eldest son, Zhang Xueliang, succeeded him as warlord of Manchuria. By July the Beiyang government in exile had reached an armistice with the Kuomintang, and by the end of 1928 the Northeast Flag Replacement nominally reunified China under the Kuomintang banner.
zhangjiakou: Zhangjiakou lies in north-western Hebei, bordering Beijing to the southeast and Inner Mongolia to the north and west. Since ancient times it has been a stronghold of military significance, and it is nicknamed the Northern Gate of Beijing. Dajingmen, an important gate and junction of the Great Wall, is located there. The urban area is surrounded by mountains on three sides, and the Qingshui River divides it into two districts, Qiaodong and Qiaoxi. The name means pass of the Zhang family. It is a clipping of Zhangjiakoubu, the earthwork fortress of the Zhang family, named for the Ming official Zhang Wen, who began fortifying the city in 1429. Europeans long knew it as Kalgan, from the Mongolian name Qaɣalɣan, meaning barrier or gate.

The region was a battleground in the Han–Xiongnu wars, and the Qin general Meng Tian joined the Great Walls of Yan, Qin and Zhao near here. In the Ming dynasty the garrison of Xuanfu, one of the Nine Garrisons, grew to 151 thousand troops between 1403 and 1424. In 1449 the Emperor Yingzong of Ming was captured by pursuing Mongol troops in Huailai County, an event called the Tumu Crisis. In 1571 Altan Khan received a title from the Longqing Emperor and agreed a lasting peace, after which Zhangjiakou changed from a military base into an important horse market for Mongolian mounts.

It was the chief northern gate for Europeans travelling along the Northern Tea Road, among them Ivan Petlin in 1619. From 1727 it was an important station in the Kyakhta trade between Russia and China, and in autumn long lines of camels carried tea chests from Zhangjiakou across the Gobi to Kyakhta. In the 19th century the town had an estimated 70–100,000 people, and some Russian merchants had permanent residences and warehouses outside the gate.

The Beijing–Zhangjiakou Railway, the first railway designed and built solely by Chinese, with Zhan Tianyou as chief engineer, connected it to Beijing in October 1909. The Japanese occupied the region in 1937 and made Kalgan the capital of the autonomous province of South Chahar, and a Federated Mengjiang Commission supervised the economy of Japanese-occupied Inner Mongolia.

Zhangjiakou is a prefecture-level city, with 4,118,908 people at the census of 2020. It is a gateway between Hebei, Inner Mongolia and Beijing, and has a notable wine industry at Huailai. It hosted skiing and snowboarding events of the 2022 Winter Olympics at Taizicheng in Chongli District.
zhanguo-ce: While editing the imperial library, Liu Xiang found six versions of writings from the School of Diplomacy, in poor condition, with confused contents and missing words, and edited them into one book under the title Zhan Guo Ce. It is therefore generally held, after Zhang Xincheng, that the book was not written by one author at one time; it is thought to have been composed by Su Qin and his peers. In 1931 Luo Genze argued that Kuai Tong, a contemporary of Han Xin, was its author, a view refuted by Zhang Xincheng in 1939.

Much of the text was lost in later centuries, and Zeng Gong of the Northern Song dynasty recovered some lost chapters and edited the version read today. Unlike many pre-Qin classics, its authenticity was not questioned from the Western Han period onward; the compiler of the Annotated Bibliography of the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries was perhaps the first to call it apocryphal, without giving grounds.

The book runs from the conquest of the Fan clan by the Zhi clan in 490 BCE to the failed attempt on the life of Qin Shi Huang by Gao Jianli in 221 BCE. Its anecdotes illustrate the strategies and tricks of the Warring States rather than tell the whole history of the period. There is no strict year-by-year dating as in the Spring and Autumn Annals: stories are ordered by the ruler under whom they fall, but within one reign there is no telling whether a day or a year separates two of them. It runs to about 120,000 words in 33 chapters and 497 sections, arranged by twelve states.

In 1973 writings on silk were excavated from the Han tomb at Mawangdui near Changsha and published in 1976 as the Zhanguo Zonghengjia Shu. Of their 27 chapters, 11 resemble passages of the Zhan Guo Ce and the Records of the Grand Historian; the copy was probably made around 195 BCE, since it avoids the word bang, the personal name of Emperor Gao of Han.

Since the 12th century writers have debated whether the book counts as history, until scholars such as Zhong Fengnian showed in 1936 that it was written as a handbook of rhetoric for the School of Diplomacy. Its stress on power politics has been criticised as at odds with Confucian ideology, while its wit and vigorous style have earned it a place as literature. English translations include James I. Crump's of 1970.
zhangye: Zhangye lies in the centre of the Hexi Corridor, in central Gansu, and its urban core, Ganzhou, stands in the oasis formed by the Ruo or Hei River. The area is on the frontier of China proper, protecting it from the nomads of the northwest and giving its armies access to the Tarim Basin. The city takes up the entire breadth of the province, from Inner Mongolia on the north to Qinghai on the south. Its streams, sunlight and fertile soil made it an important agricultural centre. Ganzhou was named for the sweet waters of its oasis, and Marco Polo's Travels gives the name as Campichu.

Zhangye Commandery was established by the Western Han in 111 BCE, with its seat at the site of modern Wuwei. The meaning of the name Zhangye is unclear; one popular theory reads it as Extending Arm, from a phrase in the Han Shu about extending the arm of the country through to the Western Realm. During the Western Han, Han armies often fought the Xiongnu in this area, and it was an important outpost on the Silk Road. Before being overrun by the Mongols it was dominated by the Western Xia dynasty, and earlier by the Uyghurs, from at least the early 10th century. Its relation to the larger Uyghur state of Qocho is obscure, but it may have been a vassal.

Kublai, the founder of the Yuan dynasty, is said to have been born in the Dafo Temple in Zhangye, now the site of the longest wooden reclining Buddha in China. Marco Polo's journal states that he spent a year in the town on his journey to China. In the 1880s a Qing official in charge of erecting poles for the telegraph network ordered the pine forests of the Babao Mountains cleared. They had regulated the flow of the Ruo River by ensuring that melt-waters lasted through the summer, and afterwards the region became prone to flooding in summer and drought in autumn. Christian missionaries arrived in 1879, after Suzhou, modern Jiuquan, was found too hostile.

Zhangye is a prefecture-level city with 1,131,016 permanent residents at the census of 2020, and 26 ethnic minorities besides the Han are represented, including many Hui, Yugur and Tibetans. The Zhangye Danxia National Geological Park, known for its colourful rock formations, lies 30 km west of the city centre. The Lanzhou–Xinjiang Railway runs through the city.
zhanjiang: Zhanjiang is a prefecture-level city that administers the entire Leizhou Peninsula and lies directly opposite Haikou, the capital of Hainan, across the Qiongzhou Strait. It is the southernmost port on the coast of mainland China and a centre of commerce and navigation for much of south-western China. The city sits on an inlet of the South China Sea, southwest of Guangzhou, and its climate is humid subtropical, with heavy rain from April to September.

During the Qin dynasty the area belonged to the Xiang Shire administrative division, and under the Han dynasty Xuwen County was set up as the seat for the whole Leizhou Peninsula. The port became one of the earliest departure points on the Maritime Silk Road. In the Song dynasty many Putian (Hinghwa) colonists settled in the region, later forming the ethnolinguistic majority of the peninsula, alongside the Baiyue, Cantonese, Tanka and foreign merchants.

In 1898 the area was a small fishing port when the French established control and forced China to lease a 99-year concession called Guangzhouwan. Much of the local population had fled, so Cantonese peasants from north of Leizhou were brought in, which made Yue Chinese the dominant local language. The French developed the port as Fort Bayard, intending it as a logistical centre for their concessions in southern China, though poverty and underdevelopment limited the effort. They held the enclave until 1943, when Japan occupied it during World War II. After the war it was briefly returned to France before being ceded to China. The Republic of China renamed the area Zhanjiang, a variant of Zhanchuan, the name of an earlier county.

After the People's Republic of China was established in 1949 the city grew in strategic and economic importance, and by 1957 it had a modern deep-water port able to handle ships of up to 50,000 tons. In 1984, under Deng Xiaoping's policy of reform and opening-up, it was designated an open city to attract foreign investment. In the early 1990s a rail line linked it to Guangzhou and was later extended to Hai'an at the southern tip of the peninsula.

The 2020 census counted a resident population of 6,981,236. Leizhou Min is the prestige language in several districts, Yue Chinese is spoken in Potou District and other areas settled in the French period, and Hakka is spoken in Lianjiang County. The local Leizhou Opera has a history of over 300 years. Zhanjiang is the headquarters of the South Sea Fleet of the People's Liberation Army Navy. Its port is a natural deep-water harbour protected by three outer islands, and the old French quarter in Chikan survives as Chikan Old Street, with arched windows, balconies and tiled roofs.
zhao-mengfu: Zhao Mengfu, whose courtesy name was Zi'ang, also used the pseudonyms Songxue, Pine Snow, Oubo, Gull Waves, and Shuijing-gong Dao-ren, Master of the Water Spirits Palace. He descended from the imperial house of the Song dynasty through Zhao Bogui, a brother of Emperor Xiaozong, who married a lady surnamed Song, a granddaughter of Emperor Huizong. Zhao Bogui in turn descended from Emperor Taizu through his son Zhao Defang.

The Censor-in-chief Cheng Jufu recommended Zhao Mengfu for an audience with Kublai Khan at the Yuan capital of Dadu in 1286, but he received no important position. The Confucian-inspired Emperor Renzong of Yuan later valued his work greatly, and Zhao was a member of the Academy of Worthies. His wife Guan Daosheng was also an accomplished poet, painter and calligrapher. Their second son, Zhao Yong, became a well-known painter and calligrapher, and their grandson through a daughter, Wang Meng, was another noted painter.

Zhao rejected the refined, gentle brushwork of his own time in favour of the cruder style of the eighth century, a change considered to have created the modern Chinese landscape painting. He was also known for his paintings of horses. In his landscapes he did not arrange a foreground, middle ground and background but layered middle grounds at various heights to create depth, which made the paintings appear simple and approachable, a quality many people valued.

One of his landscapes, held by the Princeton University Art Museum, is titled The Mind Landscape of Xie Youyu. In 2019 the Dutch scholar Lennert Gesterkamp argued that its colophon naming Xie Youyu is a forgery and that Zhao meant to honour his own spiritual master, the Daoist scholar Du Daojian (1237-1318). His former residence in Huzhou, Zhejiang, has been a museum since 2012, and a crater on Mercury bears his name.
zhao-tuo: Zhao Tuo was born around 240 BCE in Zhengding, in what is now Hebei, in a region annexed by the Huaxia state of Zhao. When Qin conquered Zhao in 222 BCE he entered Qin service and became a general in its conquest of the Baiyue peoples. The conquered Yue lands were divided into the provinces of Guilin, Nanhai and Xiang, and Zhao served as magistrate in Nanhai.

Nanhai's military commander, Ren Xiao, fell ill and advised Zhao to stay out of the affairs of the declining Qin and to build an independent kingdom around the remote city of Panyu, modern Guangzhou. Zhao closed the roads at Hengpu, Yangshan and Huangqi, replaced the Qin officials with his own appointees and, by the time Qin fell in 206 BCE, had conquered Guilin and Xiang as well. He declared himself king of Nanyue, the Southern Yue.

In 196 BCE Emperor Gaozu of Han sent Lu Jia to recognise Zhao as king of Nanyue in return for nominal submission. In 185 BCE Empress Lü's officials banned the trade of iron and horses with Nanyue, and Zhao proclaimed himself emperor and attacked the kingdom of Changsha. A Han army sent in 181 BCE failed to cross the mountains because heat and damp sickened its men. Zhao then menaced Minyue, Western Ou and Luo until they submitted. In late 180 BCE Emperor Wen of Han tried to appease him, tending the graves of Zhao's parents at Zhengding and appointing his cousins to high office. Zhao dropped the imperial title in dealing with the Han but kept it at home.

The conquest of Âu Lạc is told differently in different sources. The Records of the Grand Historian mention neither King An Dương nor a military conquest, while later records and a legend tell of a turtle-claw crossbow that gave its holder power. In the legend Zhao's son Zhong Shi married An Dương's daughter, tampered with the crossbow's trigger and returned to his father, who then defeated An Dương. Zhao left the local chiefs in place and posted two legates, in the Red River Delta and the Mã and Cả river area. For the first time the region formed part of a polity headed by a Chinese ruler.

Zhao died in 137 BCE, reportedly aged 103, and his grandson Zhao Mo succeeded him. Some traditional Vietnamese historians counted him founder of the Triệu dynasty, while some contemporary historians contest that he was a foreign invader.
zhaoqing: Zhaoqing lies 110 km west of Guangzhou, in the west of the Pearl River Delta, on the north shore of the Xi River, which flows from west to east. Gaoyao stands opposite on the south bank. A plain lies to the south and west of the city, with mountains to the east and north. Its name, meaning Beginning Auspiciousness, was bestowed on the area by Emperor Huizong of the Song in 1118. Earlier it was known to the Qin as Sihui and to the Han as Gaoyao, and under the Sui it was renamed Duanzhou as the seat of Duan Prefecture.

In the late 6th and early 7th centuries the administration moved from Gaoyao to Duanzhou on the opposite bank, which became an important administrative and military centre of the southern Sui Empire. The city wall was built in Duanzhou during the reign of Emperor Renzong of Song (1022–1063).

When the Portuguese arrived in the 16th century Zhaoqing was still an important centre, the seat of the Viceroy of Liangguang, meaning Guangdong and Guangxi. In 1582 the Italian Jesuit Michele Ruggieri came from Macao, sent in place of the governor and bishop whom the viceroy Chen Rui had summoned. After several false starts he and Matteo Ricci were allowed to settle in the city, in the first Jesuit mission house on mainland China, after the governor Wang Pan learned of Ricci's skill as a mathematician and cartographer.

Ricci drew the first modern Chinese map of the world in Zhaoqing in 1584. Ruggieri left for Rome in 1588, and Ricci was expelled by a new viceroy the next year, which obliged the Jesuits to move to Shaozhou, now Shaoguan.

In the fall of the Ming in the mid-17th century Zhaoqing was the capital of the Southern Ming resistance of the Prince of Gui, who styled himself the Yongli Emperor. The town fell in 1650 and the prince moved to Guilin and then to places in Guangxi, Yunnan and Kokang. The Jesuits Andreas Wolfgang Koffler and later Michał Boym stayed for some time at his court. Under the Qing the viceroy moved to Guangzhou, but Zhaoqing remained the seat of a commandery.

Once one of the most important cities of southern China, Zhaoqing lost that standing under the Qing dynasty. It has six National Key Cultural Relic Protection Sites, among them the Song city walls, the Seven Star Crags carvings and the Yuejiang Tower in Duanzhou District. Dinghu Mountain, beside the Seven Star Crags, was the first nature reserve established in China.
zhejiang: Zhejiang is a coastal province of East China, bordered by Jiangsu and Shanghai to the north, Anhui to the northwest, Jiangxi to the west and Fujian to the south, with the East China Sea to the east. Hills account for about 70 per cent of its area, rising towards the south and west, and the highest peak, Huangmaojian Peak, reaches 1,929 metres. It has a longer coastline than any other mainland province and about three thousand islands, the most in China. The Qiantang River, formerly the Zhe River, gives the province its name. Hangzhou stands at the end of the Grand Canal on Hangzhou Bay.

The Kuahuqiao settlement near Hangzhou dates from 6000 to 5000 BCE, and the Neolithic Hemudu culture began in 5500 BCE and the Liangzhu culture in 3400 BCE. In the second millennium BCE the area lay outside the main sphere of Shang civilisation and was populated by peoples known as the Dongyue. The Kingdom of Yue controlled it in the Spring and Autumn period, and the Qin dynasty annexed it in 222 BCE. Kuaiji Commandery was the power base of Xiang Liang and Xiang Yu in their rebellion against the Qin.

Qiantang, the former name of Hangzhou, was one of three major southern centres that supplied tax revenue to the north in the Six Dynasties period, and in 589 it was raised in status and renamed Hangzhou. As the heartland of the Jiangnan, Zhejiang was the wealthiest area under the Six Dynasties, Sui and Tang, and its grain and resources travelled north along the Grand Canal that the Sui restored and expanded. After the Tang fell in 907, King Qian Liu established the kingdom of Wuyue, with Hangzhou as its capital. The Song annexed it around 960. In 1127 Hangzhou became the Song capital under the name Lin'an, noted for its prosperity and beauty and suspected to have been the largest city in the world.

The Mongols occupied the province in the late 13th century and merged it with neighbouring provinces, and the present-day province was established in 1368. In the late Ming and Qing periods its ports were centres of international trade. During the Second World War much of Zhejiang was occupied. After the Doolittle Raid, the Imperial Japanese Army began the Zhejiang-Jiangxi Campaign against locals who had helped downed American airmen; at least 10,000 civilians died in Jiangxi.

Zhejiang has a population of about 64.6 million, and its capital and largest city is Hangzhou, with Ningbo, Yiwu and Wenzhou also notable. Hangzhou includes the West Lake. Various varieties of Chinese are spoken, the most prominent being Wu Chinese. The province is the birthplace of Chiang Kai-shek.
zhelyu-zhelev: Zhelev was born on 3 March 1935 into a modest village family in Veselinovo in north-eastern Bulgaria. He studied philosophy at Sofia University, graduating in 1958 and gaining a PhD in 1974. A member of the Bulgarian Communist Party, he was expelled from it for political reasons in 1965. All employment in Bulgaria was state-regulated, so he was unemployed for six years, a condition termed social parasitism in communist terminology. He spent much of that time in virtual internal exile in his wife's village, scraping a living from odd jobs on farms.

In 1982 Zhelev published his book Fascism. Three weeks after publication it was removed from bookstores and libraries throughout the country, because its description of the fascist states of Italy, Germany and Spain made these regimes comparable to the Communist regimes of the Eastern Bloc. In 1988 he founded the Ruse Committee, and in 1989 he became a founding member and chairman of the Club for Support of Openness and the Reform. This helped him to the chairmanship of the Coordinating Council of the Union of Democratic Forces. He was one of the most prominent figures of the 1989 Bulgarian Revolution, which ended the 35-year rule of Todor Zhivkov.

Zhelev was elected a member of parliament in June 1990 to the 7th Grand National Assembly, whose main task was to draft a new democratic constitution. After President Petar Mladenov resigned, the Assembly elected Zhelev his successor on 1 August 1990, the first head of state in 44 years who was neither a Communist nor a fellow traveller. The constitution of July 1991 provided for direct election of the president, for at most two terms, and made the office largely representative.

In the first such election, in January 1992, he led the first round on 12 January and won the runoff a week later against Velko Valkanov, backed by the Socialists, with 52.8% of the votes. He suspended his membership in the Union of Democratic Forces, believing the presidency should be above politics. In 1996 he lost the party's nomination for a second term to Petar Stoyanov.

After his presidency ended in 1997 Zhelev became honorary chair of the Liberal Democratic Union and of Liberal International and set up a foundation named after him. He also founded and presided over the Balkan Political Club, a union of former political leaders from Southeast Europe. He died in Sofia on 30 January 2015, aged 79.
zhenbao-island: Zhenbao Island, literally Rare Treasure Island, lies in Hulin, Jixi, in Heilongjiang Province, China, and covers only 0.74 square kilometres. It sits in the Ussuri River on the border between Primorsky Krai in Russia and Heilongjiang. Its Russian name, Damansky, comes from the railway engineer Stanislav Damansky, who died there in an incident in 1888 while charting the future route of the Trans-Siberian Railway.

Before the Sino-Soviet Border Agreement of 1991 the island was disputed between China and the Soviet Union. China held that, in the absence of an explicit treaty provision, the central line of the main channel, the Thalweg principle, was the legal basis for fixing the boundary in the two rivers. On that basis Beijing claimed that 600 of the rivers' 700 islands, Zhenbao among them, belonged to China. The island lay only about 180 miles southwest of the Soviet city of Khabarovsk.

Battles were fought there with considerable loss of life during the Sino-Soviet border conflict of 1969. The dispute raised fears that it could ignite a third world war, until an initial resolution in November 1969. In his memoir US President Richard Nixon recalled a story told to him by Premier Zhou Enlai: when the Soviet premier Alexei Kosygin used a hot line to ask for Chairman Mao, the Chinese operator, on his own initiative, called him a revisionist and refused to connect him, and did the same when Kosygin asked for Zhou. On 19 May 1991 both sides agreed that the island was part of China, and Soviet troops withdrew.
The 1969 fighting has been recalled in later works, among them a Russian documentary film of 2004, Damansky Island Year 1969. The island is still known by both its Chinese and its Russian name.
zheng-he: Zheng He was born Ma He into a Muslim, Hui, family of Kunyang, Kunming, in Yunnan, then ruled by the Principality of Liang, which was loyal to the Northern Yuan dynasty. He was a great-great-great-grandson of Sayyid Ajjal Shams al-Din Omar, who governed Yunnan in the early Yuan period, and his grandfather and father bore the title hajji. The Ming armies captured him in Yunnan in 1381. He was castrated and enslaved as a eunuch servant in the household of Zhu Di, Prince of Yan, who later became the Yongle Emperor.

Ma He took part in the prince's campaigns against the Mongols, assisted him in the Jingnan campaign that overthrew the Jianwen Emperor in 1402, and took the surname Zheng, conferred by the Yongle Emperor. Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming government sponsored seven naval expeditions under his command, with Wang Jinghong as second in command. The Yongle Emperor designed them to establish a Chinese presence, impose imperial control over the Indian Ocean trade and extend the tributary system. The first voyage left Suzhou on 11 July 1405 with a fleet of 317 ships carrying almost 28,000 crewmen. The Xuande Emperor commissioned the last voyages.

One theory holds that Zheng He died in 1433, during or shortly after his seventh voyage, probably at Calicut. Another has him continuing as defender of Nanjing and dying in 1435. His tomb in Nanjing is a cenotaph believed to contain his clothes and headgear. In the decades after the last voyage imperial officials minimised the expeditions in the official histories. His voyages became well known in China and abroad after Liang Qichao's biography of 1904, and the Chinese diaspora in Southeast Asia venerates him, often under the alias Sam Po.
zheng-jing: Zheng Jing was born on 25 October 1642, the eldest son of Koxinga and a grandson of the pirate-merchant Zheng Zhilong. After his father took Fort Zeelandia in 1662, he commanded the forces on Amoy and Quemoy. He fell out with his father when he had a son, Zheng Kezang, by his brother's wet nurse, although he was married. Koxinga ordered his execution, but the forces on Amoy refused to carry it out, and Koxinga died of malaria in June 1662.

Zheng Jing then fought his uncle Zheng Shixi for the throne of Tungning, defeated his forces on Taiwan and took Fort Zeelandia; his uncle withdrew his claim and surrendered to the Qing the next year. Zheng Jing meant to pursue his father's plan to invade Spanish Luzon, but gave it up in the face of a Manchu-Dutch alliance. In 1664 his fleet defeated a combined Qing-Dutch force and killed its commander, the Han Banner general Ma Degong, but Amoy and Quemoy fell to the Qing and he withdrew all his troops to Taiwan. In 1672 his navy sank the Dutch fluyt Cuylenburg off north-eastern Taiwan and executed thirty-four of its sailors.

During his nineteen years of rule he reorganised the forces on Taiwan and exchanged envoys with the Kangxi Emperor. By the time he invaded Fujian at the invitation of Geng Jingzhong, one of the leaders of the Revolt of the Three Feudatories, he had largely given up any pretence of restoring the Ming. He held key cities there for a time but lost them to the Manchus by the end of 1677, then returned with 30,000 men to take Haicheng and capture the provincial commander.

In 1680 he lost a major naval battle to the Qing admiral Shi Lang and had to abandon Amoy, Quemoy and Tang-soaⁿ. He withdrew to present-day Tainan, where he died on 17 March 1681. He named Zheng Kezang as his successor, but Zheng Kezang was quickly overthrown in favour of his younger son Zheng Keshuang.
zheng-keshuang: Zheng Keshuang was born on 13 August 1670 in Chengtian Prefecture, whose administrative centre was Fort Provintia. He was the second son of Zheng Jing, king of Tungning, by his concubine Lady Huang. While campaigning against the Qing dynasty in the late 1670s, Zheng Jing named his elder son, Zheng Kezang, heir apparent and married his sons to daughters of his two most trusted officials: Kezang to the daughter of Chen Yonghua, Keshuang to the daughter of Feng Xifan.

Chen Yonghua was ousted by his rivals Feng Xifan and Liu Guoxuan and died in 1680. After Zheng Jing's death, Feng allied with Liu, Zheng Cong and others, told Queen Dowager Dong that Zheng Kezang was not Zheng Jing's own son, and killed him in a coup. The twelve-year-old Zheng Keshuang was installed as Prince of Yanping; he rewarded the officials who had supported the coup with titles of nobility and gave posthumous titles to his ancestors.

In 1683 the Kangxi Emperor sent Shi Lang with a fleet against Tungning, and Shi Lang defeated Liu Guoxuan at the Battle of Penghu. The court then split between a war faction, led by Zheng Dexiao and others, and a surrender faction led by Feng and Liu. Zheng Keshuang took their advice. On 5 July 1683 Feng ordered Zheng Dexiao to write the surrender, and on 13 August Shi Lang entered Taiwan and received it.

In Beijing the Kangxi Emperor enrolled Zheng Keshuang in the Plain Yellow Banner and made him hereditary Duke of Hanjun. Some former Tungning units, such as the rattan shield troops, joined the Qing army and fought the Russian Cossacks at Albazin. He died of illness in Beijing. His brother Zheng Kexue was ordered to rebury Koxinga and Zheng Jing in Quanzhou, the family's ancestral home, but Lady Huang failed to recover the family's property in Fujian, which local officials had taken. His descendants served as bannermen in Beijing until the Xinhai Revolution of 1911, then moved back to Anhai and Nan'an in southern Fujian. He appears as an antagonist in Louis Cha's novel The Deer and the Cauldron.
zheng-xiaoxu: Zheng was born on 2 May 1860 in Suzhou, Jiangsu, though his family traced its roots to Minhou, near Fuzhou in Fujian. He obtained the intermediate degree in the imperial examinations in 1882 and three years later joined the secretariat of the statesman Li Hongzhang. In 1891 he became secretary to the Chinese legation in Tokyo and went on to consular duties in Tsukiji, Osaka and Kobe, where he helped establish the Chinese guild. In Japan he met politicians and scholars such as Itō Hirobumi, Mutsu Munemitsu and Naitō Torajirō.

The First Sino-Japanese War forced him to leave Japan in 1894. He joined the secretariat of the reformer Zhang Zhidong in Nanjing, followed him to Beijing and took a post in the Zongli Yamen, the Qing foreign office. After the failure of the Hundred Days' Reform in 1898 he held important posts in central and southern China. When the imperial system collapsed in 1911 he refused to serve the Republic and retired to Shanghai, devoting himself to calligraphy, poetry and art and writing articles that called the Kuomintang leaders thieves.

In 1923 Puyi summoned him to Beijing to reorganise the imperial household. Zheng became a close adviser, helped arrange Puyi's flight to the foreign concession at Tianjin after General Feng Yuxiang expelled him from the Forbidden City, and met Japanese officials and the Black Dragon Society to discuss a Qing restoration in Manchuria. After the Mukden Incident of 1931 he helped found Manchukuo and wrote the words of its national anthem. He hoped it would be a springboard for restoring the Qing across China, but the Kwantung Army, its real rulers, did not share that aim.

Pressed to resign after repeated clashes with the Japanese army leadership, he left office in May 1935. He died suddenly on 28 March 1938 in unclear circumstances, which led to speculation that the Japanese had poisoned him, and was given a state funeral in April. Remembered chiefly for his collaboration, he was also one of the most respected calligraphers of the 20th century: he supported himself in later life by selling his work, his style appears in the logos of Chinese companies, and historians still value his extensive diary.
zheng-zhilong: Zheng Zhilong was born in Fujian, the son of Zheng Shaozu, a mid-level financial official, and Lady Huang. He left home as a teenager on a merchant ship, either because he wanted to or because his father threw him out for constant fighting, and went to his uncle in Macau, where he was baptised a Catholic as Nicholas Gaspard. Sent with cargo to Hirado in Japan, he met Li Dan, the city's Kapitan Cina, who found him work as an interpreter for the Dutch. In Japan he married Tagawa Matsu, who bore their son Koxinga in 1624.

In 1624 Zheng became a privateer for the Dutch East India Company, and after Li Dan's death in 1625 he took over his fleet and led the Chinese pirates unopposed. In 1625 he founded the Shibazhi, a band of eighteen pirate leaders. By 1627 he commanded four hundred junks and tens of thousands of men, and he sold protection passes to fishermen and merchants. In 1628 he defeated the Ming fleet, then switched to official service and was made a major general.

As Admiral of the Coastal Seas he defeated a force of Dutch ships and junks under the renegade Liu Xiang at the Battle of Liaoluo Bay on 22 October 1633. The spoils let him buy as much as 60% of the land of Fujian, and his annual income was later estimated at three to four times that of the whole Dutch East India Company. After the fall of Beijing in 1644 he stayed loyal to the Ming, and after Nanjing was captured in 1645 he was ordered to defend the new capital at Fuzhou under the Prince of Tang.

When he defected to the Manchus in 1646 he left the passes of Zhejiang unguarded, and Qing forces took Fuzhou. His brothers and Koxinga refused to follow him, and seeing that his army had not come over, the Qing placed him under house arrest and took him to Beijing; his bodyguard of former African slaves died trying to stop the arrest. Accounts differ on whether Tagawa Matsu was raped and then killed herself, or died directing the fight against the Qing at Anhai. Because Koxinga kept up his resistance, Zheng was beheaded at the Caishikou execution grounds in Beijing in 1661.
zhengtong-emperor: Zhu Qizhen was born on 29 November 1427, the elder of the two sons of the Xuande Emperor, the fifth emperor of the Ming dynasty. His mother, Lady Sun, was one of the emperor's concubines. He was designated heir on 20 February 1428, and his mother was promoted to empress in March. In 1433 the Ministry of War assembled a detachment of 7,112 youths aged 11 to 12, and the prince was appointed their commander. His teacher was likely the court eunuch Wang Zhen.

The Xuande Emperor died on 31 January 1435, when his son was eight. A proposal arose to place the late emperor's younger brother Zhu Zhanshan, Prince of Xiang, on the throne, and the 17th-century historian Mao Qiling claims that Empress Dowager Zhang supported him. Empress Sun intervened and prevented it, and Zhu Qizhen was crowned, the first child emperor of the Ming.

Because the dynasty's laws had no provision for a child ruler, Grand Empress Dowager Zhang became regent in effect, leading a council of the three grand secretaries known as the Three Yangs (Yang Shiqi, Yang Rong and Yang Pu) and three eunuchs. Later generations saw this period of stability as a golden age. After her death in 1442 the emperor listened more to Wang Zhen, who pushed the ageing grand secretaries aside after Yang Shiqi died in 1444 and Yang Pu two years later. Floods, droughts and famines struck in the late 1430s and 1440s, and rebellions broke out in Fujian in 1448.

In the summer of 1449 the Oirat leader Esen launched a large raid, and on 1 August the emperor ordered the Beijing garrison mobilised and resolved to lead the campaign himself, over the protest of the Minister of War Kuang Ye and his deputy Yu Qian. Esen's army defeated the Ming army at Tumu Fortress and captured him. On 17 September 1449 his brother Zhu Qiyu took the throne as the Jingtai Emperor and declared him Emperor Emeritus. Esen returned his prisoner in September 1450, and he was confined to the Southern Palace.

After the Jingtai Emperor fell ill in early 1457, Yingzong regained power in a palace coup and took the era name Tianshun. He gradually removed the coup's organisers, among them Xu Youzhen, dismissed in August 1457, and Cao Jixiang, executed for treason in August 1461. Many followers of his brother were falsely accused, among them Yu Qian. The purges made his regime unpopular. He died on 23 February 1464 and was succeeded by his eldest son, the Chenghua Emperor.
zhengzhou: Zhengzhou lies in north-central Henan, on the southern bank of the Yellow River, at the eastern foothills of the Xiong'er Mountains where the river's valley widens into the North China Plain. It borders Luoyang to the west, Kaifeng to the east and Xinxiang to the northeast. The city stands at the crossing of the north–south route skirting the Taihang Mountains and the mountains of western Henan. Its prefecture covers 7,567 km2, of which the city centre occupies 709.69 km2. It lies in the Zhongyuan region, an area inhabited continuously for over 4,000 years and regarded as a cradle of Chinese civilization.

Several city ruins from the early Shang dynasty have been found in the Zhengzhou area, including candidate sites for the early Shang capitals Ao, Bo or Yan. Since 1950 excavations at Zhengzhou Shang City, near the historical centre of the modern city, have provided evidence of Shang settlement around 1600 BCE. About 20 km to the northwest, remains of large public buildings and a complex of small settlements have been found at a site that some identify as the Shang capital of Ao. Parts of the Shang city wall, built some 3,600 years ago, still stand in the downtown.

After the Shang the area remained an important regional city because of its position on the North China Plain. The settlement was first known as Guancheng, the city of the Guan family, who held it as a city-state. It later became the seat of a prefecture under the Sui dynasty, and the character Zheng in its modern name refers to the Zheng state that once governed the region. In June 1938, during the Second Sino-Japanese War, Nationalist forces breached the dikes at Huayuankou, north of Zhengzhou, to slow the Japanese advance. The flood inundated large areas of Henan, Anhui and Jiangsu, and the Yellow River did not return to its original course until 1947.

Zhengzhou is the capital and largest city of Henan, with a population of about 12.6 million in the 2020 census. It is a main national transport hub, and it has been a major industrial city of the People's Republic since 1949, with textiles as its staple industry. The Zhengzhou Commodity Exchange, approved by the State Council in October 1990, was the first futures exchange in China. The Zhengzhou Confucius Temple, first built in the Eastern Han dynasty, is among the oldest Confucian temples in China. About 90 km southwest, in Dengfeng, the Shaolin Monastery and its Pagoda Forest were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010.
zhi-dun: Zhi Dun's birth surname was Guan and his courtesy name Daolin. Zhi is a surname that points to an origin among the Yuezhi or in the Kushan Empire, but his biography in the Liang-dynasty Memoirs of Eminent Monks says that his family came from Henan; he took the name on ordination, after the origin of his preceptor rather than his own. Kenneth Tanaka describes him as a respected scholar of Neo Daoist philosophy who became a Buddhist.

Erik Zürcher calls him the most representative of the gentleman-monks, men of the gentry class who became prominent monks in fourth-century China, schooled in the secular arts as well as Neo Daoism, pure conversation and exegesis. The Shishuo Xinyu tells that a friend gave him two young cranes. He clipped their wings so that they would not fly away, but seeing them despondent he let them go once their feathers had grown again.

In his works Zhi Dun explained the metaphysical meaning of li, the noumenon. One of his eulogies, translated by Zürcher, is the earliest surviving example of Chinese Pure Land Buddhism. It describes Sukhavati as a country without royal regulations, ranks or titles, where the Buddha is the ruler, and holds that whoever serves the Buddha, keeps the commandments, recites the scripture of Amitabha and vows to be reborn there will be transported there at death. He had a painting made as an object of his devotion.

His works were collected in ten juan, most of them now lost. Titles recorded in the Memoirs and in Lu Cheng's 5th-century collection, the Falun, include a treatise on wandering in the Mystery through the identity of emptiness with matter, a commentary on the Zhuangzi chapter Unfettering quoted in the Shishuo Xinyu, an essay of 365 on the death of his close friend Zhi Faqian, and a memorial of the same year to Emperor Ai of Jin asking leave to withdraw from the capital. A letter to a monk from Koguryŏ is the first record connecting that kingdom with Buddhism. He also left seventeen miscellaneous poems, and five of his poems are written in the style of Ruan Ji's Singing of My Cares.
zhizhi: Zhizhi's original name in Chinese transcription was Luandi Hutuwusi; he was of the Luandi clan and one of the Worthy Princes of the East. When his father, Xulüquanqu Chanyu, died in 60 BCE, power was seized by a distant relative, Woyanqudi. In 58 BCE Huhanye, a younger son of Xulüquanqu, revolted and made himself chanyu, and Woyanqudi took his own life soon after.

In 56 BCE Hutuwusi rose against his younger brother, took the title Zhizhi Chanyu and drove Huhanye out of the royal domain. Huhanye moved south, submitted to the Han in 53 BCE and used Chinese support against him. Zhizhi too offered tribute and sent a son as hostage, but the Han court favoured Huhanye. Growing weaker, Zhizhi began moving west in 49 BCE; he killed Yilimu, another claimant, fought the Wusun, gained control of the Dingling and made his capital among the Jiankun, who may have been the Yenisei Kirghiz.

By 44 BCE he was on the north slope of the Tian Shan. The Han returned his son, but for unknown reasons Zhizhi murdered the envoy who came with him. He made a marriage alliance with the rulers of Kangju near Lake Balkhash and led his tribe west; they suffered greatly from cold, and only 3,000 people arrived. With the Kangju he plundered the Wusun, then quarrelled with his hosts, killed several hundred of them, forced them to build him a fortress on the Dulaishui River and took tribute from Dayuan.

Fearing that Zhizhi meant to build a large empire, the Han commander of the Western Regions struck first. In 36 BCE the generals Chen Tang and Gan Yanshou led 40,000 men through Wusun territory to Kangju, near modern Taraz. They beat off Kangju raiders and a Xiongnu attack on their camp, then advanced on the city with shields and spears in front and crossbowmen behind, drained the moat and piled firewood against the palisade. The city fell, and Zhizhi was killed and beheaded; his head was presented to Emperor Yuan of Han at Chang'an.

During the battle an infantry unit on the Kangju side fought in a formation said to look like fish scales, which has led to speculation that its men were Greek hoplites from Dayuan; the evidence is inconclusive.
zhou-daguan: Zhou Daguan was a native of Yongjia, a name often used in his time for modern Wenzhou in Zhejiang. Other records call him Zhou Jianguan or Zhou Dake, and in later life he used the assumed name Thatched Courtyard Recluse. He was neither the first nor the last Chinese envoy to the Khmer Empire, and official Chinese records do not mention his mission. Little is known of his life after his return, though he may have lived until the 1350s.

He sailed from Mingzhou, today's Ningbo, on 20 February 1296 aboard a compass-guided ship, calling at Fuzhou, Guangzhou and Quanzhou and stopping in Champa. The ship then entered the Mekong and the Tonle Sap River to Kampong Chhnang, from where a small boat took him across Tonle Sap Lake to Yaśodharapura, or Angkor Thom, in August. He was received at the court of King Indravarman III, admitted to the Royal Palace though not to its inner part, lived near the north gate of the city, and travelled into the countryside. He left in July 1297, after eleven months.

He wrote his book, the Zhenla fengtu ji, within fifteen years of his return; the surviving text is believed to be about a third of the original. He describes a square city with five gates and a wide moat crossed by bridges lined with 54 figures pulling a nine-headed nāga, and above the gates five Buddha heads, the central one gilded. He notes that dress marked social class, that women carried on all trade, selling from mats in markets where officials collected rent, and that households cooked in earthen pots and ate from bowls of woven leaves. He recounts a royal procession in which Indravarman III stood on an elephant with gilded tusks, holding his sacred sword.

The sinologist Jean-Pierre Abel-Rémusat translated the book into French in 1819 and Paul Pelliot again in 1902; Pelliot's version, later revised, was itself translated into English and German. The linguist Peter Harris made the first direct translation from Chinese into modern English in 2007, and Chaloem Yongbunkiat published a Thai translation in 1967. Today the book is one of the most important sources for the understanding of historical Angkor and the Khmer Empire.
zhou-dynasty: In Chinese tradition the Zhou lineage began with Qi, the Lord of Millet (Houji), a culture hero credited with improving agriculture. Later chiefs settled at Bin and then moved to Zhou in the Wei River valley, which remained their heartland. Wen moved the capital to Feng, and his son Wu, with his ally Jiang Ziya, led an army of 45,000 men and 300 chariots across the Yellow River and defeated the Shang king Di Xin at the Battle of Muye. The Zhou made a member of the Shang royal family Duke of Song and appear to have spoken a language much like the Shang's.

King Wu died early, leaving a young heir, and the Duke of Zhou assisted his nephew King Cheng. When the Three Guards, Zhou princes stationed in the east, rebelled with Shang partisans, the Duke put them down and extended the kingdom eastward. He set up the fengjian system of hereditary fiefs and expounded the Mandate of Heaven. Over generations the kinship ties between the kings and the regional lords thinned, and peripheral states gained power on par with the Zhou.

In 771 BCE the Quanrong, joined by the Marquis of Shen, whose daughter King You had demoted as queen, sacked the capital Haojing and killed You. Nobles declared the marquis's grandson King Ping and moved the capital east to Wangcheng. Royal authority then declined. The court recognised Han, Zhao and Wei as independent states in 403 BCE, and in 344 BCE Duke Hui of Wei was the first to claim the title of king. Qin captured Wangcheng in 256 BCE and killed King Nan, traditionally the last Zhou king.

The Mandate of Heaven held that Heaven gave power to the one ruler who upheld harmony, and withdrew it from a king whose people suffered. The Zhou used it to justify replacing the Shang. Farming was done mainly by ordinary rural households owing labour, taxes and military service, with slaves a minority. Five ranks of nobility stood below the king: duke, marquis, count, viscount and baron.

The Zhou period is often seen as the high point of Chinese bronze casting, and in the Eastern Zhou the Hundred Schools of Thought arose, including Confucianism, Taoism, Mohism and Legalism. The ritual system called li was later set down in texts compiled under the Han.
zhou-enlai: Zhou was born on 5 March 1898 in Huai'an, Jiangsu, and studied at the Nankai Middle School in Tianjin. His Chinese biography makes him a leader of the Tianjin student protests of the May Fourth Movement, but many modern scholars think it unlikely that he took part. In 1924 he returned from Europe to join the Whampoa Military Academy at Guangzhou as its chief political officer, and he married Deng Yingchao on 8 August 1925.

After the split between Nationalists and Communists in 1927 he went underground. From 1929 he built a network of Communist cells in Shanghai, changing residence at least once a month. In the Jiangxi Soviet he reorganised the Red Army, and when the Communists abandoned it he organised the logistics of the withdrawal that became the Long March. In 1936 he helped bring about the Xi'an Incident through contact with Zhang Xueliang. During the war against Japan he led the Communist liaison office at the Nationalist capital, first at Wuhan and then at Chongqing.

After the People's Republic of China was proclaimed on 1 October 1949, Zhou became Premier and Minister of Foreign Affairs, holding the second post until 1958. He became the architect of early foreign policy. He cultivated Jawaharlal Nehru and helped formalise the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence from the 1954 Sino-Indian Agreement. At the Geneva Conference of 1954 he was credited with helping the powers reach the agreement ending the Indochina War, and at the Bandung Conference of 1955 he spoke for peace and the abolition of nuclear arms.

During the Cultural Revolution he was the main force keeping the government and economy running. He tried to protect scientists, academics and artists, though he could not shelter most officials in the institutions he controlled. After the fall of Lin Biao he was elected first-ranking Vice Chairman of the Party in 1973.

Zhou withdrew from public life after 13 January 1975 and died on 8 January 1976. He had willed that his ashes be scattered over the hills and rivers of his hometown, so there was no burial ceremony. After a single memorial on 15 January, further public mourning was prohibited. On 4 April 1976 thousands gathered at the Monument to the People's Heroes in Tiananmen Square to commemorate him, and some slogans attacked the Gang of Four and even Mao.
He has been remembered as a skilled negotiator and a pragmatic statesman. Deng Xiaoping held that without him the Cultural Revolution might have been worse, but might not have lasted as long.
zhou-fohai: Zhou Fohai was born on 29 May 1897 in Yuanling County. Between the ages of 17 and 22 he studied in Japan, at the Seventh Higher School Zoshikan, the forerunner of Kagoshima University, and then at Kyoto Imperial University. There he was drawn to Marxism, and on his return to China he became one of the founders of the Chinese Communist Party, attending its First Congress in Shanghai in July 1921. He left the party in 1924 for the Kuomintang, where he worked as a secretary in the central government's public relations department and kept close ties with its leftist wing under Wang Jingwei and Liao Zhongkai.

Zhou opposed Chiang Kai-shek's Northern Expedition and his conduct of the Second Sino-Japanese War. When Wang Jingwei broke with the Kuomintang and set up the collaborationist government at Nanjing, Zhou followed and became Vice Premier and Minister of Finance, with control over part of its army. He was Minister of Police until 1941 and in 1944 succeeded Chen Gongbo as Mayor of Shanghai, while keeping secret contacts with the Nationalists in Chongqing.

According to his associate Jin Xiongbai, editor of the newspaper Zhongbao, Zhou led the Nanjing network of the CC Clique and coordinated political appointments, so that his office held authority over diplomatic, financial, military and intelligence matters even where Chen Gongbo formally ranked above him. Jin also recorded his rivalry with the so-called Mansion Clique and his patronage of the intelligence chiefs Ding Mocun and Li Shiqun.

At the end of the war Zhou was captured and held in Chongqing for nearly a year, then tried for treason in Nanjing. He argued that in the first half of his service he had kept in touch with the enemy to help his country, and in the second half had worked against the enemy by keeping in contact with Chongqing. He was sentenced to death, but after his wife interceded Chiang Kai-shek commuted the sentence to life imprisonment. Suffering from heart and stomach problems, he died in prison on 28 February 1948, aged 50.
zhu-fan-zhi: Its author, Zhao, who lived from 1170 to 1231, was a member of the Song imperial clan posted to Fujian to supervise maritime trade at Quanzhou. There he met merchants of many countries, noted the goods they traded and studied the maps of his time. In his preface he wrote that he spent his days reading maps, listed the names and customs of the countries, and removed hearsay to keep the facts. He never travelled overseas himself, so his information is secondhand, unlike that of the Yuan traveller Wang Dayuan in the Daoyi Zhilüe.

Many entries draw on older works, among them Zhu Yu's Pingzhou Ketan of 1116 and Duan Chengshi's 9th-century Miscellaneous Morsels from Youyang, and above all the Lingwai Daida written in 1178 by the geographer Zhou Qufei.

The book has two volumes. The first describes 58 countries and regions and their customs: in South East Asia, Jiaozhi, Champa, Chenla, Langkasuka, Sanfoqi, Java and Bagan, as well as Japan, Korea and Taiwan, and in India Gujarat, Malabar and the Chola. It tells more than earlier Chinese sources about the Islamic world, describing Dashi, the Arabs, as a realm of 24 territories with its capital in Egypt, including Baghdad, Oman, Mecca and Ghazni. In Africa it names Egypt and Alexandria, with a long account of its lighthouse, Berbera, Zanzibar and Damietta, and its furthest western state is Mulanpi, the Al-Murabitun, which included southern Spain. Sicily is also mentioned.

The second volume lists 47 products, 22 of them from Central Asia and Africa. It explains, for example, that frankincense came from the remote mountains of Arabia, was carried by elephant to the coast and shipped to Sanfoqi, where it was traded on and so became known as a product of that country. Some passages are fanciful, such as a bird of Madagascar large enough to swallow a camel, probably taken from the Lingwai Daida.

The original book was lost, but extracts survived in other compilations and in the 15th-century Yongle Encyclopedia, from which Li Diaoyuan recompiled it for his collection Han Hai in 1781. Friedrich Hirth and William W. Rockhill published an annotated partial English translation in 1911, and Shao-yun Yang a new annotated translation of the first volume in 2020.
zhu-wen: Zhu Wen was born on 5 December 852, the youngest of three sons of Zhu Cheng, an instructor in the Five Classics in Dangshan County. His father died while he was a boy, and his mother took her sons to the household of Liu Chong of Xiao County. He formed a bandit gang and in about 877 joined the rebel army of Huang Chao. After Huang Chao took the capital Chang'an in January 881, Zhu received a separate command and captured Tong Prefecture.

By 882 Huang Chao was effectively surrounded. Zhu surrendered to the Tang governor Wang Chongrong. Emperor Xizong of Tang rewarded him with a command and a new name, Quanzhong, wholeheartedly loyal. On 3 May 883 he was appointed military governor of Xuanwu Circuit at Bian Prefecture, the modern Kaifeng. In spring 884 he and Li Keyong, chief of the Shatuo Turks, routed Huang Chao's generals. On the night of 11 June 884 Zhu tried to have Li Keyong assassinated, which began a struggle of forty years between their houses.

He destroyed rival warlords such as Qin Zongquan, Shi Pu, Zhu Xuan and Zhu Jin. In 902 he besieged Li Maozhen at Fengxiang, where Emperor Zhaozong of Tang was held, and in 903 Li Maozhen handed the emperor over; all the palace eunuchs were then slaughtered. In spring 904 Zhu forced the emperor, his household and the people of Chang'an to move to Luoyang. That autumn he had Emperor Zhaozong murdered and a child, Emperor Ai of Tang, enthroned. Nine of the dead emperor's sons were killed, and some 30 senior officials of aristocratic family were forced to commit suicide at Baima and their bodies thrown into the Yellow River.

The deposed Emperor Ai was made Prince of Jiyin and poisoned in 908. Most circuits submitted to the new emperor, but the realms of Li Keyong, Li Maozhen, Yang Wo and Wang Jian did not. A siege of the Jin city of Lu was broken in 908 by Li Keyong's son Li Cunxu, and in spring 911 the Later Liang army was crushed at Boxiang.

The histories describe him as violent towards his subordinates and say that he raped the wives of his officers and of his own sons. In summer 912, gravely ill, he meant to leave the throne to his adoptive son Zhu Youwen and ordered another son, Zhu Yougui, away from the capital. Fearing execution, Zhu Yougui led imperial guards into the palace and killed him on 18 July 912.
zhu-xi: Zhu Xi was born in Fujian on 18 October 1130, where his father worked as subprefectural sheriff. His family originated in Wuyuan County, Huizhou, in modern Jiangxi province. After his father was forced from office in 1140 for opposing the government's appeasement policy towards the Jurchen, Zhu Xi was taught at home by him. When his father died in 1143, he studied with his father's friends Hu Xian, Liu Zihui and Liu Mianzhi. In 1148, at the age of 19, he passed the imperial examination and became a presented scholar (jinshi). From 1153 he studied under Li Tong, who followed the Neo-Confucian tradition of Cheng Hao and Cheng Yi, and he became Li's formal student in 1160.

Zhu Xi's first official post was Subprefectural Registrar of Tong'an, from 1153 to 1156. He then held no office until 1179, when he was appointed Prefect of Nankang Military District and revived the White Deer Grotto Academy. Three years later he was demoted for attacking the incompetence and corruption of some influential officials. After his last dismissal he was accused of numerous crimes and a petition was made for his execution, with much of the opposition led by the Prime Minister Han Tuozhou, a political rival. He wrote, compiled and edited almost a hundred books and taught groups of students, many of whom studied under him for years.

Rather than concentrating on the I Ching as other Neo-Confucians did, Zhu Xi emphasised the Four Books: the Great Learning, the Doctrine of the Mean, the Analects and the Mencius. His commentaries on them were not widely recognised in his time but later became the standard ones, and from 1313 to 1905 they formed the basis of the civil service examinations. He held that all things arise from the union of qi, a vital or material force, and li, a rational principle, and that the source and sum of li is the taiji, the Supreme Ultimate. Qi obscures each person's perfect moral nature, so moral cultivation means clearing the qi. He advocated the investigation of things and practised a daily meditation called jingzuo.

He died on 23 April 1200. Almost a thousand people attended his funeral, although his teachings had been severely attacked. In 1208 Emperor Ningzong of Song rehabilitated him, and in 1241 a memorial tablet was placed to him in the Confucian Temple at Qufu. His teaching became influential in Japan, where it is called Shushigaku, in Korea, where it became an orthodoxy known as Jujahak, and in Vietnam.
zhu-youzhen: Zhu Youzhen was born at Bian Prefecture, modern Kaifeng, the fourth son of the warlord Zhu Quanzhong and the only known son of his wife Lady Zhang. He was described as handsome, quiet and fond of scholars. When his father ended the Tang dynasty in 907 and founded the Later Liang as Emperor Taizu, Zhu Youzhen became Prince of Jun and a commander of the new imperial guard, the Tianxing Army. In 912 his brother Zhu Yougui murdered Taizu and, keeping the death secret, ordered Zhu Youzhen in their father's name to kill the adopted son Zhu Youwen, which he did.

When his brother-in-law Zhao Yan and cousin Yuan Xiangxian plotted against Zhu Yougui, Zhu Youzhen joined them and won over Yang Shihou, military governor of Tianxiong. Yuan and Zhao rose at Luoyang and killed Zhu Yougui, and Zhu Youzhen took the throne at Daliang, later renaming himself Zhu Zhen. His attempt to split Tianxiong Circuit after Yang's death in 915 led its soldiers to mutiny and hand it to Jin, and by autumn 916 nearly all Later Liang territory north of the Yellow River had fallen to Li Cunxu. He survived a mutiny at Daliang and an assassination plot by his brother Zhu Youjing, and afterwards trusted only Zhao and the brothers and cousins of his late Consort Zhang, ignoring the senior chancellor Jing Xiang.

The battle at Huliu Slope early in 919 was a draw in which each side lost two-thirds of its army. Zhu Zhen had his general Liu Xun poisoned in 920, suspecting him of sparing a rebel. In 921 he declined Jing Xiang's advice to aid Zhang Wenli of Zhao against Jin, though Dai Siyuan's capture of Wei Prefecture briefly restored a foothold north of the river.

In 923 Li Cunxu proclaimed the Later Tang and Li Siyuan seized Yun Prefecture. Zhu Zhen replaced his commanders, breached the Yellow River levee at Hua Prefecture, and approved Duan Ning's four-pronged counterattack, but the officer Kang Yanxiao defected and revealed that it left Daliang undefended. Li Cunxu defeated Wang Yanzhang and Zhang Hanjie at Zhongdu and marched on the capital. Seeing no hope, Zhu Zhen ordered his general Huangfu Lin to kill him, and Huangfu then took his own life. Li Cunxu buried the body with respect but kept the head in the imperial temple until Shi Jingtang of the Later Jin had it buried. Sima Guang judged him temperate and frugal but ruined by trusting Zhao and the Zhangs.
zhuanxu: Zhuanxu, also called Gaoyang, is a mythological emperor of ancient China, counted by many sources among the Five Emperors. In the account of Sima Qian he was a grandson of the Yellow Emperor and Leizu through their son Changyi. His mother is named Changpu of the Shushan clan by Sima Qian and Niuqu in the Bamboo Annals, while the Classic of Mountains and Seas makes him a son of Hanliu, in a passage written last. He is said to have led the Shi clan east to Shandong at the age of ten with Shaohao.

Sima Qian says that when the Yellow Emperor died, Zhuanxu was chosen as the tribe's new leader in preference to his father and all his uncles, and that his uncle Shaohao never reigned. The Bamboo Annals instead make him an assistant to Shaohao at ten and a king in his own right at twenty. Some sources give him a reign of seventy-eight years. He defeated Gonggong, a descendant of the Emperor Yan.

Zhuanxu is credited with introducing sacrifice to the soil and grain, which stayed essential to Chinese government until the fall of the Qing, and with religious reform against shamanism, a unified calendar, a patriarchal order and a ban on marriage between close kin. The Bamboo Annals say that in the thirteenth year of his reign he invented calendric calculations, and the Qin called their calendar the zhuanxuli after him. He is also linked with the separation of heaven and earth: the Book of Documents says the Lord on High had Chong and Li cut communication between them. Some mythologists read this as a sign of growing social stratification between Yangshao and Longshan culture.

Zhuanxu was succeeded by his cousin Ku, a grandson of Shaohao. According to Sima Qian his line included a son derided as Taowu, and Qiongchan, from whom Emperor Shun descended. Gun, father of Yu the Great, was another descendant. Many ruling houses claimed him as an ancestor, among them the Mi of Chu and Yue, the Ying of Qin, the Cao of Wei and the Qian of Wuyue. The Samguk Sagi says the kings of Goguryeo regarded themselves as descended from Chinese heroes including Gaoyang.
zhuge-liang: Zhuge Liang's ancestral home was in Yangdu County, Langya Commandery, in present-day Shandong. Orphaned young, he was raised by Zhuge Xuan, a cousin of his father, whom he accompanied to Jing Province, where Zhuge Xuan lived with the governor Liu Biao. Zhuge Liang later lived in seclusion at Longzhong and earned the sobriquet Sleeping Dragon. The hermit Sima Hui and Xu Shu both recommended him to the warlord Liu Bei, who visited him three times. Zhuge Liang then proposed the Longzhong Plan: to secure Jing and Yi provinces, ally with Eastern Wu and resist Cao Wei.

In the autumn of 208 Cao Cao invaded Jing Province. Liu Bei fled to Xiakou, was defeated at the Battle of Changban, and sent Zhuge Liang to Sun Quan to propose an alliance. Sun Quan sent Zhou Yu, Cheng Pu, Lu Su and others with 30,000 troops, and in the winter of 208 the allies won a decisive victory over Cao Cao at the Battle of Red Cliffs. Defeated at the Battle of Xiaoting in 222, Liu Bei fell ill and in early 223 summoned Zhuge Liang, telling him to assist the heir but to make his own decision if the heir proved incompetent.

As regent for Liu Shan, Zhuge Liang refused letters from Wei officials urging Shu to submit. In 225 to 227 he led a southern campaign into Nanzhong against rebellions, following Ma Su's advice to win the hearts of the people. In 227 he sent Liu Shan the memorial Chu Shi Biao and gathered troops at Hanzhong. In 228 his army reached Mount Qi, and three Wei commanderies went over to Shu. In 234 he camped more than 100,000 troops on the Wuzhang Plains, where soldiers grew crops alongside civilians.

After a stalemate of more than 100 days, Zhuge Liang became critically ill and died in camp, between 11 September and 10 October 234, aged 54 by East Asian reckoning. Liu Shan gave him the posthumous title Marquis Zhongwu. As governor of Yi Province he ruled by strict law and helped write the legal codes of Shu Han. The Chu Shi Biao is regarded as a masterpiece of Chinese prose. In the 14th-century Romance of the Three Kingdoms he is a near-sage of wisdom and loyalty, and temples to the Marquis of Wu stand in Chengdu and Baidicheng.
zia-ol-din-tabatabaee: Zia was born in Shiraz in June 1889 and grew up mostly in Tabriz, where his father, Seyyed Ali Tabataba'i Yazdi, was an influential cleric. At sixteen he started his first newspaper, Nedaye Islam, and later Ra'ad, Shargh and Bargh, which attacked leading politicians of the Qajar monarchy and were closed several times; he took part in the Persian Constitutional Revolution. After a stay in Europe, mainly in France, he revived Ra'ad and supported the British during the war. In 1917 he was sent to St. Petersburg, where he witnessed the Bolshevik Revolution.
