After the coup Ahmad Shah Qajar appointed him prime minister, and he formed his cabinet on 24 February 1921. The new government declared a state of siege, stopped the newspapers, closed bars, theatres and gambling clubs, and with Reza Khan arrested some four hundred rich men and aristocrats, whom Zia accused of having sucked the blood of the people. His programme spoke of forming an army, ending the capitulations, friendly ties with the Soviet Union, land reform, education for every Iranian and a legal system modernised on European lines, under a commission headed by Mohammad Ali Foroughi.

Money for these plans was lacking. The ban on alcohol and the closing of shops on Fridays angered merchants, and the families of the arrested campaigned against what they called the black cabinet. Ahmad Shah turned against him, and on 23 May 1921 Reza Khan asked him to resign and leave the country. His government had lasted 93 days.

In exile he sold carpets in Berlin and Montreux, and in December 1931 he was elected Secretary General of the World Islamic Congress in Jerusalem, where he and Amin al-Husseini tried and failed to raise money for an Islamic university. He then farmed in Palestine. He returned to Iran in 1943 and in his last fifteen years advised Mohammad Reza Pahlavi. He openly called himself a friend of the British, arguing that their friendship cost a price while their enmity meant destruction. He died of a heart attack in Tehran on 29 August 1969 and was buried at the Shah Abdol-Azim Shrine in Ray.
ziauddin-barani: Barani came from an Indian Muslim family of Baran, which gave him his nisba; his ancestors had come there from Kaithal in Haryana but regarded Baran as their home. His family served the sultans of Delhi in high posts. His maternal grandfather Husam-ud-Din was an important officer of Balban, his father Muwayyid-ul-Mulk was naib to Arkali Khan, son of Jalal-ud-Din Firuz Khalji, and his uncle Qazi Ala-ul-Mulk was kotwal, or police chief, of Delhi under Ala-ud-Din Khalji. Barani himself never held office. As a companion of Muhammad bin Tughluq he was close to the poet Amir Khusrau.

The Fatwa-i-Jahandari is written as advice to Muslim kings on how to earn religious merit and the gratitude of their subjects. It holds that religion and temporal government are twins. Scholars read its defence of aristocracy by birth differently: M. Athar Ali saw its model in Sassanid Iran rather than in race or caste, while Muzaffar Alam argued that Barani chose it to serve the narrow interests of the early Muslim regime in India. Barani also divided law into the Sharia and the Zawabit, state laws made by the monarch with the nobility, which in his view had to keep to the spirit of the Sharia.

The Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, completed in 1357, covers the sultanate from Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq to the first six years of Firuz Shah Tughluq. It presents the sultans who followed Barani's rules as succeeding and those who sinned as meeting their downfall. Because he did not consult contemporary works, his accounts of Ala-ud-Din Khalji's wars at Chittor, Ranthambhor and Malwa and of Malik Kafur's Deccan campaigns are sketchy. His other works include the Hasratnama and the Sana-i-Muhammadi.

After Muhammad bin Tughluq's death Barani wrote his two works on government, religion and history in the hope of winning the favour of Firuz Shah Tughluq, but he received no reward. His gravestone lies in the courtyard of the dargah of Nizamuddin Auliya in Delhi, near the tomb of Amir Khusrau. Later historians, among them Nizam-ud-Din Ahmad, Abd al-Qadir Badayuni and Firishta, relied on his Tarikh for the period, and Abd al-Haqq al-Dehlawi drew on it for his lives of Nizam-ud-Din Auliya and other Sufi saints.
ziaur-rahman: Ziaur Rahman was born on 19 January 1936 in the village of Bagbari in Gabtali, Bogura District. He graduated from the Pakistan Military Academy in September 1955 and was commissioned in the Pakistan Army, serving in the Punjab Regiment and from 1957 in the East Bengal Regiment. In June 1969 he was posted to Chittagong as second-in-command of the 8th East Bengal Regiment.

After the army crackdown and the arrest of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman on 26 March 1971, he revolted, and on 27 March he broadcast the declaration of independence from the Kalurghat radio station, becoming known as the Announcer of the Liberation. He commanded Sector 1 of the Bangladesh Forces, then Sector 11 from June and Z Force from mid-July.

After Mujibur Rahman was assassinated on 15 August 1975, Ziaur Rahman became Chief of Army Staff. A coup on 3 November forced him out and put him under house arrest, and on 7 November the Sipahi-Janata Revolution freed him and returned him to the post. He then held de facto power under martial law, took over the presidency on 21 April 1977 and retired from the army in 1978 as a lieutenant general.

Ziaur Rahman lifted martial law and in 1978 won a five-year term as president; elections to the National Assembly followed the next year, and opponents questioned their integrity. In 1978 he founded the Bangladesh Nationalist Party and reinstated multi-party politics and freedom of the press. He announced a 19-point programme stressing self-reliance, rural development, decentralisation, free markets and population control, set up village councils called Gram Sarkar, and launched a food-for-work programme in 1977.

He improved relations with the West and China and moved away from Mujib's close alignment with India. He also amended the constitution to open its preamble with an invocation of Allah and to replace the commitment to secularism with trust and faith in Almighty Allah. Critics say this changed the nature of the republic.

Ziaur Rahman faced many coup attempts, for which military tribunals were set up and at least 200 soldiers of the army and air force were executed. On 29 May 1981 he travelled to Chittagong to settle a dispute in the regional BNP and stayed at the Circuit House. In the early hours of 30 May a group of army officers assassinated him; six bodyguards and two aides were also killed. Nearly two million people are estimated to have attended his funeral. Opinion on his legacy is divided: he is credited with ending disorder and restoring multi-party politics, while critics say he suppressed opposition and gave posts to men accused in the killing of Mujibur Rahman.
ziebice: The area became part of the emerging Polish state under its first historic ruler, Mieszko I, in the 10th century. The town was first mentioned in 1234 under the Old Polish spelling Sambice. This Polish town was probably destroyed in 1241 during the first Mongol invasion of Poland. According to records, a new town under German town law followed, called Munsterberck in 1253 and Sambiz videlicet Munsterberg in 1268. It became home to a German-speaking population as a result of Ostsiedlung.

As Poland fragmented, the town formed part of the duchies of Silesia until 1290 and of Świdnica until 1322. It then became the capital of a small duchy of its own and remained under the rule of the Piast dynasty until 1521. In 1344 the Piast dukes established a court in the town. In 1521 it passed to the Podiebrad family. The town suffered in the Hussite Wars and the Thirty Years' War, and in 1643 it was hit by an epidemic.

In 1742 Münsterberg became part of Prussia and the capital of Kreis Münsterberg. In 1871 it became part of the German Empire with the bulk of Silesia. After World War II the town returned to Poland in 1945, under a Soviet-installed communist regime, and the German population was expelled. The Polish anti-communist resistance was active in Ziębice in the following years.

Ziębice lies in Ząbkowice County, in the Lower Silesian Voivodeship of south-western Poland. It has an Old Town with a preserved Market Square and the Romanesque-Gothic Saint George Basilica, listed as a Historic Monument of Poland, and it holds Poland's only Museum of Home Appliances.
ziggurat: The word ziggurat comes from the Akkadian ziqqurratum, from a verb meaning to protrude or to build high. Before the ziggurats there were raised platforms, which date from the Ubaid period in the sixth millennium BCE. The ziggurats began as platforms, usually oval, rectangular or square. Ziggurats mark Mesopotamian cities from about 2200 until 500 BCE. The Great Ziggurat of Ur was built by King Ur-Nammu in about the 21st century BCE, in the period of the Third Dynasty of Ur, and dedicated to Nanna, or Sîn. Sumerians, Akkadians, Kassites, Elamites, Eblaites and Babylonians all built them for local religions.

A ziggurat was a terraced structure of receding stories, each step slightly smaller than the one below. Its core was of sun-baked brick with a facing of fired brick on the outside. The facings were often glazed in different colours, which may have had astrological significance, and kings sometimes had their names engraved on the bricks. The number of levels ranged from two to seven. Each ziggurat stood in a temple complex that included a courtyard, storage rooms, bathrooms and living quarters, around which a city spread.

Designs ranged from a simple base carrying a temple, such as the White Temple of Uruk, to tall structures of many terraces. The ziggurat at Babylon, called Etemenanki, meant House of the foundation of heaven and earth in Sumerian. Chogha Zanbil in western Iran is one of the best-preserved examples.

The Mesopotamians believed the ziggurat was a dwelling place of the gods, and each city had its own patron god. It was not a place for public worship. Only priests could enter the ziggurat or the rooms at its base, and it was their duty to care for the gods and attend to their needs. The priests were very powerful members of Sumerian and Assyro-Babylonian society. Access to the top was by ramps on one side or by a spiral ramp.

The archaeologist Harriet Crawford observes that the only evidence for a shrine on top comes from Herodotus, and no physical remains of one exist, since erosion has reduced the surviving ziggurats to a fraction of their height. She suggests as a working hypothesis that small shrines stood on the highest stages. Scholars also suggest that the height offered priests refuge from the annual floods.
ziggurat-of-ur: The Sumerian name of the ziggurat was Etemenniguru, meaning house whose foundation creates terror. King Ur-Nammu of the Third Dynasty of Ur dedicated it to Nanna, the moon god and patron deity of Ur, in about the 21st century BCE on the short chronology. It was part of a temple complex that served as an administrative centre for the city. Its completion fell to King Shulgi, who proclaimed himself a god to win the allegiance of cities, and during his 48-year reign Ur became the capital of a state controlling much of Mesopotamia.

The Sumerian structure was a massive stepped pyramid measuring 64 metres in length, 45 metres in width and over 30 metres in height, though the height is speculative, since only the foundations survived. By the 6th century BCE it had crumbled to ruins. King Nabonidus, the last king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, found little left but the last stage and nothing to guide him as to its original appearance, and had it restored in seven stages rather than three.

What remains is a three-layered solid mass of mud brick faced with burnt bricks set in bitumen. The lowest layer corresponds to Ur-Nammu's construction, and the two upper layers belong to the Neo-Babylonian restoration. It is the best preserved of the ziggurats known from Mesopotamia after that of Dur Untash (Chogha Zanbil).

William Loftus rediscovered the remains in 1850, and John Taylor's excavations in the 1850s led to the identification of the site as Ur. Sir Leonard Woolley excavated it extensively between 1922 and 1934 for the University Museum of the University of Pennsylvania and the British Museum. In the 1980s the facade of the lowest level and the monumental staircase were rebuilt under Saddam Hussein. Small arms fire in the Gulf War of 1991 damaged the rebuilt ziggurat, leaving over 400 bullet holes in its walls.
zimbabwe: Zimbabwe is a landlocked country between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers, bordered by South Africa, Botswana, Zambia and Mozambique. Most of it sits on the Zimbabwean Plateau, generally over 1,000 metres high. The Eastern Highlands are mountainous, and Mount Nyangani, at 2,592 metres, is the highest point. About 20 per cent of the country is low-lying veld under 900 metres. Victoria Falls lies in the extreme north-west on the Zambezi. The climate is subtropical, the rainy season runs from late October to March, and the country faces recurring droughts.

The earliest known inhabitants were most likely the San, who left arrowheads and cave paintings, and Bantu-speaking farmers arrived approximately 2,000 years ago. Societies speaking proto-Shona languages emerged in the middle Limpopo valley in the 9th century, and the plateau became the centre of Shona states from about the 10th century. Trade with Arab merchants on the coast helped develop the Kingdom of Mapungubwe in the 13th century. By 1300 the Kingdom of Zimbabwe eclipsed it, building on its stone architecture at Great Zimbabwe, near Masvingo. These states traded gold, ivory and copper for cloth and glass.

From about 1450 to 1760 the Kingdom of Mutapa ruled much of present-day Zimbabwe and parts of central Mozambique. The British South Africa Company of Cecil Rhodes demarcated Rhodesia in 1890 and conquered Matabeleland in 1893 after the First Matabele War. Southern Rhodesia became a self-governing colony in 1923, and in 1965 the white minority government unilaterally declared independence as Rhodesia. A 15-year guerrilla war ended in a peace agreement, and Zimbabwe gained sovereignty in April 1980.

Robert Mugabe became Prime Minister in 1980 and was President from 1987 until he resigned in 2017 following a coup. The name comes from a Shona term for Great Zimbabwe, often explained as dzimba-dza-mabwe, houses of stones; the archaeologist Peter Garlake instead derives it from dzimba-hwe, venerated houses. The Shona are about 82 per cent of the population and the Ndebele 14 per cent. Zimbabwe has 16 official languages, of which English, Shona and Ndebele are most used, and its population is roughly 17.3 million.
zimbabwe-african-national-union: ZANU was founded on 8 August 1963 at the house of Enos Nkala in Highfield, Salisbury, when Ndabaningi Sithole, Henry Hamadziripi, Mukudzei Midzi, Herbert Chitepo, Edgar Tekere and Leopold Takawira decided to break with the Zimbabwe African People's Union, dissatisfied with the tactics of Nkomo, ZAPU's leader. At first both parties drew members from the Shona and the Ndebele. Each had a political wing inside the country and a military wing abroad: ZANU's Zimbabwe African National Liberation Army operated from Mozambique and Zambia, ZAPU's Zimbabwe People's Revolutionary Army from Zambia and Botswana.

Through the 1970s the leadership was based in exile, with offices in Lusaka, Dar es Salaam, Maputo and London. In 1973 Nathan Shamuyarira and others left for the Front for the Liberation of Zimbabwe after his bid for the leadership was defeated by Chitepo. After Chitepo was assassinated on 18 March 1975, Sithole took over, but as a proponent of détente he faced opposition from the more militant wing, and in the Mgagao Declaration ZANLA's leaders and guerrillas rejected him.

The party then split, both sides keeping the name. Sithole's group renounced armed struggle and in 1979 joined the transitional government of Bishop Abel Muzorewa, then took part with him in the Lancaster House Agreement. The faction of Robert Mugabe and Simon Muzenda, backed by ZANLA, formed the Patriotic Front with ZAPU in 1976 and became known as ZANU–PF.

At the 1980 general election in the newly constituted state of Zimbabwe, ZANU–PF won a majority, with ZAPU, registered as PF–ZAPU, second, while Sithole's group, registered as ZANU, won no seats. ZAPU merged into ZANU–PF in 1987. Sithole's party later won a few seats as ZANU–Ndonga, a minor party with its support among the Ndau.
zimbabwe-african-peoples-union: ZAPU was formed on 17 December 1961, ten days after the Rhodesian government banned the National Democratic Party. Joshua Nkomo was its president, Samuel Parirenyatwa vice-president, Ndabaningi Sithole chairman, Jason Moyo treasurer, Robert Mugabe information and publicity secretary and Leopold Takawira external secretary. The white minority government banned the party in 1962, and ZAPU later took up a guerrilla war against it.

Its armed wing, the Zimbabwe People's Revolutionary Army (ZIPRA), was founded by Moyo and commanded by General Lookout Masuku. ZIPRA was aligned with the Soviet Union and put its effort into mobilising urban workers, while the rival Zimbabwe African National Union looked to the People's Republic of China and worked among the rural peasantry. The difference in outlook kept the two movements apart through the war for majority rule.

In the 1980 elections ZAPU stood as the Patriotic Front and lost to ZANU. After the Gukurahundi massacres the two parties signed the Unity Accord and merged in 1987 as the Zimbabwe African National Union-Patriotic Front (ZANU-PF). The accord made Robert Gabriel Mugabe first secretary and president of the united party, committed it to a socialist society on Marxist-Leninist principles and to a one-party state, and bound both parties to end the insecurity and violence in Matabeleland.

In October 2008, led by Benny Ncube and Dumiso Dabengwa, a group of former PF ZAPU and ZIPRA members pressed to leave the alliance, and a meeting on 8 November decided that the party would again operate as ZAPU under its own constitution. Former ZIPRA fighters also left the Zimbabwe National Liberation War Veterans Association and revived ZIPRA as an association. A convention on 13–14 December 2008 elected Dabengwa interim chairperson, a congress on 16 May 2009 endorsed the withdrawal from ZANU-PF, and a congress in August 2010 elected Dabengwa president and Emilia Mukaratirwa vice-president.
zimri-lim: Zimri-Lim belonged to the clan of Yahdun-Lim, who headed the tribal confederation of the Bensimalites, and was probably Yahdun-Lim's nephew or grandson. His name is Amorite and means 'the tribe is my help' or 'the tribe is my strength'. When Samsi-Addu ousted his family from Mari, he spent some fifteen years in exile, probably in the kingdom of Yamhad or under its protection. He was likely a teenager when the family fled, since by his accession he already had daughters of marriageable age.

His mother was Addu-duri, who died in the sixth year of his reign and who managed the palace when he was away. His father was Hadni-Addu, about whom little is known, though Zimri-Lim officially presented Yahdun-Lim as his father to support his claim to the throne.

The death of Samsi-Addu in 1775 BCE set off revolts that brought down his kingdom. Zimri-Lim set out for Mari with the Bensimalites who had fled earlier, advancing along the Euphrates through Tuttul and Terqa, and was crowned at Terqa in the temple of the god Dagan. He then resisted Eshnunna, put down a revolt of the Benjaminite tribes that began in 1773, and consolidated his authority over the small kingdoms of Upper Mesopotamia as a 'great king' equal to the other major powers. His rival Ishme-Dagan lost the throne of Ekallatum and fled to Babylon.

Zimri-Lim ruled a dual entity, as king of Mari and as leader of the Bensimalites, some of whom lived as nomads. He pursued alliances, marrying several of his daughters to vassals, consulted oracles frequently, and relied on a palace administration in which Queen Shibtu, from Aleppo, had a major role. In 1765 he allied with Hammurabi of Babylon to lead a coalition that defeated an invading Elamite force at Hiritum. The royal palace at Mari, covering about 25,000 square metres, was the centre of the kingdom, and its archives make his reign one of the best documented in ancient history.

Tension between Mari and Babylon grew as Babylon sought influence further north. In 1762, when Babylon captured Eshnunna, Zimri-Lim appears to have sided with Eshnunna against his ally Hammurabi, which could explain why he became a target himself. He probably died during the capture of Mari in 1761 BCE, which preceded the city's destruction.

After the fall of Mari, the region regained its independence under the Kings of Hana, one of whom bore the name Zimri-Lim. The king also appears in a Babylonian literary text, known only in fragments, that tells of Hammurabi's capture of Mari and Eshnunna.
zinder: Zinder lies 861 km east of the capital Niamey and 240 km north of the Nigerian city of Kano. Locally it is also called Damagaram. The centre consists of three main areas. In the north is Zengou, or Zango, the old Tuareg suburb, known for its vernacular architecture. In the south lies Birni, the old Hausa town, which holds the Zinder Great Mosque, Fort Tanimoune, the Sultan's Palace and a museum. Between them is Sabon Gari, the new town, which is the commercial centre and has a large market, the Grand Marché. The city has many distinctive granite rocks and a long history of water shortages.

The site was first a small Hausa village called Zengou. The town grew greatly in importance after Kanuri aristocrats arrived in 1736, built a fortified quarter named Birni to the south and made Zinder the capital of the Sultanate of Damagaram. It became an important centre of the trans-Saharan trade, with routes south through Kano and east to Bornu. The sultanate stayed nominally subject to the Borno Empire until the mid-to-late 19th century, when Sultan Tanimoune Dan Souleymane declared independence and began a period of vigorous expansion.

Europeans reached the region in the 19th century, beginning with the German explorer Heinrich Barth, who stayed in Zinder in 1851. The French explorer Marius Gabriel Cazemajou was killed in the city in 1897. After a brief resistance Zinder was occupied in July 1899 by Lt. Pallier of the Voulet-Chanoine mission. The French barracks was called Fort Cazemajou, and it served as the capital of the Niger Military Territory when that was created in 1911. In 1926 the capital was moved back to the village of Niamey, after fears of Hausa revolts and as relations improved with the Djerma of the west. After Niger became independent the fort was renamed for Sultan Tanimoune.

The city's economy rests largely on the agriculture of its surroundings. It is divided into five urban municipalities, Zinder I to Zinder V, and has an airport a few kilometres to the southwest and the André-Salifou University, founded in 2010. The oil refinery SORAZ, commissioned in November 2011, stands 50 km to the north and was the country's first.
zionism: The word Zion derives from Mount Zion, a hill in Jerusalem named in the Hebrew Bible, and has been used poetically for the Land of Israel since the Babylonian Exile. Religious tradition held that a future messianic age would bring a return to Zion, recalled in the phrase next year in Jerusalem, and that the return should come through Divine Providence rather than human action. Forerunners of Zionism were thinkers and activists such as the rabbis Judah Alkalai and Zvi Hirsch Kalischer, whose Seeking Zion of 1862 was the first written work to demand mass migration of Jews to Palestine.

Modern Zionism emerged in Central and Eastern Europe as a secular nationalist movement in the late 19th century, in reaction to new waves of antisemitism and in response to the Haskalah, or Jewish Enlightenment. By the early 20th century the movement, led by Theodor Herzl, tied this national revival to Palestine, then under Ottoman rule.

Fundamental to Zionism is the belief that Jews constitute a nation with a right and need of self-determination. Early Zionism was ambiguous about the form this would take: the Basel declaration spoke of a Jewish homeland and the Balfour Declaration of 1917 of a national home, and according to Shlomo Avineri a sovereign state became the fully articulated goal only in the 1930s.

Zionist views have not been uniform. The mainstream has included Liberal, Labor, Revisionist and Cultural Zionism. Revisionist Zionism, developed by Ze'ev Jabotinsky, who founded the Revisionist Party in 1925, sought a state on both sides of the Jordan and held that Arab resistance would have to be met with an iron wall of military force. Cultural Zionism, founded by Ahad Ha'am, looked to Palestine as a spiritual and cultural centre, and Religious Zionism, associated with Abraham Isaac Kook, combines religious conservatism with nationalism.

Britain's 1917 Balfour Declaration supported a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine, and the 1922 Mandate placed Britain in control until 1948, when the State of Israel declared its independence and war broke out. Advocates view Zionism as a national liberation movement for the return of an indigenous people to the homeland of its ancestors. Opponents often describe it as a colonialist or racist ideology; scholars such as Edward Said and Joseph Massad place it within European colonialism, while Anita Shapira and Shlomo Ben-Ami frame it as a liberation movement that used colonial methods. Before the Second World War many Jews also opposed it, among them Orthodox Jews, who held that it pre-empted the Messiah.
zipaquira: Zipaquirá is a municipality and city in the department of Cundinamarca, about 48 kilometres north of Bogotá, to which it is linked by road and by train. It lies in the Greater Bogotá Metropolitan Area and is the capital of the Sabana Centro province and the seat of a diocese. In Chibcha, the language of the Muisca, the name means the land of the zipa, the ruler of the territory; another origin suggested is city of our father. The Muisca name was Chicaquicha.

In the Abra Valley between Zipaquirá and Tocancipá lie some of the most ancient human remains in South America, about 12,500 years old by carbon dating, the oldest evidence of settlement on the Altiplano Cundiboyacense. The area belonged to the domain of the zipa of Bacatá, the leader of the southern Muisca. Inhabitants of Nemocón, Gachancipá and Tocancipá came by canoe over the small lakes to Chicaquicha for salt, which they traded for pottery and tiles, and salt also went to the Panche, the Pantágora and the Muzo. Early Spanish descriptions of 1537 speak of a few hundred dwellings and a population of 12,000.

On 18 July 1600 the oidor Luis Henríquez established a settlement on the site, and in 1605 the area became the Corregimiento de Zipaquirá. In 1778, by order of the Viceroy Manuel Antonio Flórez, the natives were moved to Nemocón to prevent constant rebellions of the previous owners of the salt deposits. On 3 August 1816, during the Spanish reconquest, the so-called Zipaquirá Martyrs were executed in the city square. Under the Constitution of Cundinamarca of 1815 the city became the capital of its province, and in 1905 it was made capital of the Department of Quesada, until 1910.

Zipaquirá is known above all for its Salt Cathedral, an underground church built in a tunnel made by the excavation of the salt mine, which the Muisca exploited before the Spanish. González Forero Square is the centre of the old town and is surrounded by colonial buildings, including a cathedral built between 1760 and 1870. Dairy and potato farming are important, and industry is tied to producing and refining salt. The population is about 130,000. Santiago Pérez (1830-1900), president of Colombia from 1874 to 1876, was born there.
zirid-dynasty: The Zirids were Sanhaja Berbers of the sedentary Talkata tribe, from the area of modern Algeria, who served as vassals of the Fatimid Caliphate in the 10th century. Their progenitor, Ziri ibn Manad, was installed as governor of the central Maghreb, roughly north-eastern Algeria today, to guard the western frontier of the Fatimid Caliphate. With Fatimid support he founded a capital and palace at 'Ashir, south-east of Algiers. In 945 he helped break Abu Yazid's siege of the Fatimid capital, Mahdia, and in 959 he aided Jawhar al-Siqili's expedition that conquered Fez and Sijilmasa. Ziri was killed in battle against the Zanata in 971.

Under Buluggin ibn Ziri, emir of Ifriqiya from 972, the Zirids extended their control westwards and briefly occupied Fez and much of present-day Morocco after 980, meeting resistance from the Zenata Berbers who gave allegiance to the Caliphate of Cordoba. In the east they took Tripolitania after 978. A kinsman, Zawi ibn Ziri, fled to al-Andalus and founded the Taifa of Granada in 1013, and the Hammadids broke away after disputes and took the central Maghreb after 1015. The main branch, the Badisides, held only Ifriqiya, ruling from Kairouan until 1057 and then from Mahdia. The early reign of al-Mu'izz ibn Badis (1016-1062) marked the height of their power, with agriculture, trade and learning flourishing at Kairouan.

In the 1040s the Zirids broke from the Fatimids by adopting Sunni Islam and recognising the Abbasids, a move popular with the urban Arabs of Kairouan. The Fatimids retaliated by sending the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym to the Maghreb. At the Battle of Haydaran on 14 April 1052, 30,000 Sanhaja cavalry were decisively beaten by 3,000 Arab cavalry of the Banu Hilal, and in 1057 al-Mu'izz abandoned Kairouan. The Normans of Sicily took Jerba in 1135, Tripoli in 1146, and Sfax, Gabès and Mahdia in 1148. The last Zirid ruler, al-Hasan, left Mahdia to them, and the Almohads took it in 1160.

The Zirid period opened an age when Berber dynasties held political power in North Africa, followed by the Almoravids, Almohads, Zayyanids, Marinids and Hafsids. Ibn Khaldun wrote that the Berbers had never seen a kingdom more vast and flourishing than that of al-Mu'izz. Wheat, olives, dates, sugar cane, cotton and horses and sheep supported the economy, and trade links reached the Kalbid emirs of Sicily. Al-Mu'izz himself wrote a treatise on the arts of the book. He restored the Great Mosque of Kairouan, whose wooden maqsura is the oldest preserved in place in the Islamic world.
ziryab: Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Nafi, known as Ziryab, was a singer, oud player, composer, poet and teacher. His nickname comes from a Persian and Kurdish word for blackbird, which Ibn Hayyan connects to his dark complexion, the clarity of his voice and the sweetness of his character. He was born in Baghdad into a family of mawali of the caliph al-Mahdi, and his ethnic origin is unclear: sources suggest Persian, Kurdish, Sindi, African or mixed Arab-African descent. He trained in music from a young age under Ibrahim al-Mawsili.

He left Baghdad some time after 813, during the reign of al-Ma'mun, and travelled to Syria and then to Kairouan, where he lived at the Aghlabid court of Ziyadat Allah. Accounts of why he left differ. Al-Maqqari says that al-Mawsili, jealous after Ziryab performed for the caliph Harun al-Rashid, told him to leave; earlier and more reliable sources say he outlived Harun and his son al-Amin and left after al-Amin's death in 813.

In 822 the Umayyad prince al-Hakam I invited him to al-Andalus. Al-Hakam had died by the time he arrived, but his son Abd ar-Rahman II renewed the invitation, and Ziryab settled in Córdoba with a monthly salary of 200 gold dinars.

He founded one of the first schools of music in Córdoba, which taught men and women and shaped performance for at least two generations. According to Ibn Hayyan he had eight sons and two daughters, and five of the sons and both daughters became musicians.

Ziryab is said to have improved the oud by adding a fifth pair of strings and using an eagle's quill instead of a wooden pick. He is also said to have popularised an early song sequence that may have been a forerunner of the nawba.

Later accounts credit him with setting fashions: clothes changed with the weather and the time of day, men shaved, and hair was cut with bangs. He is said to have promoted daily baths and introduced an early toothpaste, asparagus and the serving of meals in three courses. The French historian Henri Terrasse argued that no single man could have brought about such a transformation of dress. The claim that he opened beauty parlours for Córdoban women is not supported by the early sources.
zittau: Zittau lies in Upper Lusatia, the southern part of Lusatia, on the Mandau and the Lusatian Neisse, in the Zittau Basin just north of the Zittau Mountains, which are part of the Sudetes. The Lusatian Neisse forms the border with Poland and touches the city in the east, and the two rivers meet in its south-east. Further south is the point where Germany, Poland and the Czech Republic meet. The city belongs to the district of Görlitz and has about 25,000 inhabitants.

The city grew from a Slavic settlement of the 12th century. The area belonged to the Bohemian duchy, later kingdom, from the 11th century. It was first mentioned as Sitavia in 1238 and received town rights in 1255 from King Ottokar II of Bohemia, who also built defensive walls. In 1319 it passed to the Piast-ruled Duchy of Jawor, and after the death of Duke Henry I of Jawor in 1346 it returned to the Bohemian Crown. Its coat of arms still shows a Czech lion and a Silesian Piast eagle. In 1469 it recognized the Hungarian king Matthias Corvinus as ruler, and after his death in 1490 it returned to Bohemia, then under Vladislaus II. In 1635 it passed to the Electorate of Saxony.

In 1346 Zittau became a member of the Six-City League of Upper Lusatia, and it was given the title Die Reiche, the Rich, because of its high proportion of well-to-do citizens. Great fires struck it in 1359 and 1422. Beer was one of its most important trading goods in the 16th century, and textiles became important in the 18th and 19th centuries, as elsewhere in Upper Lusatia. After the Battle of White Mountain in 1620, many Protestant refugees from Bohemia were taken in by the Protestant Saxon rulers at Zittau. The near-complete destruction of the city in the Seven Years' War means that its earlier prosperity survives in only a few exceptional buildings and in the cemeteries where the well-to-do were buried.

The Great Zittau Lenten Cloth of 1472, a veil of 56 square metres that hid the altar during Lent, is shown in the former Church of the Holy Cross, and a smaller Lenten cloth of 1573 is kept in the Museum of Cultural History in the former Franciscan monastery. The city hall, designed by Karl Friedrich Schinkel in the style of an Italian palazzo, was built between 1840 and 1845, and the Church of Our Lady is first mentioned in 1355. Several historic fountains stand in the squares, among them the Roland or Mars Fountain of 1585. The composer Heinrich Marschner was born in Zittau in 1795.
ziusudra: One version of the Sumerian King List, the recension known as WB-62 or the Weld-Blundell prism, names Ziusudra of Shuruppak as the last king of Sumer before the flood. It makes him the son of Ubara-Tutu, from whom he inherited the rule, and says that he reigned as both king and gudug priest for ten sars, periods of 3,600 years, a figure that is probably a copyist's error for ten years.

Sediment layers at Shuruppak, the modern Tell Fara, and at Uruk, Kish and other sites attest a river flood radiocarbon-dated to about 2900 BCE, and Kish flourished soon after it. On this ground Max Mallowan held that there were good reasons to believe Ziusudra was a prehistoric ruler of a historic city.

The Sumerian tale survives on a single fragmentary tablet, dated by its script to the 17th century BCE and published in 1914 by Arno Poebel. Its first part tells of the creation of humans and animals and the founding of the first cities, Eridu, Bad-tibira, Larak, Sippar and Shuruppak. The passages in which the gods decide on the flood and in which the boat is described are lost. Where the text resumes, a storm rages for seven days. The sun god Utu then appears, and Ziusudra opens a window, prostrates himself and sacrifices an ox and a sheep.

After another gap he bows before the gods An and Enlil, who give him breath eternal. The rest of the poem is lost. The word used for his new home in Dilmun, kur, is ambiguous. Samuel Noah Kramer explained that its first meaning is mountain, from which came the senses of foreign land and of land in general.

Ziusudra is one of several heroes of Near Eastern flood stories, with Atrahasis, Utnapishtim and the biblical Noah, and many elements are shared among the versions. The eleventh tablet of the Epic of Gilgamesh calls Utnapishtim man of Shuruppak. Ziusudra is also named in The Death of Gilgamesh, The Poem of Early Rulers and a late version of the Instructions of Shuruppak, a text Kramer dated to about 2600 BCE.

In Greek he became Xisuthros, known from the writings of Berossus, a priest of Bel in Babylon. In that version the god Enki is identified with the Greek Cronus, Xisuthros is the son of one Ardates and reigns 18 saroi, reckoned as 64,800 years, and his reed boat is said to have survived until Berossus's own day in the Corcyrean Mountains of Armenia.
ziya-gokalp: Mehmed Ziya was born in Diyarbakır on 23 March 1876, the second son of Muhammad Tefvik Bey, an Ottoman bureaucrat, and Zeliha Hanım. His maternal family was of Kurdish origin. He described his paternal family as Syrian Turkmen, and he concealed traces of Kurdish ancestry. Diyarbakır was a cultural frontier of Turks, Kurds and Armenians, which has often been suggested as an influence on his sense of national identity. He later held that nationality rests on upbringing. In 1895 he went to Istanbul, studied at a veterinary school, spent ten months in prison for underground nationalist politics and joined the Committee of Union and Progress.

Gökalp opened the first Committee office in Diyarbakır in July 1908, took the pen name Gökalp, meaning celestial hero, after the Young Turk Revolution, and moved to Salonika in 1909. He joined the Central Committee in 1910. Hans-Lukas Kieser describes him and Talaat Pasha as a political duumvirate, with Talaat the executive leader and Gökalp the chief ideologue. After the war he was exiled to Malta from 1919 to 1921, then taught in Diyarbakır and later worked in Ankara in support of Mustafa Kemal, in the Ministry of Education. He sat in the Grand National Assembly until his death in Istanbul on 25 October 1924, aged 48.

Influenced by Émile Durkheim, whom he translated into Turkish, Gökalp held that a nation needs a shared consciousness and that a modern state should be homogeneous in culture, religion and national identity. In The Principles of Turkism, published in 1923, he described a nation as people who share a language, religion, morality and aesthetics through the same education. He thought Turkification, Islamization and Westernization were complementary. He also wrote poetry, including Turan in 1911.

His legacy is controversial. Many historians and sociologists suggest that his nationalism contributed to the Armenian genocide, and Kieser characterises his thought as proto-fascist. Some readings see his Turanism as cultural rather than a call for expansion. Atatürk is quoted as calling him the father of his thought.
ziyad-ibn-abihi: Ziyad was probably born in Ta'if, the illegitimate son of Sumayya, a woman of obscure origins whom the 9th-century historians al-Baladhuri and Awana ibn al-Hakam describe as a slave; his father was probably Abu Sufyan. He was raised among the Banu Thaqif and embraced Islam under Abu Bakr. He was among the first settlers of the garrison town of Basra, where its founder Utba ibn Ghazwan al-Mazini gave him tasks in the treasury and later made him his secretary. Caliph Umar rewarded him with 1,000 silver dirhams, which he used to buy the freedom of his mother or his stepfather Ubayd.

Ziyad stayed neutral at the Battle of the Camel in 656, then served Ali as collector of Basra's land tax and as acting governor, putting down a pro-Umayyad rising. Sent to Fars, he held out longest of Ali's appointees against Mu'awiya I, surrendering only in 662/63 through al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba. Mu'awiya's recognition of him as a half-brother scandalised the Umayyad family, and Muslim scholars generally counted it among the caliph's most disreputable acts. As governor of Basra from 665 he opened with a speech praised for its eloquence, threatening death to anyone found in the streets at night, and he gave the city a congregational mosque and buildings of baked brick.

From 670 he governed Kufa as well, wintering in Basra and summering in Kufa. In 671 he had the Alid leader Hujr ibn Adi al-Kindi and thirteen followers arrested and sent to Damascus, where six, Hujr among them, were executed. He regrouped the tribes of both garrisons under leaders he appointed, minted Sasanian-style dirhams in his own name and settled 50,000 Arab soldiers and their families in the Merv oasis, from which his lieutenants campaigned in Tukharistan, Balkh and Quhistan.

Ziyad died in al-Thawiyya near Kufa on 23 August 673. His sons Ubayd Allah, Abd al-Rahman, Salm, Abbad and Yazid governed Iraq, Khurasan and Sijistan. Hugh N. Kennedy notes that the descendants of the Khurasan settlers helped destroy the Umayyad Caliphate in 750, and Hujr's execution, the first political execution in Islamic history, made him a martyr for Shia Muslims. Ziyad is counted among the four shrewd Arab statesmen of his era, with Mu'awiya, al-Mughira and Amr ibn al-As.
ziyadat-allah-i: Abu Muhammad Ziyadat Allah ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Aghlab succeeded his brother Abd Allah in 817. Ifriqiya was then reputed a hard province to rule. Nasr b. Habiib, adviser to the emir of the day, warned the caliph that it was a large frontier zone that would not be safe without a strong ruler. When Ziyadat Allah came to power the Abbasid Caliphate was in turmoil, with no caliph in Baghdad, and outlying provinces such as Ifriqiya were left to fend for themselves.

Two groups threatened every governor. The jund, the Arab army of the province, may have numbered over 100,000 and had risen repeatedly since 765, probably because it often went unpaid; under the caliphate, provinces such as Egypt had sometimes helped meet its costs. The Berber tribes, many of them Ibadi and long used to war, had also defied Abbasid authority, and by 770 an emir had recognised Berber-Ibadi rule over the hinterland.

In 824 the jund began what was possibly the largest of its revolts, and most of Ifriqiya fell into its hands. Earlier emirs had faced the soldiers and the Berbers at once, each trouble feeding the other. Ziyadat Allah instead seems to have built a working relationship with the Berbers and used them to defeat the rebels. It was the last jund revolt in Ifriqiya.

Some historians argue that he opened the conquest of Sicily to draw the jund's fighters into holy war; another view, criticised because it rests on a much later source, holds that he had already mastered the rising and launched the campaign to prevent further revolts and gain resources.

Ziyadat Allah died on 10 June 838. Because he ended the conflict with the jund and the Berbers and turned the dynasty towards conquest, he is sometimes called the second founder of the Aghlabid regime, and his reign is seen as a shift towards greater control and stability for the emirs.

Sources for his rule are sparse. Al-Tabari, close to the caliph al-Mu'tazz in Baghdad, wrote chiefly about the Abbasid centre, and al-Baladhuri wrote about the Aghlabids more than a century after their fall. A story told by al-Bakri over two hundred years after Ziyadat Allah's death, that he sent Idrisid gold dinars to the caliph al-Ma'mun as a warning, is doubted by scholars. A character loosely based on him, played by Kal Naga, appears in the fifth season of the television series Vikings.
ziyarid-dynasty: The Ziyarid dynasty was an Iranian dynasty of Gilaki origin that ruled Tabaristan during the Iranian Intermezzo. They descended from Vardanshah, leader of the Shahanshahvand tribe, which traced its descent to Arghush Farhadan, a ruler of Gilan in the time of Kai Khosrow. Vardanshah's son Ziyar married a sister of the Gilaki king Harusindan, and their son was Mardavij. Mardavij served the Gilaki military leader Asfar ibn Shiruya, betrayed him and conquered Tabaristan, and named the dynasty after his father.

Mardavij killed Asfar and took Hamadan, Dinavar, Kashan, Isfahan, Shiraz and Ahvaz from the Abbasids. He planned to restore the Sasanian Empire by conquering Baghdad, but was murdered in 935. His brother Vushmgir, crowned at Ray, spent the next decades in a struggle for Gorgan, Tabaristan and Ray, relying on Samanid support against the Buyids. He was killed by a boar during a hunt in 967.

His sons Bisutun and Qabus then fought for influence. Qabus succeeded in 977, but the Buyid ruler Adud al-Dawla expelled him in 980, and the Buyids dominated Tabaristan for 17 years. Qabus returned in 998 and kept good relations with Mahmud of Ghazni. His army overthrew him in 1012, and his son Manuchihr recognised Mahmud's sovereignty. In 1035 the Ghaznavids sacked the capital Amol when Abu Kalijar, the power behind the throne of Anushirvan, stopped paying tribute. The Seljuqs forced Anushirvan to accept their authority in 1041 or 1042, and in 1090 the Nizari Ismaili state under Hassan-i Sabbah conquered the domains of Keikavus's son Gilanshah.

Under Qabus the kingdom attracted scholars, among them al-Biruni, who dedicated his Chronology to Qabus around 1000 and observed eclipses of the moon in the capital Gorgan. Qabus himself wrote in Arabic and patronised poets, and the poet Manuchihri took his pen name from Qabus's son Manuchihr. Keikavus wrote the Persian work Qabus-nama, a major text of Persian literature. The best-known monument is the Gonbad Kavous, the tomb of Qabus, a fired-brick cylinder 49 metres high with a conical roof, one of the earliest surviving monuments in post-Islamic Iran with a dated inscription.
ziying: There is no firm consensus on Ziying's relationship to the Qin royal family. Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian calls him in different chapters a son of the elder brother of Qin Er Shi, who according to Yan Shigu's commentary was Fusu, an elder brother of Qin Er Shi, or a younger brother of Qin Shi Huang. Xu Guang's commentary calls him a son of Qin Shi Huang's younger brother.

The historian Wang Liqun argued that Ziying was at most 19 when Zhao Gao killed Qin Er Shi, which makes it unlikely that he consulted two sons as Sima Qian implies, and that he was therefore unlikely to be a grandson of Qin Shi Huang. Li Kaiyuan notes that Qin Shi Huang had only three brothers of any kind, so another brother would have been mentioned more often.

After the death of Qin Er Shi, Zhao Gao chose Ziying as successor and changed the title from emperor back to king, because the Qin dynasty was by then as weak as the former Qin state and held only Guanzhong. Ziying ruled the fragmented empire for 46 days, from mid-October to early December 207 BCE. He had been the only person at court to try to persuade Qin Er Shi against the wrongful executions of Meng Tian and Meng Yi. According to Sima Qian, he feigned illness and conspired with the eunuch Han Tan and his sons to murder Zhao Gao, and he lured the regent into a trap and killed him.

He later surrendered to Liu Bang, the leader of the first group of rebels to occupy the capital Xianyang. Another rebel leader, Xiang Yu, killed him and the male members of his family, in about January 206 BCE. Some sources give him the posthumous name Emperor Shang of Qin, though the Qin dynasty had abolished the practice of posthumous names.

Ziying sometimes appears as a door god in Chinese and Taoist temples, usually paired with his successor Emperor Yi of Chu. Historians differed about him. The Han dynasty writer Jia Yi (200-169 BCE) judged him a mediocre sovereign. Ban Gu (32-92 CE) disagreed, holding that Ziying had done everything he could by killing the conspiring eunuch whose actions had caused the political chaos, and that by surrendering the kingdom to the rebel forces he prevented further loss of life and dignity.
zlin: The first written mention of Zlín is from 1322, when it was acquired by Queen Elizabeth Richeza. It was already a market town and a craft guild centre for the surrounding region of Moravian Wallachia. From 1358 the estate belonged to Bishop Albrecht of Šternberk and became the seat of the Moravian branch of the Šternberk family, and in 1397 its town privileges were extended. The Hussite Wars forced the family to sell it in 1437. The 16th century brought peace and prosperity, with drapery, pottery and shoemaking flourishing.

Tomáš Baťa and his siblings founded a shoe factory in 1894. By 1922 it was the leading maker of footwear in Czechoslovakia, and the company moved into engineering, chemistry and rubber technology. Baťa was elected mayor in 1923. Between 1923 and 1938 the company built a large complex on the outskirts with thousands of flats, schools, department stores, scientific facilities and a hospital, in a controlled development shaped by modern urban ideas. The plan was the work of František Lydie Gahura, who had studied in Le Corbusier's atelier, and the city drew on both Ebenezer Howard's garden city and Le Corbusier's vision of urban modernity.

Buildings of the period include Baťa's Hospital of 1927, the Grand Cinema of 1932, with 2,270 seats the largest cinema in Central Europe in its time, and the Tomas Bata Memorial of 1933. Baťa's Skyscraper, built in 1936–1939 to a design by Vladimír Karfík, rose 77.5 m.

Tomáš Baťa died in 1932 and the company was run by others. German occupation halted development in the Second World War, and in 1944 American bombing destroyed large parts of the factories. Soviet and Romanian armies liberated the city on 2 May 1945, and in October 1945 the Bata company in Czechoslovakia was nationalised. The city name returned to Zlín on 1 January 1990. Zlín has about 75,000 inhabitants, lies on the Dřevnice River about 70 km east of Brno, is the seat of the Zlín Region and has been home to Tomas Bata University since 2001. Much of its centre is protected as an urban monument zone.
znojmo: Znojmo lies in the South Moravian Region, about 54 kilometres south-west of Brno and near the border with Austria. It stands mainly on a rock outcrop on the steep left bank of the Thaya, along the eastern edge of Podyjí National Park. The name is of uncertain origin. The likeliest explanations derive it either from the Old Czech words znoj, heat, and znojný, exposed to heat, or from a personal name, Znojem or Znojim.

A settlement may have existed in the time of Great Moravia in the 9th century, when the main gord stood on the hill across the Gránický brook and was one of the first places in Moravia where Christianity appeared. After 1029 the gord was the residence of a Přemyslid principality within the Bohemian March of Moravia and a strategic outpost near the Bavarian March of Austria. Around 1100 the administrative centre moved to a new castle, and in 1101 Duke Luitpold of Znojmo built the Rotunda of Saint Catherine there. Duke Vladislaus II of Bohemia seized and demolished the castle in 1145, and in 1190 Duke Conrad II founded the Premonstratensian Louka Monastery.

King Ottokar I of Bohemia founded the royal town shortly before 1226, in front of the rebuilt castle, and fortified it; it was one of the first royal towns in Moravia. Znojmo survived the Hussite Wars unscathed, as the Hussites failed to capture it. In the 15th and 16th centuries burgher houses with a system of underground passages were built as part of the fortifications. The population was mixed Czech and German, and the burghers mainly spoke German. The Thirty Years' War ended the town's development, and it took over a hundred years to recover. The Armistice of Znaim was concluded there on 12 July 1809, after the Battle of Wagram.

Znojmo has about 34,000 inhabitants and is the second most populated town of its region. Its well-preserved historic centre is protected as an urban monument reservation, and the Rotunda of Saint Catherine, the Louka Monastery and the Town Hall Tower, built in 1445-1448, are national cultural monuments. The town is known for its gherkins, grown in the region since 1571 when George II, abbot of Louka, introduced them, and for winemaking.
zoe-porphyrogenita: Zoe was called Porphyrogenita, born into the purple, the name given to a child born in the capital to a reigning emperor. She was the second daughter of Constantine VIII and his wife Helena. Her uncle Basil II, the senior emperor, prevented his nieces from marrying into the Byzantine nobility, since a husband would have gained a claim on the throne, and Zoe lived in obscurity in the women's quarters of the palace for many years. A marriage to the Holy Roman Emperor Otto III was planned in 996. In 1001 an embassy under Arnulf II, Archbishop of Milan, chose Zoe, then 23, from the emperor's three daughters, and she sailed for Italy in January 1002, only to learn at Bari that Otto had died.

Constantine became sole emperor in December 1025. Hoping to continue the dynasty, he sought an aristocratic husband for one of his daughters. Constantine Dalassenos was rejected, and Romanos Argyros, the urban prefect of Constantinople, was chosen after her sister Theodora refused him. Zoe and Romanos married on 10 November 1028, and the next day Constantine died and they took the throne.

Zoe was desperate to bear a child and used charms and potions without effect. Romanos grew distant, and in 1033 she took up with a low-born servant named Michael. Romanos was found dying in his bath on 11 April 1034. Michael Psellus says some of his retinue held his head under the water; John Scylitzes says he was drowned on Michael's orders; Matthew of Edessa has Zoe poisoning him. Zoe and Michael married that day, and Michael IV was crowned the next. He excluded her from politics, and his brother John the Orphanotrophos governed in his name.

In 1041 John forced Zoe to adopt his nephew Michael Kalaphates, who became Michael V when Michael IV died on 10 December. He banished her to a monastery on Principus, which provoked a popular uprising. On 19 April 1042 the mob rose for Zoe and Theodora, and they were crowned on 21 April as joint empresses. After two months Zoe married Constantine Monomachos on 11 June 1042, and he was crowned Constantine IX. She remained Augusta.

Constantine IX brought his mistress Maria Skleraina to court and gave her the title of sebaste. Rumours that she planned to murder Zoe led to a popular uprising in 1044, quieted when Zoe and Theodora appeared on a balcony. Psellos describes Zoe in later life as deeply pious, consulting a jewelled statue of Christ for omens, and also as extravagant and vindictive. She died in 1050, aged 72, and was buried in Constantinople. Constantine tried to have her canonised, but the attempt foundered on her history of affairs.
zog-i: Zog was born Ahmed Muhtar Bey Zogolli in 1895 at Burgajet Castle, near Burrel in northern Albania. His landowning family was of beylical rank, with feudal authority over the region of Mati, and his mother belonged to the Toptani family, who claimed descent from the sister of Skanderbeg. He was educated at the Galatasaray High School in Istanbul and became governor of Mat when his father died in 1911. In 1912 he took part in the Albanian Declaration of Independence. In the First World War he volunteered on the side of Austria-Hungary and was detained in Vienna and Rome before returning to Albania in 1919.

In the early 1920s he served as Governor of Shkodër, Minister of the Interior and chief of the military, and in 1922 changed his surname to Zogu, which sounds more Albanian. He became prime minister that year at 27, and in February 1924 he was shot and wounded in Parliament. A leftist revolt drove him into exile in June 1924, and he came back with Yugoslav and White Russian military backing.

The Constituent Assembly elected Zogu the first President of Albania on 21 January 1925. A new constitution gave him sweeping executive and legislative powers, so that he was in effect a dictator. His government enacted major reforms, and its principal ally was Italy, which lent money in exchange for a greater role in Albanian finances. It was also a police state in which civil liberties were almost non-existent, the press was censored and opponents were imprisoned and often killed. In 1925 he ceded Sveti Naum to Yugoslavia.

On 1 September 1928 Albania became a kingdom and Zogu proclaimed himself Zog I, King of the Albanians. He was never formally crowned. In 1929 he abolished Islamic law and adopted a civil code based on the Swiss one. In 1938 he opened Albania's borders to Jewish refugees fleeing Nazi Germany, and he married Countess Geraldine Apponyi in April of that year. Their son Leka was born on 5 April 1939. Zog reputedly survived more than 55 assassination attempts.

Through the 1930s Albania became almost wholly dependent on Mussolini's Italy. Italy invaded in April 1939, and Zog went into exile, never to return. He lived in England during the Second World War. The new Communist-dominated government under Enver Hoxha barred his return and formally dethroned him in 1946. He spent the rest of his life in France and died on 9 April 1961. His remains were moved from the Thiais Cemetery near Paris to a royal mausoleum in Tirana in 2012.
zograf-monastery: Zograf Monastery, named for Saint George the Zograf, is one of the twenty Eastern Orthodox monasteries of Mount Athos. It was founded by three Bulgarians from Ohrid and is regarded as the historical Bulgarian monastery on Athos, traditionally inhabited by Bulgarian Orthodox monks. The earliest written evidence of it dates from 980. The monastery takes its name from a 13th- or 14th-century icon of Saint George. Zograf means painter in Greek, and the icon is believed to have painted itself on the prepared board.

Bulgarian rulers such as Ivan Asen II and Ivan Alexander supported the monastery generously, since it was a matter of pride for the Bulgarian Orthodox Church to keep a house on Athos. It also received land from Byzantine rulers, the first being Leo VI the Wise, and from Serbian rulers. In 1275 Crusaders acting on the orders of the Byzantine emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos plundered and burned it and killed 26 monks, including the abbot Thomas. The cause was the opposition of the Athonite monks to the Union of Lyons, which the emperor supported for political reasons. Their martyrdom is commemorated each year on 10 October.

Mercenaries of the Catalan Grand Company raided the Holy Mountain in 1307–9, and of some 300 monasteries on Athos at the start of the 14th century only 35 were left by the end. Zograf recovered quickly with grants from the Palaeologue emperors and the princes of Moldavia and Wallachia, and its buildings were reconstructed with the aid of Andronicus II Palaeologus. The present buildings date from the middle of the 18th century: the south wing was built in 1750, the east in 1758, the small church in 1764 and the large one in 1801. Large-scale construction ended in 1896.

The monastery library is of major importance to Bulgarian culture. It holds 388 manuscripts in Church Slavonic, 126 in Greek and about 10,000 printed books, among them the original draft of Paisius of Hilendar's Istoriya Slavyanobolgarska. Two medieval Bulgarian royal charters, the Zograf Charter and the Rila Charter, were found there. The monastery and its seal appear on the Bulgarian 2 lev banknote issued in 1999 and 2005, and a 10 lev silver coin of 2011 features it.
zollverein: By the 1790s the Holy Roman Empire had about 1,800 customs barriers, and in the early 19th century Prussia itself had more than 67 local tariffs. A shipment from Königsberg to Cologne was inspected and taxed about 80 times. The Congress of Vienna created the German Confederation in 1815 but made no effort at trade standardisation. In 1818 Prussia abolished its own internal tariffs, and it then began inviting other states to do the same. Historians have identified three Prussian aims: to eliminate Austrian influence in Germany, to improve the economies, and to strengthen Germany against French aggression while reducing the economic independence of the smaller states.

The middle-sized states had their own plans. In 1825 an agreement at Stuttgart between Württemberg and Bavaria founded the South German Customs Union, and Hanover, Saxony, Hesse and others made trade agreements of their own. Organised by the treaties of 1833, the Zollverein formally started on 1 January 1834, and that year Baden and Württemberg joined the Prussian union, which was renamed the German Customs Union. By 1835 it included most of the states of the German Confederation. Austria stayed out because of its highly protectionist trade policy and Prince von Metternich's opposition.

The union was not ended by the Austro-Prussian War of 1866 but was reorganised in 1867, when no individual state any longer had a veto. By then its members covered about 425,000 square kilometres. After the founding of the German Empire in 1871 the Empire took over control of the union, though Hamburg acceded only in 1888, with part of its port left outside. Luxembourg remained a member until 1919, when the Treaty of Versailles ended its membership.

It was the first instance in history in which independent states formed a full economic union without a political federation. Economic historians Helmut Böhme and H.-U. Wehler hold that it laid the groundwork for unification under Prussian guidance. Hans-Joachim Voth and others dispute this, arguing that smaller states joined for fiscal reasons and used the revenue to consolidate their independence, and that membership brought no political commitment to Berlin in 1866. In 1840 the poet August Heinrich Hoffmann von Fallersleben published an ironic song, Der deutsche Zollverein.
zolta: Zoltán, also written Zolta, Zsolt, Solt or Zaltas, is the third Grand Prince of the Hungarians in the Gesta Hungarorum, a late twelfth-century chronicle by the writer known as Anonymus, which is the main source for his life. According to Anonymus he was the only son of Árpád and was born during his father's second campaign against Menumorut, one of the local rulers who appear only in that chronicle among the opponents of the Hungarians during the conquest of the Carpathian Basin.

Menumorut was forced to surrender and give his daughter in marriage to Zoltán, in 904 or 905. When he died, Zoltán inherited his father-in-law's duchy east of the river Tisza. His name seems to derive from the Arabian title sultan through Turkic mediation, though scholars have not unanimously accepted this.

Anonymus says that Zoltán, still a minor, succeeded Árpád, who died around 907, and describes him as a lisping, pale, warlike duke, merciful to his subjects but covetous of power. When he was thirteen, the leading men appointed rectors beneath the prince to settle lawsuits by customary law. In this account he later abdicated in favour of his son Taksony and died in the third year of his son's reign.

Modern historians reject most of these details. Gyula Kristó places his birth around 880 rather than 903, and Alexandru Madgearu writes that either he was born many years earlier or his marriage came years after 904. Pál Engel calls Menumorut an imaginary figure invented to describe the heroic wars of the conquerors, while Charles R. Bowlus takes him for a Moravian ruler whose daughter's marriage symbolized the end of Great Moravia, and Tudor Sălăgean considers him a real ruler of a duchy inhabited by Romanians, Slavs and other peoples.

That Zoltán ever ruled the federation of Hungarian tribes is also challenged. Sándor L. Tóth observes that as the youngest of Árpád's four sons he could hardly precede his elder brothers in the succession, and Kristó notes that other Hungarian chroniclers do not mention his rule, suggesting that Anonymus inserted him into the incompletely preserved list of grand princes because all Hungarian monarchs of the House of Árpád descended from him. There is consensus that, even if he never ascended the throne, all rulers of Hungary from that house after around 955 descended from him through Taksony.
zoltan-kodaly: Kodály was born in Kecskemét, in the Kingdom of Hungary within Austria-Hungary, on 16 December 1882, and learned the violin as a child. In 1900 he entered the Department of Languages at the University of Budapest and at the same time Hans von Kössler's composition class at the Royal Hungarian Academy of Music. After his studies he spent a year in Paris with Charles-Marie Widor.

In 1905 he visited remote villages to collect songs on phonograph cylinders, and in 1906 he wrote a thesis on Hungarian folk song, Strophic Construction in Hungarian Folksong. About then he met Béla Bartók, whom he took under his wing and introduced to some of the methods of folk-song collecting. The two became lifelong friends and champions of each other's music.

In 1919 Kodály was appointed alongside Bartók to the Music Directory by the People's Commissariat for Education and Culture in the short-lived Hungarian Soviet Republic. His works blend western European styles, including classical, late-romantic, impressionist and modernist traditions, with the folk music of Hungary and of the Hungarian-inhabited areas of what are now Slovakia and Romania.

Partly because of the Great War and the geopolitical changes that followed, and partly because of a diffident temperament in youth, he had no major public success until 1923. In that year Psalmus Hungaricus was first performed at a concert for the fiftieth anniversary of the union of Buda and Pest, at which Bartók's Dance Suite also had its premiere.

His later works include the stage work Háry János (1926) and its suite, the Dances of Marosszék (1929), the Dances of Galánta (1933), the Variations on a Hungarian folk song, The Peacock (1939), the Concerto for Orchestra (1940) and the Symphony in memoriam Toscanini (1961).

Beginning in 1935 Kodály worked with his colleague Jenő Ádám on a project to reform music teaching in Hungarian schools. He wrote down no comprehensive method but set out principles: music is for everyone, teaching should be sequential and begin with the child, singing is the first and most valuable tool, and teachers should draw on quality folk songs in the pupils' mother tongue. These principles were widely taken up after World War II, above all in Hungary but also in many other countries. Kodály died in Budapest on 6 March 1967, at the age of 84. The city of Pécs commissioned a bronze statue of him by Imre Varga in 1976.
zoltan-tildy: Zoltán Tildy was born on 18 November 1889 in Losonc, now Lučenec in Slovakia, then in the Austro-Hungarian Empire, into the family of a Hungarian official in the local government. He took a degree in theology at the Reformed Theological Academy in Pápa and then spent a year at Assembly's College in Belfast, Ireland. From 1921 he was an active minister of the Reformed Church, and he edited the church's daily paper, Keresztény Család (Christian Family), and other periodicals.

In 1929 Tildy joined the Independent Smallholders' Party with other noted Hungarian figures, among them Ferenc Nagy, and soon became its executive vice-president. He was elected to the Hungarian parliament in 1933 and re-elected in 1936 and 1939. He pressed the government of Horthy to take Hungary out of the Second World War, and after the German occupation he was forced into hiding.

When the Soviets occupied Hungary and drove out the Germans, Tildy became leader of the Smallholders' Party and was appointed prime minister, serving from 15 November 1945 until 1 February 1946, when he was elected President of Hungary, the first president of the republic.

He was forced to resign in July 1948, after allegations emerged that his son-in-law had been arrested for corruption and adultery, and was held under house arrest in Budapest until 1 May 1956. During the Hungarian Revolution of 1956 he was appointed a state minister in the coalition government, and when Warsaw Pact intervention crushed the revolution Soviet forces arrested him.

On 15 June 1958 the Supreme Court sentenced him to six years' imprisonment in the trial of Imre Nagy and his associates. He was released under an individual amnesty in April 1959 in view of his advanced years, and lived in complete retirement until his death in Budapest on 3 August 1961.
zong-massacre: The ship was the Dutch slaver Zorg, captured by the British brig HMS Alert on 10 February 1781 and bought at Cape Coast Castle for a Liverpool syndicate that included William Gregson, a former mayor of Liverpool. Renamed Zong, it was insured with its captives for £8,000. Its captain, Luke Collingwood, had been a ship's surgeon with no experience of command, and the crew numbered only 17.

Zong sailed from Accra on 18 August 1781 with 442 enslaved people, more than twice what it could safely carry. Near Jamaica on 27 or 28 November the crew mistook the island for Saint-Domingue and sailed on; by then about 62 Africans had died. Collingwood was gravely ill and the first mate, James Kelsall, suspended, so command had broken down.

Insurance paid nothing for captives who died a natural death, but under the principle of general average a claim could be made for cargo jettisoned to save the rest. On 29 November the crew agreed to throw people overboard, and 54 women and children were pushed through the cabin windows. On 1 December 42 men were thrown into the sea, and 36 more followed over the next days; another 10 jumped in defiance. By Kelsall's later affidavit it rained heavily on 1 December, filling six casks. In all 142 Africans were killed. Zong reached Black River, Jamaica, on 22 December with 208 captives, who were sold in January 1782.

At the trial at the Guildhall on 6 March 1783 the only witness was Robert Stubbs, the ship's passenger. At the King's Bench hearing on 21 and 22 May 1783 the owners' counsel, John Lee, argued that the captives perished just as a cargo of goods perished. There is no evidence that the retrial was ever held, and despite Granville Sharp's efforts no crew member was prosecuted for murder.

Sharp's account moved the London Yearly Meeting of Quakers to campaign against slavery, and the massacre was told by Thomas Clarkson, Ottobah Cugoano and John Newton. The Slave Trade Act 1788 limited the number carried per ship, and its renewal in 1794 narrowed insurance on enslaved people. J. M. W. Turner's painting The Slave Ship of 1840 and M. NourbeSe Philip's Zong! of 2008 draw on it, and a memorial stone was raised at Black River in 2007.
zongli-yamen: Zongli Yamen is a traditional abbreviation of the office's official name, literally the Office in Charge of Affairs Concerning All Nations; in Manchu, the other official language of the Qing Empire, it was Geren gurun i baita be uherileme icihiyara yamun. The name is often taken to mean the Premier's Office, because zongli is now used for a premier or prime minister, but it named an office of foreign affairs; contemporary English sources called it the Board of Ministers for Foreign Affairs. Prince Gong established it on 11 March 1861.

The office was the first significant institutional innovation in the central bureaucracy at Beijing since the Yongzheng Emperor created the nucleus of the Grand Council in 1729. Qing officials insisted that it would be temporary, kept only until the crisis of the time had passed. Its formal status was low, its members held posts in other agencies at the same time, and policy in foreign affairs remained the emperor's prerogative. The Tongwen Guan, set up to translate Western languages as successor to the Bureau of Translators, was placed under it rather than under the Hanlin.

Within a few decades the office was overshadowed by powerful officials such as Zeng Guofan and Li Hongzhang, but it remained the channel between the Qing government and the foreign ministers in Beijing's legation quarter. In 1873 it quarrelled with those ministers over the protocol of their audience with the Tongzhi Emperor, since they refused to perform the kowtow; the impasse was resolved partly through the Japanese ambassador, Soejima Taneomi, and similar protocol was followed for their audience with the Guangxu Emperor in 1891.

The missions it opened abroad were staffed by Qing diplomats with foreign staff and interpreters trained at the Tongwen Guan, and gave it some autonomy in presenting its own views in other capitals. Its successor under Article XII of the Boxer Protocol, the Waiwubu, ranked above the six boards, yet one judgement holds that it was as ineffective in establishing good relations with the outside world as the Zongli Yamen had been. The former site of the office, at No. 49 Dongtangzi Hutong in Dongcheng District, Beijing, lies in a historical conservation site, and nearly all its buildings are preserved in good condition.
zoroastrianism: The roots of Zoroastrianism lie in a common prehistoric Indo-Iranian religious system dating back to the early 2nd millennium BCE, and the religion shares many elements with Vedic religion. Zoroaster, whom tradition places in the 6th century BCE, is thought by many modern historians to have lived much earlier, in the second half of the second millennium BCE; the date is uncertain. He was born into the Spitama clan and calls himself a poet-priest and prophet in the Gathas. The religion enters recorded history in the mid-5th century BCE, when Herodotus describes Iranian customs that may be recognizably Zoroastrian, among them exposure of the dead.

Zoroastrians exalt Ahura Mazda, the uncreated, all-wise creator, and hold the Gathas, hymns thought to be Zoroaster's own, to be the most sacred texts. In the Gathas the central dualism is ethical, a choice between Asha, truth and order, and Druj, the lie. Evil is embodied in Angra Mainyu, the destructive spirit, and Ahura Mazda is served by the Amesha Spentas and by divine beings called Yazatas. Scholars disagree whether the faith is monotheistic, polytheistic, henotheistic or a mixture. At death each soul crosses the Chinvat Bridge, judged by the Yazatas Mithra, Sraosha and Rashnu. The Avesta is the central collection of texts, and today worship centres on fire temples.

For about a thousand years Zoroastrianism was the official religion of successive Iranian polities, from the Achaemenid Empire, which formalised many of its rituals, to the Sasanian Empire, which revived the faith and standardised its teachings. Over 22 years in the 7th century the Muslim caliphate conquered most of the Sasanian Empire, and the faith began to decline. Persecution by the early Muslims prompted many to migrate to India, where they became the Parsis. Zoroastrians now live mainly in India, Iran and diaspora communities, and India's census of 2011 recorded 57,264 Parsis. Some credit the faith with an imprint on Second Temple Judaism and, through it, on later monotheistic religions.
zou-yan: Zou Yan came from the coastal state of Qi, in present-day Shandong, and was a noted scholar of the state-sponsored Jixia Academy. He lived in the age of the Hundred Schools of Thought and is counted as the representative thinker of the Yin and Yang School, also called the School of Naturalists. The fullest account of him is the brief biography in the Records of the Grand Historian, written in the 1st century BCE by Sima Qian, which presents him as a polymath: philosopher, historian, politician, naturalist, geographer and astrologer.

According to Sima Qian, Zou Yan saw the rulers of his day growing ever more dissolute and unable to value virtue, and so studied the increase and decrease of yin and yang, writing essays of more than 100,000 words on their permutations and on the cycles of the sages. His method was to begin with small things and reason from them to large ones, and to begin with his own time and work back to the age of Huang Di. He classified the notable mountains, great rivers, valleys, birds, beasts, soils and rare products of China, and extended his survey to lands beyond the seas.

Starting from the separation of Heaven and Earth, he traced the revolutions of the Five Powers through history until each found its place. He held that what the Confucians called the Middle Kingdom made up only one part in eighty-one of the whole world. His teachings, Sima Qian wrote, at first frightened princes, dukes and officials, who later proved unable to practise them. None of his writings survive; they are known only through quotations in early Chinese texts.

The British biochemist and sinologist Joseph Needham called Zou Yan the real founder of all Chinese scientific thought. He is also commonly linked with Daoism and the beginnings of Chinese alchemy, a link that goes back to the Book of Han, of about 100 CE, which calls him a fangshi, a master of techniques such as alchemy, magic, exorcism and divination. The scholar Holmes Welch argued that Zou Yan himself knew nothing of alchemy and gained that reputation over time, and that the art was probably developed by followers who experimented with the Five Elements.
zouaves: The Zouave corps was created during the conquest of Algeria in 1830 by recruiting men from the local population. Its name comes from the Zwawa group of tribes in Algeria, who had a martial reputation from fighting for the rulers of the Regency of Algiers. The new French regiments in fact included few Kabyles and had a more diverse recruitment of Arabs, Turks, Moors and others. A royal decree of 21 March 1831 formally recognised the corps, which began with 404 men and officers.

Local recruitment gave patchy results in battle and frequent desertion: over 15 months 46 per cent of the force deserted. From 1833 the battalions took in European recruits, and from 1842 the men recruited were exclusively French or people of French descent born in French Algeria. The uniform was of North African origin, with a short open-fronted jacket, baggy trousers, sashes and a fez-like chéchia.

The zouaves served in the French conquest of Algeria, at the Mouzaia Pass in March 1836, at Mitidja in September 1836 and at the siege of Constantine in 1837. They were reorganised as separate regiments in 1852, linked to Algiers, Oran, Constantine and Tunis. Armed with the rifled fusil rayé, they served in the Crimean War, the Franco-Austrian War of 1859, the Mexican Intervention of 1864 to 1866 and the Franco-Prussian War of 1870.

After 1871 the zouaves became a force mainly of conscripts from the French settlers in Algeria and Tunisia. Provisional zouave regiments were raised for both world wars. The 9th Zouaves took a major part in the Battle of Algiers in 1957. The remaining regiments were disbanded in 1962, after Algerian independence, since their recruiting base was the European population of Algeria, which dispersed when French rule ended.

In the 1860s zouave units arose in many other countries. Louis Juchault de Lamoricière, a former commander of North African zouaves, organised the Papal Zouaves, renamed on 1 January 1861, volunteers who came to help Pope Pius IX against the Italian Risorgimento. By May 1868 they numbered 4,592 men. In 1863 the former French zouave François Rochebrune organised the Polish Zouaves of Death in the January Uprising against Russia. The Union Army had more than 70 volunteer zouave regiments during the American Civil War, and the Confederates about 25 companies, after Elmer E. Ellsworth made the style known with his drill company, the Zouave Cadets.
