zoucheng: Zoucheng lies in the south of Shandong province, about 20 km south of the city of Qufu, and like Qufu it falls under the prefecture-level city of Jining. Until it was made a city in October 1992 it was known as Zou County, or Zouxian. It is divided into three subdistricts and thirteen towns, and it lies on the Beijing-Shanghai Railway, with frequent buses to Qufu and Yanzhou.

Mencius was born here, in what was then the State of Zou, and his descendants have lived in the town ever since; some went to Korea during the Tang dynasty and others to Taiwan after the Chinese Civil War. Four sites in the city are linked with him: the Mencius Temple, the Mencius Family Mansion, the Mencius Forest and the forest of Mencius' mother.

The temple, on the south side of the town, covers more than 4 hectares, with five courtyards and sixty-four halls and rooms, and its history goes back to 1037 in the Northern Song dynasty. The mansion beside it, where his descendants lived, has 116 halls and rooms. The temple grounds hold over 270 stone steles and sculptures, some from the Song dynasty, among them Yuan dynasty stelae inscribed in 'Phags-pa script.

Immediately north of the city lies the tomb of the Ming King of Lu, Zhu Tan (1370–1389), the tenth son of the Hongwu Emperor, and there is also a royal tomb of the Han dynasty. The city had 1,116,692 people at the 2010 census.
zu-chongzhi: Zu Chongzhi, courtesy name Wenyuan, came from a family that originated in what is now Baoding, Hebei. His grandfather Zu Chang moved to the Yangtze during the mass population movement of the Eastern Jin and later held the post of Chief Minister for the Palace Buildings under the Liu Song, directing government construction. His father Zu Shuozhi also served the court and was respected for his learning.

Zu was born in Jiankang. His family had long been involved in astronomical research, so he met both astronomy and mathematics from childhood, and his talent won him a reputation while he was still a youth. Emperor Xiaowu of Song sent him to the Hualin Xuesheng academy and later to the Imperial Nanjing University, known as Zongmingguan, to carry out research.

In 461 Zu worked in the office of the local governor at Nanxu, today Zhenjiang in Jiangsu. In 464 he moved to Louxian, today the Songjiang district of Shanghai, where he compiled the Daming calendar and calculated pi. In 488 he was responsible for erecting water-powered trip hammer mills, which Emperor Wu of Southern Qi inspected in the early 490s.

He is also credited with the Chinese paddle boat, or Qianli chuan, in the late 5th century, and many paddle-wheel ships were built in the Tang era. In 478 he reconstructed the south-pointing chariot, first made by Ma Jun. The Book of Qi says Emperor Wu of Liu Song had captured Yao Xing's carriage as an empty shell with no machinery, so a man inside had to turn the figure, and Zu made new bronze machinery that turned without a hitch.

Zu used Liu Hui's algorithm, inscribing a polygon of 12,288 sides, and bounded pi between 3.1415926 and 3.1415927, a precision that stood for centuries. His other notable approximations were 355/113, called milü or the close ratio, and 22/7, the yuelü. The Japanese mathematician Yoshio Mikami noted that 355/113 appears in no Greek, Indian or Arabian manuscript before 1585 and urged that it be called Zu's fraction. He and his son Zu Gengzhi also derived the volume of a sphere as πd³/6.

In astronomy he distinguished the sidereal year from the tropical year, and calculated the year as 365.24281481 days. He gave the Jupiter year as about 11.858 Earth years. With his son he wrote the mathematical text Zhui Shu, which was lost after the Song dynasty, and his book Accounts of Strange Things survives.
zubaidah-bint-jafar: Zubaidah's date of birth is unknown, but she was at least a year younger than Harun al-Rashid. Her father, Ja'far, was a brother of the caliph al-Mahdi, and her mother, Salsal, was an elder sister of al-Khayzuran, the second and most powerful wife of al-Mahdi and mother of the caliphs Musa al-Hadi and Harun al-Rashid. Zubaidah was a pet name, meaning little butter ball, given by her grandfather, the caliph al-Mansur; her birth names were Sukhainah or Amat al-'Aziz. She later took the kunya Umm Ja'far. The exploits of her and Harun form part of the basis for The Thousand and One Nights.

Zubaidah married Harun in 781 or 782 at the Baghdad residence of Muhammad bin Sulayman. Her son Muhammad, the future caliph al-Amin, was born in April 787. She also raised Abdallah, the future al-Ma'mun, born in September 786 to Harun and the concubine Marajil, who died soon afterwards. Zubaidah employed staff to manage her properties and business ventures independently of Harun.

Her household was luxurious: meals were served on gold and silver plates, she brought in sandals stitched with gems, and she travelled in a palanquin of silver and ebony. It is said that her palace sounded like a beehive because she employed a hundred women who had memorised the Qur'an.

On her fifth pilgrimage to Mecca she found a drought had reduced the Zamzam Well to a trickle. She had it deepened and spent over 2 million dinars on the water supply of Mecca and its province, including an aqueduct from the spring of Hunayn, 95 kilometres to the east, and the Spring of Zubayda on the plain of Arafat. Ibn Khallikan records that she told her engineers she would build even were every stroke of a pickax to cost a dinar.

She also improved the route across nine hundred miles of desert between Kufa and Mecca, paving it, clearing boulders and building water storage at intervals. Ibn Battuta wrote that every reservoir, pool or well on the road from Mecca to Baghdad was due to her bounty. She rebuilt Tabriz after the earthquake of 791. Harun died in March 809, and her son al-Amin was killed by al-Ma'mun's supporters in 813; al-Ma'mun gave her the same respect as a son. She died on 10 July 831.
zubarah: Zubarah lies on the north-western coast of the Qatar peninsula in the Al Shamal municipality, about 105 km from Doha. The site covers around 400 hectares, 60 of them inside the outer town wall, and is Qatar's most substantial archaeological site. It stands on a low coastal hillock between sabkha flats and stony desert. Fresh water was scarce, so Murair Fort was built 1.8 km to the east, on the edge of the desert scarp, to protect wells that tapped shallow freshwater lenses. The name is most often linked to an Arabic word for a raised sand mound.

The Bani Utbah clans, among them the Al Sabah, Al Khalifa and Al Jalahma, migrated from the Najd in response to drought, travelling through Al Aflaj, Qatif and Al Ahsa to Freiha in north-western Qatar. In the 1760s the growing influence of the Al Khalifa brought conflict with the Al Musallam clan, which acted for the Bani Khalid. Sheikh Muhammad bin Khalifa refused its demand for tribute, and a fortified settlement, Qal'at Murair, was finished by 1768. The town was attacked at the behest of Nasr Al-Madhkur in 1778 and 1782.

Zubarah lived by pearling and trade. Its boats sailed to pearl beds along the southern shore of the Gulf for weeks at a time, and the pearl trade employed up to a third of the male population of the region until cultured pearls appeared in the early 1900s. The population at its height is estimated at 6,000 to 9,000. The Wahhabis occupied the town in 1809. In 1811 Said bin Sultan of Muscat attacked their garrisons and the fort was burned. Most remaining residents left in the early 20th century because the water supply was inadequate.

The town was laid out on a grid of streets, with courtyard houses of local stone coated in gypsum plaster, a market with storage rooms and a wall 2.5 km long defended by 22 semi-circular towers. Excavation found 27 date presses. Danish expeditions first surveyed the site in 1956, and the Qatar Museums Authority excavated in the 1980s and from 2002 to 2003. Since 2009 Copenhagen University has worked there with the Qatar Islamic Archaeology and Heritage Project. The Al Zubara Fort, built in 1938, also stands there.
zugdidi: Zugdidi lies in the north-west of the historical province of Samegrelo, also called Mingrelia, 318 kilometres west of Tbilisi. It stands at an elevation of 100 to 110 metres, about 30 kilometres from the Black Sea coast and 30 kilometres from the Egrisi Range. The name first appeared in the 17th century and means big hill in the Mingrelian language, after a hill in the eastern part of the city where small remains of an ancient fortress can still be seen. The city is the seat of the Metropolitan of Zugdidi and Tsaishi of the Georgian Orthodox Church.

Zugdidi was the capital of the Principality of Mingrelia, also called Odishi, until the Russian Empire abolished the principality in 1867. It then became the administrative centre of the Zugdidi Uyezd in the Kutais Governorate until 1918, when it passed to the Democratic Republic of Georgia. Between the 17th and 19th centuries it was an important political and cultural centre of Mingrelia and of Georgia as a whole. In 1646 the medieval epic The Knight in the Panther's Skin was rewritten there by Mamuka Tavakalashvili at the court of Prince Levan II Dadiani.

During the Crimean War Ottoman forces under Omar Pasha seized the town in 1855, and at the end of 1855 and the beginning of 1856 it was liberated by the Mingrelian Militia under Major General Prince Grigol Dadiani. On the order of Iskender Pasha the Ottomans plundered, burned and destroyed the whole city, especially the palaces and the botanical garden, and its population fell from 2,000 to 800. From 1930 it was the centre of the Zugdidi Raion of the Georgian Soviet Socialist Republic. Many buildings were heavily damaged in the Georgian Civil War of 1992–1993, and refugees from Abkhazia moved to the city.

The Dadiani Palace, built in the 19th century, was home to the last ruling family of the Principality of Samegrelo. The complex includes the palace of Ekaterine Dadiani, a residence for her son Niko Dadiani, a monastery and the botanical garden. The palace is now a museum.

The Shalva Dadiani Drama Theatre staged its first performance, Molière's Le médecin malgré lui, on 11 April 1869, and the first public library opened in 1887, though the library tradition goes back to Prince David Dadiani, who ruled from 1812 to 1853 and collected many books. Zugdidi is the regional centre of Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti.
zuiderzee: The Zuiderzee was a shallow bay of the North Sea in the northwest of the Netherlands. It extended about 100 km inland and at most 50 km in width, with a depth of about 4 to 5 m, a coastline of about 300 km and an area of 5,000 square kilometres. Its name is Dutch for southern sea, which shows that it originates in Friesland, to the north. Five small islands lay within it, Wieringen, Urk, Schokland, Pampus and Marken, whose people lived mainly by fishing. Around it fishing villages grew up and several became walled towns with extensive trade, in particular Kampen, and later Amsterdam, Hoorn and Enkhuizen.

In classical times the water here was called Lake Flevo by Roman authors, the largest of a region of lowland and freshwater lakes, separated from the sea by a belt of marsh and fen and fed by streams including the Vecht, Eem and IJssel. It drained to the North Sea through the Vlie. The Roman geographer Pomponius Mela describes it in 44 CE. In the early Middle Ages it was called Almere, a name in a life of saints by the Anglo-Saxon Boniface in 753, perhaps meaning eel lake.

Rising sea levels, peat digging by the Frisians and floods turned the lake into an inland sea. The All Saints' Flood of 1170 broke through the barrier dunes near Texel and washed away land between Stavoren, Texel and Medemblik, and its disaster marked the rise of Amsterdam, since traders from the Hanseatic cities could now reach the area. Further surges in 1173 and 1196 and in the 13th century completed the change, and about 1400 the Zuiderzee had reached its full extent. Storms pushing North Sea water into the inlet often caused floods and lost ships. On 18 November 1421 a seawall broke and flooded 72 villages and killed about 10,000 people, in the Second St Elizabeth's Flood.

Closing the Zuiderzee was first proposed in 1667, though a feasible method did not appear until the 20th century. The Flood of January 1916 hastened plans originating from Cornelius Lely, and the Afsluitdijk was built between 1927 and 1932.

With the completion of the Afsluitdijk in 1932 the Zuiderzee became the freshwater IJsselmeer, and the outer part became part of the Wadden Sea. Large areas were reclaimed by polders: the Wieringermeer Polder in 1930, the Northeast Polder in 1942, Eastern Flevoland in 1957 and Southern Flevoland in 1968. Together they form the Zuiderzee Works, and the reclaimed land became the province of Flevoland. The Markerwaard, begun in 1963, was abandoned in the mid-1980s.
zuiderzee-works: Half the land of the Low Countries lies below or less than a metre above sea level, and between 1200 and 1900 the Dutch reclaimed some 520,000 hectares while losing about 570,000 to the Zuiderzee. Hendrik Stevin published the first study proposing to drain it in 1667. In 1891 Cornelis Lely presented his plan: a dam from North Holland to the coast of Friesland and four polders in the enclosed water. Fishermen who would lose their living opposed it, as did people on the Wadden Sea who feared higher water, and others doubted its cost.

Work on the Afsluitdijk began in 1927, from Den Oever on Wieringen to Zurich in Friesland, 32 km long and 90 metres wide. Ships laid two parallel lines of glacial till dredged from the sea bed, with sand between them, and the dam was finished in sand and clay planted with grass. It was closed two years earlier than forecast, when the last trench of the Vlieter was filled with a bucket of till; the new lake still held salt water.

The polders followed. The Wieringermeer was drained in 1930, flooded by the Wehrmacht on 17 April 1945 and drained again by the end of that year. The Noordoostpolder, 480 square kilometres, was drained by September 1942 and sheltered members of the Dutch resistance. Eastern Flevoland, the largest at 540 square kilometres, was drained in 1957, with a ring of lakes left to keep groundwater from draining away from the old land. The Houtribdijk, built from 1963 to 1975, divided the IJsselmeer from the Markermeer.

The planned fifth polder, the Markerwaard, was abandoned in the early 2000s as environmental issues came to be seen differently than in the 1920s. On 1 January 1986 the new land, without the Wieringermeer, became Flevoland, the 12th province of the Netherlands, home to Lelystad, named after Lely, and Almere. Old ports such as Lemmer and Vollenhove lost their direct access to the sea, and Urk and Schokland became part of the mainland. The American Society of Civil Engineers named the works, with the Delta Works, among the Seven Wonders of the Modern World.
zulfikar-ali-bhutto: Zulfikar Ali Bhutto was born on 5 January 1928 near Larkana in Sindh, the third child of Shah Nawaz Bhutto, dewan of the princely state of Junagadh, and Khursheed Begum. He studied at the University of Southern California, the University of California, Berkeley and the University of Oxford, and trained as a barrister at Lincoln's Inn. In 1958 he became Pakistan's youngest cabinet minister, in charge of Commerce under President Iskander Mirza.

He then served President Ayub Khan and became foreign minister in 1963, drawing Pakistan close to China. After the 1965 war with India and the Tashkent Declaration he was dismissed. On 30 November 1967 he and others founded the Pakistan Peoples Party in Lahore, whose creed he summed up as Islam as faith, democracy as policy and socialism as economy.

In the general election of 7 December 1970 the Awami League won a majority in the legislature, while Bhutto's party was the largest in West Pakistan. Bhutto refused to accept an Awami League government. Talks failed, the army began Operation Searchlight on 25 March 1971, and civil war and a war with India led to the creation of Bangladesh. On 20 December 1971 Bhutto took over from Yahya Khan as president and as the first civilian Chief Martial Law Administrator.

He secured the release of 93,000 prisoners of war and, through the Simla Agreement of July 1972, the return of five thousand square miles of territory. A constitution drafted with the opposition was approved in 1973 by 97 percent of parliament, and on 14 August 1973 he was sworn in as prime minister. He nationalised industry and brought in Abdul Qadeer Khan to begin a nuclear programme. In Balochistan he dismissed the provincial government in 1973 and ordered a military operation.

After the 1977 elections the opposition Pakistan National Alliance alleged vote rigging and unrest spread. On 5 July 1977 General Zia-ul-Haq seized power and detained Bhutto. He was arrested again on 3 September, charged with authorising the murder of Nawab Muhammad Ahmed Khan Kasuri in March 1974, sentenced to death on 18 March 1978, and executed on 4 April 1979.

His legacy remains disputed. Supporters call him Quaid-e-Awām, the People's Leader, and praise his nationalism and the 1973 constitution. Critics point to the economic setbacks they blame on nationalisation and to the suppression of opponents and abuses in Balochistan. His daughter Benazir Bhutto served twice as prime minister.
zulfiqar-khan: Zulfiqar Khan was born Muhammad Ismail, in 1649 according to the historian Satish Chandra or in 1657 according to William Irvine. His father, Asad Khan, became the long-serving wazir of Emperor Aurangzeb, and his mother, Mehrunissa Begum, was a daughter of Asaf Khan, wazir under Shah Jahan. The family was Iranian on the father's side: his grandfather had moved to India after his great-grandfather, the governor of Safavid Shirvan, was executed around 1600 by Shah Abbas I. In 1677 he married a daughter of the noble Shaista Khan and received the title Itiqad Khan.

In 1689 he captured the Maratha fort of Raigad. The Maratha king Rajaram Bhonsle escaped to Jinji, but the family of his predecessor Sambhaji, including the young Shahu, was taken, and Muhammad Ismail was given the title Zulfiqar Khan. Assigned in 1690 to the Siege of Jinji, he made slow progress against a strong fort and disrupted supply lines, and the length of the siege led contemporaries to accuse him of collusion with the enemy. In 1693 he and his father arrested Prince Kam Bakhsh for negotiating with Rajaram against orders. He became mir bakhshi, or paymaster general, in 1702.

In the war of succession of 1707 he reluctantly sided with Prince Azam Shah but deserted him at the Battle of Jajau. The victor, Bahadur Shah I, reconciled him, confirmed him as mir bakhshi and in 1709 made him governor of the Deccan. When Bahadur Shah lay dying in 1712, Zulfiqar Khan allied three of his sons against the strongest, Azim-us-Shan, and then helped Jahandar Shah, the weakest, to kill the others. For this the historian Munis Faruqui calls him the first kingmaker in Mughal history. As wazir he held effective power, abolished the jizya and continued to conciliate the Marathas.

Farrukhsiyar, a son of Azim-us-Shan, rebelled with the support of the Sayyid brothers and defeated Jahandar Shah at Agra in January 1713. The emperor sought shelter in Delhi at the house of Asad Khan, but father and son handed him over in the hope of winning the victor's favour. Despite assurances, Zulfiqar Khan was executed on 11 February 1713, and his body and that of Jahandar Shah were paraded on elephants and left before the Delhi Gate. According to Richard Eaton, his kingmaking set the precedent for power brokers raising puppet emperors to the Mughal throne.
zulu-kingdom: The kingdom arose during the Mfecane, a period of instability and state formation in southern Africa that followed earlier trends of political centralisation, sharpened by international trade, environmental instability and European colonial expansion. Shaka, born about 1787, was the illegitimate son of Senzangakhona, Chief of the Zulus. Exiled with his mother Nandi, he found refuge with the Mthethwa and fought under their leader Dingiswayo. After Dingiswayo was killed by Zwide, king of the Ndwandwe, about 1816, Shaka took leadership of the whole Mthethwa alliance.

Shaka's clan numbered a few thousand at first and grew to 45,000 by absorbing neighbours. He replaced long throwing spears with short stabbing spears and trained conscripted men, kept apart from the rest of society, as a standing army, the amabutho. The alliance survived Zwide's assault at Gqokli Hill in 1818 and broke the Ndwandwe at the Mhlatuze River in 1820. By 1822 it ruled about 210,000 km2.

Shaka was murdered in 1828 by his half-brothers Dingane and Mhlangana and the induna Mbopa. Dingane killed Mhlangana and executed his royal kin and many of Shaka's supporters. In February 1838 he had the Voortrekker leader Piet Retief and his party seized and killed after a land treaty, and his army then attacked Voortrekker camps near present Weenen. On 16 December 1838 Andries Pretorius's party of about 600 repelled some 15,000 Zulu warriors at the Battle of Blood River. Dingane's half-brother Mpande then joined the Voortrekkers against him and took the throne.

Mpande's sons Cetshwayo and Mbuyazi fought at Ndondakusuka in 1856, where Mbuyazi died. In 1878 Sir Henry Bartle Frere presented Cetshwayo with an ultimatum he could not accept. The Zulu army killed more than 1,000 British soldiers at Isandlwana on 22 January 1879, but the British won at Ulundi. Zululand was divided among thirteen chiefs, civil conflict followed, and the British annexed it in 1887.

Cetshwayo died in February 1884, possibly poisoned. His son Dinuzulu was convicted of high treason in 1909 after the Bambatha Rebellion and sent to St Helena, and died in 1913. In the apartheid era KwaZulu was a bantustan, led by Mangosuthu Buthelezi until its abolition in 1994, when it merged with Natal to form the province of KwaZulu-Natal.
zunyi: Zunyi lies in northern Guizhou between the provincial capital Guiyang to the south and Chongqing to the north, and borders Sichuan to the northwest. It stands at an elevation of 865 m, in the transition from the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau to the Sichuan Basin and the hill country of Hunan. Its climate is humid subtropical, with fairly mild winters and hot, humid summers, and rain is common throughout the year.

The area was first inhabited, in the Paleolithic, by the Tongzi people, and later belonged to several kingdoms. Zunyi is considered to have been the centre of the Yelang kingdom. The region first came under Chinese rule in the Han dynasty, during the reign of Emperor Wu. After the Han collapsed it remained under nominal Chinese control, with much of the administration left to local non-Han chiefs. In the 7th century it came under regular Chinese administration in the Tang dynasty, as part of the new Bo Prefecture, Bozhou.

Towards the end of the Tang, Bozhou was conquered by the Nanzhao Kingdom, but it soon gained independence as the Chiefdom of Bozhou, in 876. The chiefdom became an autonomous prefecture of the Song and later dynasties, and the ruling Yang family held power in Zunyi for more than seven centuries. Bozhou rebelled against the Ming in 1589, resisted for more than a decade and was destroyed in 1600. Zunyi Prefecture was then established, with the present city as its seat, and kept that status through the Qing dynasty. After the Xinhai Revolution it became a county in 1914.

In 1935 the Zunyi Conference took place in the city during the Long March and raised Mao Zedong to a dominant position within the Chinese Communist Party. During the First Five-Year Plan Zunyi was made a city, and it grew considerably.

Zunyi is a prefecture-level city of 6,606,675 people at the census of 2020, including the surrounding counties. Its ethnic groups include the Gelao, Miao, Tujia, Buyi, Yi, Dong, Hui and Manchu. The Zunyi Conference Memorial Museum in Honghuagang District consists of several sites connected with the conference. The rice liquor Maotai is produced in the town of Maotai in the prefecture, and chili peppers and red sorghum are grown there.
zuo-zhuan: Little is known of how the work came into being. Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, of the 1st century BCE, calls it Master Zuo's Spring and Autumn Annals and says that Zuo compiled it from the scribal records of Confucius to preserve the true teachings. The identification of this Zuo with the Zuo Qiuming praised in the Analects rests on no specific evidence and was challenged as early as the 8th century. Excavated manuscripts and analysis of its language suggest that its composition was largely complete by 300 BCE.

In the early 19th century Liu Fenglu argued that the text was not originally a commentary on the Annals, a view now generally accepted. Kang Youwei went further and held that the Han scholar Liu Xin had forged it; that theory is now considered discredited. The present arrangement, in which each entry of the Annals is followed by the matching narrative, was made by Du Yu in the 3rd century CE.

The work has 30 chapters and tells its events from the perspective of the State of Lu. Each year opens with the terse entry of the Annals, followed by narratives that are often long and detailed: battles, assassinations, intrigue, oppression and uprisings, ghosts and portents. Because the order is strictly chronological, connected episodes may be separated by the events of intervening years. Its account of the Battle of Chengpu in 632 BCE, in which the State of Jin under Chong'er defeated the State of Chu, is typical in giving more space to preparations, omens and the division of spoils than to the fighting.

The narration stays in the third person and conveys its lessons through speech and action: the haughty and wicked generally bring disaster on themselves, and ritual propriety governs all conduct, including war, though the good are also shown suffering senseless violence. Many anecdotes end with a brief verdict attributed to Confucius or to an unnamed gentleman; these were added later by Confucian scholars.

The work was canonised as one of the Chinese classics in the 1st century CE and remained a cornerstone of education in China, Japan and Korea until modern times. It is the source of more chengyu, or set idioms, than any other work, and the Qing anthology Guwen Guanzhi took 34 passages from it, more than from any other source. The oldest surviving manuscripts are six fragments found among the Dunhuang manuscripts by Paul Pelliot, dating from the 3rd to the 7th century.
zuo-zongtang: Zuo Zongtang was born on 10 November 1812 into a land-holding family in Xiangyin County, Hunan, and mastered the Confucian classics at a private school from the age of five. He failed the imperial examination seven times and withdrew to his home by the Xiang River to farm silkworms and read, and in those years he first turned to Western science. He liked to compare himself with Zhuge Liang, and his stubbornness earned him the nickname Zuo the mule.

When the Taiping Rebellion broke out he became an adviser to Zeng Guofan, and in 1860 he was given command of 5,000 volunteers of the Xiang Army. He drove the rebels into Zhejiang, became governor of that province in 1863, took Hangzhou in 1864 and was made First Class Count Kejing. He, Zeng Guofan and Li Hongzhang were remembered together as the leaders who put down the rebellion. As viceroy of Fujian and Zhejiang he founded China's first modern shipyard and naval academy at Fuzhou.

As viceroy of Shaanxi and Gansu he put down the Nian Rebellion in 1868 and then marched west with 120,000 men, armed with Dreyse needle rifles and Krupp artillery, against the Dungan Revolt. Hui generals who had defected to him, among them Ma Zhan'ao and Ma Anliang, helped him crush the rebels. He suppressed Yakub Beg's uprising in 1878, massed troops toward Kuldja, then occupied by Russia, and won the court debate against Li Hongzhang, who wanted to abandon what he called useless Xinjiang. He was raised to Second Class Marquis Kejing in 1878.

Uneasy with court politics, he asked to leave the Grand Council and became viceroy of Liangjiang in 1881. At the outbreak of the Sino-French War he took charge of coastal defence in Fujian, and he died at Fuzhou on 5 September 1885, receiving the posthumous name Wenxiang. In the northwest he had promoted cotton in place of opium, written pamphlets on intensive small-field farming and set up a press that printed the classics. The American dish General Tso's chicken, created by the chef Peng Chang-kuei, was named in his honour.
zviad-gamsakhurdia: Zviad Gamsakhurdia was born in Tbilisi on 31 March 1939. His father, Konstantine Gamsakhurdia, was a prominent Georgian writer and historical novelist who held nationalist views and promoted Georgian culture within the Soviet Union. In 1958 he was arrested for distributing anti-communist literature and held for six months in a mental hospital, where he was diagnosed with psychopathy with decompensation, making him an early victim of the political abuse of psychiatry in the Soviet Union.

In mid-1974 he co-founded a human rights group with Kostava, and in 1977 they set up the Georgian branch of the Helsinki Rights Watch Group, which monitored the Soviet Union's compliance with the 1975 Helsinki Agreement. He also contributed to samizdat periodicals. A professor of English and American literature at Tbilisi State University, he published monographs on subjects including Georgian literature and American poetry and translated Shakespeare and Baudelaire into Georgian.

Under glasnost the dissident movement revived, and in 1988 Gamsakhurdia helped found the Society of Saint Ilia the Righteous. The suppression of a large peaceful demonstration in Tbilisi by Soviet forces on 9 April 1989 was a pivotal event in discrediting Soviet rule. The pro-independence opposition split over whether to contest the official elections. Gamsakhurdia's Round Table—Free Georgia coalition took part and won the elections of 28 October 1990, while a rival faction organised an alternative National Congress.

Once in office in November 1990 the Supreme Council renamed the republic the Republic of Georgia and restored the flag, emblem and state hymn of the First Republic. In September 1990 Ossetian nationalists in South Ossetia declared independence from Georgia, and after clashes Gamsakhurdia declared a state of emergency there on 12 December 1990.

After his overthrow in early 1992 by Tengiz Kitovani and Jaba Ioseliani, he fled to Chechnya, where Dzhokhar Dudayev welcomed him, and he continued to claim to be the legitimate president. He returned on 24 September 1993, arriving at Zugdidi, and led an uprising that took several places in western Georgia. After Eduard Shevardnadze obtained Russian help, Zugdidi fell on 6 November, ending the six-week insurgency. Gamsakhurdia went into hiding in Samegrelo, and the circumstances of his death at the end of December 1993 remain disputed. In 2004 President Mikheil Saakashvili rehabilitated him, and in 2013 he was posthumously given the title National Hero of Georgia.
zweibrucken: Zweibrücken lies on the Schwarzbach River in the south-western part of the Western Palatinate, bordering the state of Saarland. It is about 26 kilometres from Pirmasens, 40 from Saarbrücken and 55 from Kaiserslautern. The name means two bridges, and older forms include Middle High German Zweinbrücken, Latin Geminus Pons and Bipontum, and French Deux-Ponts.

From the end of the 12th century Zweibrücken was the seat of the County of Zweibrücken, whose counts descended from Henry I, youngest son of Count Simon I of Saarbrücken. The line died out with Count Eberhard II in 1394, who had sold half his territory to the Count Palatine of the Rhine in 1385. Louis, who died in 1489, founded the House of Palatinate-Zweibrücken, a branch of the House of Wittelsbach. In 1533 Count Palatine Wolfgang made the territory Protestant, and in 1559 he founded the town's first grammar school. When Charles X Gustav, son of John Casimir, Count Palatine of Kleeburg, succeeded Queen Christina on the Swedish throne, Palatinate-Zweibrücken was in personal union with Sweden until 1718.

In 1680 Louis XIV's Chambers of Reunion awarded Zweibrücken to France, but the Treaty of Rijswijk in 1697 restored it to the King of Sweden. In 1731 it passed to the Birkenfeld-Zweibrücken branch. France occupied it in 1793, and on 4 November 1797 it became a canton centre in the department of Mont Tonnerre. After the French annexation was confirmed at the Peace of Lunéville in 1801, the greater part of the territory went to Bavaria. The ducal printing office published the Bipontine Editions of the classics from 1779.

The ducal castle, built in its present form in 1720-1725 by Jonas Erikson Sundahl, was destroyed in the Second World War and rebuilt in 1965; it is now the seat of the Palatinate Higher Regional Court. The Herzogvorstadt consists of baroque buildings put up between 1762 and 1772. The town has one of the largest rose gardens in the world and is sometimes called the Rose City. The Bibliotheca Bipontina holds the remains of the ducal libraries, including first editions of the 16th century. Zweibrücken has a campus of the Hochschule Kaiserslautern.
zwentibold: Zwentibold, a member of the Carolingian dynasty, was born about 870 during the long reign of his great-grandfather Louis the German in East Francia. He was the first-born but illegitimate son of Arnulf of Carinthia and his concubine Vinburga. His name is a Frankish form of Svatopluk, the ruler of Great Moravia, who was his godfather.

Arnulf, himself an illegitimate son of Carloman of Bavaria, succeeded King Charles the Fat as king of East Francia in 887. Zwentibold was at first marked out as his heir, and when he came of age he intervened in the struggle for the West Frankish throne between Count Odo of Paris and Charles the Simple, who began to cooperate against him when it became clear that he intended to become king of West Francia.

When Arnulf's wife Ota gave birth to a legitimate son, Louis the Child, Zwentibold received the Lotharingian royal title in compensation; it had last been held by Lothair II. Lotharingia, the former Middle Francia, had fallen to the East Frankish realm under the Treaty of Meerssen of 870 and the Treaty of Ribemont of 880. In the summer of 893 Arnulf, answering pleas from Pope Formosus and Berengar of Friuli against Wido of Spoleto, sent Zwentibold over the Brenner Pass with an army. With Berengar he besieged Pavia without success.

According to Liutprand of Cremona, Zwentibold accepted money from Wido to leave. His retreat was seen as a failure, and Arnulf led a stronger army to Italy and took Pavia a few months later. Zwentibold's rule in Lotharingia was enforced by his father, supported by Archbishop Herman I of Cologne and Archbishop Ratbod of Trier, against the resistance of the local nobility. The account holds that he helped the common people too much and came to be hated. He was fighting unruly nobles when Arnulf died in 899 and Louis the Child became king at the age of six.

Zwentibold tried to use his half-brother's youth to make Lotharingia fully independent. Having lost his father's backing, he saw the whole nobility support Louis, who was asked to intervene. In 900 Count Reginar I of Hainault and Odoacer rose against him and killed him in battle on the River Meuse, near present-day Susteren, on 13 August. He is buried at Susteren Abbey. Louis the Child then ruled Lotharingia, but his realm disintegrated, and from 903 the Lahngau count Gebhard, of the Conradine dynasty, administered Zwentibold's former kingdom with the title Duke of Lorraine. Zwentibold had three daughters, Benedetta, Cecilia and Relenda, named in the Gesta episcoporum Leodensium, and a son, Otto de Lorraine, who died in 949.
zwickauer-mulde: The Zwickauer Mulde is the left tributary of the Mulde. Its source lies in the Ore Mountains near Schöneck, in the Vogtlandkreis. It runs northeast to Aue and then northwest to Zwickau, from which it takes its name, before turning north through Glauchau, Rochlitz and Colditz to meet the Freiberger Mulde and form the united Mulde. Above Zwickau, at Cainsdorf, the river cuts through the Rußkohlenflöz, a soot coal seam whose permanently exposed outcrop is unique in Saxony and is protected as a geological natural monument.

From the end of the last cold stage the valleys of the Mulde were presumably used as routes into the densely forested Ore Mountains, as finds left by Old Stone Age hunters and Bronze Age and Iron Age remains suggest. Later the western Ore Mountains became the territory of Germanic and Slavic tribes. Trade routes and military roads linked the old settled areas around Leipzig and Altenburg with Bohemia, keeping to the ridges rather than the rivers, and castles, villages and monasteries arose at crossings and junctions. When rich silver deposits were found in the late Middle Ages, mining towns grew up around the headwaters.

Along the valley survive the palaces and manor houses of Rochsburg, Rochlitz, Wolkenburg, Waldenburg, Forderglauchau, Hinterglauchau and Osterstein, the castles of Wiesenburg, Stein and the Isenburg, and fortifications in the side valleys at Hartenstein, Wildenfels and Schwarzenberg. The river also feeds the Eibenstock Dam, and demonstrations of timber rafting are held each year on the Muldenberg rafting waterway.
zwiefalten: Zwiefalten lies in the district of Reutlingen in Baden-Württemberg, halfway between Stuttgart and Lake Constance. The name comes from its position in the valleys of the Zwiefalter Aach and the Kessel-Aach, and the place was first mentioned as Zwivaltum in a document of King Ludwig IV dated 15 June 904. The town's coat of arms shows two interlocking rings for the confluence of the two streams and seven golden stars taken from the arms of the former counts of Achalm.

The municipality includes seven villages, one hamlet and three farmsteads, among them Baach, Gauingen, Sonderbuch and Upflamör, which were incorporated between 1938 and 1975. Nearby is the Heuneburg of Upflamör, a Celtic rampart of 4.5 hectares in the forest that was settled no later than the 7th century BCE, and the Wimsener Höhle, a cave accessible by boat and known since 1447.

The town owes its standing to the Benedictine abbey, founded in 1089 by monks from Hirsau. Counts Luitold von Achalm and Kuno von Wülflingen made extensive donations to it. A convent had once stood on the spot, but by the 14th century it had gone. The monastery bought a large territory on the Swabian Jura and stayed influential until the 15th century. In 1525, during the German Peasants' War, peasants looted it. In 1750 it received the status of an imperial abbey, an independent power answerable only to the Imperial Crown and free of Württemberg's rule.

The monastery was forcibly dissolved in the secularisation, and in 1812 the royal Württemberg sanatorium was established in its buildings. During the Nazi killing action known as T4, the state hospital at Zwiefalten served as an intermediate station for the killing centre at Grafeneck Castle. At least 1 673 mentally ill people of all ages were moved from Zwiefalten in 1939 and 1940. The first transport, of 50 women, left on 2 April 1940, and by 9 December more than 1,000 patients had been taken in 22 transports to Grafeneck. Killing by injection continued in Zwiefalten itself. In 1949 the former director Martha Fauser was sentenced to one year and six months for manslaughter, and a memorial stone in the cemetery recalls the victims.

The former abbey church, begun in 1739 and completed by 1765, is considered a masterpiece of the German late Baroque. Its interior holds a late Gothic miraculous image of 1430, frescoed ceilings and an altarpiece by Franz Joseph Spiegler, frescoes by Andreas Meinrad von Au and stucco by Johann Michael Feuchtmayer. The former monastery now forms part of the psychiatric hospital, and the town lies on the B 312 between Reutlingen and Riedlingen.
zwinger-dresden: The name Zwinger is the medieval German term for the outer ward between the outer and inner defensive walls of a fortress. Dresden's outer wall was added after 1427, during the Hussite Wars, and the strip between the walls served the court as a garden. When work on the palace began, that function was gone, but the name passed to the new building, whose south-western parts and the Kronentor stand on remains of the outer curtain wall.

Augustus the Strong returned from a tour of France and Italy in 1687–89, as Louis XIV moved his court to Versailles, and after his election as King of Poland in 1697 he wanted something comparably spectacular. The unneeded fortifications gave him the space.

Matthäus Daniel Pöppelmann designed the complex, which was built in stages from 1710 to 1728, with sculpture by Balthasar Permoser. Pavilions and arcaded galleries with balustrades, figures and vases surround a great courtyard. The Kronentor, or crown gate, was finished in 1714 in the shape of the Polish crown, with four Polish eagles and figures of Hercules and Mars.

In the elector's original conception the Zwinger was the forecourt of a new castle between it and the Elbe, so the river side stayed provisionally closed by a wall. Pöppelmann's early plans also took in gardens down to the river.

The Zwinger was inaugurated in 1719 for the marriage of the electoral prince Frederick August to the Archduchess Maria Josepha, daughter of the Habsburg emperor. The interiors were completed in 1728, so that the buildings could serve as galleries and library halls. Augustus died in 1733, work stopped and the plan for a castle was abandoned. Gottfried Semper closed the open side with the Semper Gallery, built from 1847 and opened in 1855.

The bombing in February 1945 largely destroyed the complex, though the art collection had been evacuated. Reconstruction began in 1945, parts opened in 1951, and by 1963 it was largely restored. It houses the Old Masters Picture Gallery, the Dresden Porcelain Collection and the Mathematisch-Physikalischer Salon, and is still used for concerts and theatre.
zwolle: Zwolle lies on the eastern side of the River IJssel, bordering the province of Gelderland, and is the second-largest municipality of Overijssel after Enschede. A woodhenge found in the Zwolle-Zuid suburb in 1993 has been dated to the Bronze Age, and in the Roman era the area was inhabited by Salian Franks.

The modern city was founded around 800 CE by Frisian merchants and troops of Charlemagne. Earlier spellings of the name include Suolle, which means hill. It refers to an incline in the landscape between the four surrounding rivers, the IJssel, Vecht, Aa and Zwarte Water. The hill was the only land that stayed dry in the frequent floods of the rivers, and Zwolle was established on it.

On 31 August 1230 the bishop of Utrecht granted Zwolle city rights. The city joined the Hanseatic League in 1294 and in 1361 took part in the war between the League and Valdemar IV of Denmark. The Treaty of Stralsund of 1370, which ended the war, awarded Zwolle a vitte, a trade colony, in Scania, then part of Denmark. The 15th century was its golden age, and between 1402 and 1450 the city's regional product multiplied about six times. Regional noblemen set the city on fire in July 1324 and October 1361; in the 1324 fire only nine buildings escaped.

Zwolle was, with Deventer, a centre of the Brethren of the Common Life. About 5 km from the city, on the Agnietenberg, stood the Augustinian convent in which Thomas à Kempis spent most of his life and died in 1471. In 1521 the city's governors broke the oath of loyalty they had sworn to the Duke of Gelre, Charles of Egmont, at a time when Zwolle and Kampen were in dispute over tolls on the IJssel. The duke was captured on entering Zwolle and was released on condition that the city keep its independence. The people of Zwolle are still known as Blauwvingers, or Bluefingers; this name is traced to the raised fingers of the oath.

Zwolle is the capital of Overijssel. St Michael's church, the Grote of Sint Michaëlskerk, was renovated in the first half of the 15th century and has a baroque organ of 1721 designed by Arp Schnitger and completed by his sons. The basilica of Our Lady of the Assumption dates to 1399, and its tower, called the Peperbus, is among the tallest and best known in the Netherlands. The town hall was first built in 1448. Born in the city were the painter Gerard ter Borch, the engraver known as Master I. A. M. of Zwolle, and the statesman Johan Rudolf Thorbecke.
